launches.title: Overjet adds hands-free hard-tissue and natural voice perio charting
launches.ai_summary: Overjet launched hands-free hard-tissue and natural voice periodontal charting in Overjet Voice, letting providers complete exams via natural speech. The natural perio feature uses a model trained on over 50 million tokens with 98% accuracy, and both features are available now to all Voice subscribers at no extra cost.
launches.author: Drbicuspid.Com Staff Writersaug

industries.name: Periodontal Diagnostics & Risk Assessment (Perio Charting/Microbial Testing)

launches.full_text:
Overjet has launched hands-free hard-tissue charting and natural voice periodontal charting within Overjet Voice, allowing providers to complete an exam using natural speech while the system captures periodontal measurements, restorative findings, billing codes, and clinical notes directly into the practice management system (PMS).

The hard-tissue charting feature listens throughout a visit and converts findings on decay, existing restorations, missing teeth, and planned treatment into structured odontogram entries for provider review before submission to the PMS.

For practices using Overjet's Vision AI, providers can verbally confirm x-ray findings flagged by Vision for the same hands-free charting. Hard-tissue charting is available now on CareStack, Eaglesoft, Open Dental, Dentrix Core, Dentrix Ascend, and Denticon, with more integrations planned, at no additional cost to existing Voice subscribers.

The natural perio charting update lets hygienists and dentists speak measurements in their own words and sequence rather than following a fixed command format. According to Overjet, the underlying model was trained on more than 50 million training-token exposures and understands natural phrasing with more than 98% accuracy.

Both features are available now to all Overjet Voice subscribers with no additional hardware or workflow changes.

launches.title: Three Trends Driving Dental Practices Into the Cloud
launches.ai_summary: The article discusses the increasing adoption of cloud-based software and AI in dental practices, driven by generational shifts, staffing challenges, and the integration of dental care with broader healthcare services. It highlights the growth of SaaS solutions such as Oryx, Vyne, Overjet, and Pearl that improve efficiency and patient outcomes.
launches.author: Dentistry Today
launches.full_text:
Todays Dental News Web Exclusives Three Trends Driving Dental Practices Into the Cloud By Rania Saleh, DDS, MSD When it comes to software, dentistry has been an under-innovated space for decades. When I was starting my own private cosmetic practice in the mid-2010s, I was shocked by how basic the traditional technology was: on-premise, clunky, and with no real clinical component. It was no wonder so many dental practices still used pen-and-paper or manual processes for taking notes, filling out charts, or communicating information to front office team members. Clinicians can bring all the components of a modern dental practice within their reach with Oryx software, a fully managed, all-in-one solution. Photo credit: Oryx Dental. Thankfully, times are changing. While dentistry was largely left out of the software as a service (SaaS) revolution that transformed so many other verticals in the 2000s, there are finally purpose-built options for dental practices. For example, Vyne provides RCM tools specific to dentistry’s quirks; Overjet and Pearl use the latest in cloud and AI for imaging; and my own company, Oryx Dental, offers an all-in-one practice management system (PMS) built only and specifically for dentists. As a result, we’ve seen a growing number of dentistry practices moving to the cloud. In fact, at Oryx, we doubled our annual recurring revenue in just 12 months. We don’t see that trend slowing any time soon, either. There are broader market forces at play that will push dental practices of all shapes, sizes, and specialties towards the cloud. 1. A New Wave of Dentists Is Entering the Workforce The Boomer generation, commonly defined as people born between 1946 and 1964, are retiring in waves. Right now, we’re in the center of the generation, which means in the next 10 years, we can expect more Boomer dentists to exit the workforce. As they do so, new opportunities arise for newer dentists in several ways: For younger dentists who are working for these soon-to-be-retirees , they may purchase the practice from their mentor or colleague.

, they may purchase the practice from their mentor or colleague. For those who have already established their own practice , they may want to open new locations by acquiring a well-established practice.

, they may want to open new locations by acquiring a well-established practice. Or, for those looking to start their own practice, they’ll find ample patients seeking a new dental practice once their old one shuts down. In all 3 of these situations, a younger, more tech-savvy generation will be making major decisions about how to run a business, including the patient experience, communication, workflows, and technology. So, whether they’re starting from scratch and want a firm, tech-forward foundation or need to integrate patient data, processes, and teams from multiple locations, a younger wave of dental decision-makers will drive more practices onto modern, cloud-first platforms. 2. The Staffing Crunch Continues Since the pandemic, hiring has been a major challenge for dental practices across the US. It’s harder than ever to find great front- or back-office team members. Practice managers are being asked to do more than ever. And with costs rising across the board—from medical school tuition to materials—dentists can’t afford to spend less time in the chair while doing administrative work. Cloud-based technology can significantly shorten workflows by reducing friction. For example: Patients can provide health, insurance, and other information ahead of time via online forms that automatically integrate with the PMS.

With clinical notes entered into charts via ambient AI voice technology, dentists don’t need to bring information to the front desk for the patient’s next appointment or procedure—the information is there by the time the patient checks out.

AI imaging providers like Overjet, Pearl, and others can quickly give dentists information to assess, diagnose, and determine treatment plans for patients.

Automation tools can append information to insurance submissions, reducing the amount of back-and-forth with carriers and leading to more timely reimbursements.

Clinical, Patient Engagement, and Practice Management modules ensure that nothing gets missed, and free up time so practices can focus more fully on their patients. These are just a few, high-level examples of ways that SaaS and AI solutions can drive efficiency in dental practices—a need that will only accelerate as costs rise and pressures mount. 3. Dental Care Will Become More Integrated with Healthcare When I was running my cosmetic dentistry practice outside DC, I used a thorough, Kois Center-inspired process for assessing patients. I often saw issues in the mouth that pointed to broader health issues like early cancers and would refer patients to medical specialists. In fact, I remember getting calls from doctors thanking me for a referral, as they were able to catch early cancers. They were amazed that a dentist would be able to spot the warning signs. But those of us who sit in the chair know it’s not unusual at all: dental care is healthcare. Oral health is increasingly shown to be tied to major conditions like cardiac disease, diabetes, and more. Organizations like the ADA and the FDI are already calling for dental information to be integrated into EHRs. Given the technological and insurance differences between dentistry and general healthcare, there’s a long road ahead to make dental/healthcare integration a reality. But by having their patient data digitized, in the cloud, and accessible, dental practices—especially large groups or DSOs—will be better positioned for an industry-wide shift towards integrated health. Dentistry’s Future Has Arrived

There’s a famous quote that’s often used in some version or another by the tech industry, widely attributed to the science fiction writer William Gibson: “The future is already here—it’s just not evenly distributed.”

When it comes to dentistry, that’s certainly true. We have incredible leaps in technology not just poised to transform but already available to dental practices all over the world. If a dental practice wants to seamlessly communicate between locations, integrate patient data, automate patient scheduling and the patient experience, and use AI to speed practice workflows, opportunities to do so exist. But not all dental practices are there yet—in fact, most dental practices still use old-fashioned, on-prem technology. That will change rapidly as purpose-built SaaS and AI technologies prove their worth and as word spreads. The future of dentistry is, indeed, already here. Rania Saleh, DDS, MSD, is the founder and CEO of Oryx Dental Software. Prior to starting the company, she was the founder and owner of a multi-site dental practice in the DC area. Dr. Rania attended McGill University, where she received both her DDS and MSD. launches.ai_summary: Dental practice overhead now averages 60-65% of collections, with anything above 70% signaling serious financial trouble and figures below 55% potentially indicating under-investment, according to industry benchmarks from Overjet and the ADA Health Policy Institute.

Understanding dental practice overhead benchmarks isn’t just good accounting practice. It’s the difference between thriving and barely surviving. If you’ve ever looked at your practice’s profit and loss statement and wondered where all the money goes, you’re not alone.

The reality is stark: overhead in dental practices now averages 60-65% of collections, with many practices creeping even higher. That means for every dollar you collect, 60 to 65 cents disappears into operating costs before you even think about taking home a paycheck.

Smart dental practice owners know that managing overhead starts with accurate tracking and inventory control. ZenOne helps practices save an average of $17,000 annually through automated inventory management and real-time price comparisons across trusted suppliers.

See how much you could save →

Dental Practice Overhead Percentages: Quick Answer (2026)

Most dental practices run 60–65% overhead (everything it costs to run the office before you pay the dentist). If you’re consistently over 70%, you’re likely bleeding profit. If you’re under 55%, you may be under-investing in team, systems, or growth.

Healthy target: 55–65% total overhead (best-run practices aim lower)

(best-run practices aim lower) Fastest “quick win” category: supplies (prices vary a lot by vendor and waste is common)

TL;DR: Summary of Dental Practice Overhead Benchmarks

Dental office overhead percentages should ideally fall between 55-65% of total collections, with high-performing practices targeting the lower end of this range. While staff costs represent the largest expense category in absolute dollars, dental supplies present the biggest opportunity for quick savings often without any sacrifice to patient care quality. The key to maintaining healthy overhead lies in monthly tracking, strategic vendor negotiations, and ruthless elimination of waste in high-impact categories like supplies, staffing, and lab fees. Real practices like Dr. Brandon Johnson save $24,000 annually through systematic supply management, while others reclaim 12 days per year by delegating ordering to their teams with proper systems in place.

Key Points:

Target overhead range: 55-65% of collections, with anything above 70% signaling serious financial trouble

Lab fees above 10% and facility costs exceeding 7% indicate inefficiency Monthly monitoring matters: Calculate your overhead percentage monthly rather than waiting for year-end surprises

Real Examples: How Dental Teams Cut Overhead Without Cutting Care

Here are practical, real-world takeaways from dental healthcare providers who focused on overhead. These are simple moves that work in real offices—not “perfect world” advice.

Supplies: Stop “panic ordering.” Set par levels so you don’t pay rush prices.



Stop “panic ordering.” Set par levels so you don’t pay rush prices. Staffing: Track production per team member each month so you don’t overstaff for slow weeks.



Track production per team member each month so you don’t overstaff for slow weeks. Lab: Review your top 10 lab cases and make sure you’re not paying premium fees for routine work.

What Are Dental Practice Overhead Benchmarks in 2026?

The dental industry continues to face mounting cost pressures, making it more crucial than ever to understand what constitutes healthy overhead. According to comprehensive analysis from Overjet in 2025, “the national median sits around 62% of collections, yet high-performing practices often maintain overhead between 55-60%.” These top-tier practices achieve lower overhead through strategic technology adoption, streamlined workflows, and efficient staffing models.

Recent data from Blue & Co., a major dental CPA firm, reveals that top-performing practices navigated 2025’s cost increases with a 39% margin before debt service, significantly outpacing industry averages.

Current Industry Standards by Category

According to ADA Health Policy Institute 2023 data, staff costs represent the largest single expense at 25-30% of collections. Clinical supplies and lab fees combined typically account for 4-7% of revenue, though many practices unknowingly exceed these benchmarks.

Here’s how your dental office overhead percentages should break down:

Category Benchmark Range Notes Staff/Personnel 25-30% Largest expense; includes salaries, benefits, payroll taxes Clinical Supplies 4-6% Controllable through inventory management Lab Fees 6-8% Varies by case mix and volume Facility Costs 6-10% Higher for smaller practices and urban locations Marketing 4-7% (established)

8-10% (growth) Depends on growth phase and competition Admin/Technology 2-8% Software, compliance, general business expenses

Benchmarks vary by location, procedure mix, and practice size—use these as a starting point, then track monthly

The ADA HPI data also reveals significant variation by practice size: practices with less than $750,000 in collections typically experience 70-80% overhead, those generating $750,000-$1.5 million see 60-70%, while practices exceeding $1.5 million achieve overhead below 60%.

What Counts as Overhead?

Overhead includes every operating expense required to run your practice except doctor compensation. This includes:

Personnel costs: Staff salaries, benefits, and payroll taxes for hygienists, assistants, and administrative team members

Staff salaries, benefits, and payroll taxes for hygienists, assistants, and administrative team members Clinical costs: Dental supplies, laboratory fees, and any in-house lab technician expenses

Dental supplies, laboratory fees, and any in-house lab technician expenses Facility expenses: Rent or mortgage payment, utilities, maintenance, equipment leases, and repairs

Rent or mortgage payment, utilities, maintenance, equipment leases, and repairs Administrative costs: Accounting fees, insurance premiums, software subscriptions, professional memberships, and office supplies

How to Calculate Your Overhead Percentage

Step-by-Step Calculation

Pull a complete P&L report covering at least 12 months to smooth out seasonal variations Locate your total collections figure after adjusting for refunds. This represents your actual revenue Identify and exclude all doctor compensation from your expense total (owner salary, associate pay, owner benefits, profit distributions) Apply this formula: (Total Overhead Expenses ÷ Total Collections) × 100

Example: If your practice collected $1 million and had $620,000 in overhead expenses (after excluding doctor pay), your overhead percentage equals 62%.

What Your Number Means

55-60%: Top-performing practices. This range provides healthy margins for doctor compensation (typically 35-40% of collections), plus retained profits for reinvestment.

Top-performing practices. This range provides healthy margins for doctor compensation (typically 35-40% of collections), plus retained profits for reinvestment. 60-65%: Average range for dental practices. Room for improvement, but not in immediate danger.

Average range for dental practices. Room for improvement, but not in immediate danger. 65-70%: Warning territory. Practices in the 67-70% range face operational inefficiency that limits profitability.

Warning territory. Practices in the 67-70% range face operational inefficiency that limits profitability. Above 70%: Serious problems requiring immediate intervention.

The #1 Overhead Category Practices Overspend On (And How to Fix It)

While staff costs represent the largest expense in absolute dollars, dental supplies present the biggest opportunity for immediate savings without impacting patient care. The average 5-chair practice spends $50,000-70,000 annually on supplies (roughly 5-7% of collections), but many practices unknowingly exceed these benchmarks.

Why Dental Supplies Are Your Biggest Leak

Dental supplies quietly drain profits through:

Emergency orders at premium prices

Expired materials that must be discarded

Excessive safety stock that ties up cash

Inconsistent pricing for identical products from order to order

Supply costs have risen steadily since 2020, with manufacturers passing along increased raw material and shipping expenses. When supply costs grow faster than production, it signals waste, theft, or pricing problems.

Real example: Dr. Brandon Johnson (Brushy Creek Dentistry) was “spending so many hours on eBay, Net32 and Amazon just trying to find the best price.” After implementing systematic price comparison through ZenOne, he now saves $2,000/month ($24,000/year) on his $10,000 monthly supply spend.

5 Ways to Cut Supply Costs Without Sacrificing Quality

1. Implement real-time price comparison across multiple suppliers

Tools like ZenOne enable instant side-by-side pricing across 50+ trusted suppliers, ensuring you never overpay for routine items. The platform’s AI-powered search helps practices identify the best deals on 150,000+ products without manual effort.

2. Establish strict inventory par levels based on actual usage

Track consumption by operatory to identify waste, and set automated alerts when stock reaches predetermined minimums.

3. Standardize your product formulary

Too many practices allow each dentist to specify preferred brands for every category, multiplying SKU counts and eliminating volume discounts.

4. Negotiate annual contracts with volume rebates

Join a group purchasing organization or use a centralized procurement platform to leverage collective buying power.

5. Conduct quarterly audits of high-value items

Implement variance logs to track discrepancies from theft, loss, or expired stock. These controls typically uncover thousands of dollars in annual leakage.

Start comparing prices across suppliers →

Average Markup From Dental Supply Companies (And Why Prices Vary)

Dental supply pricing includes markups at different steps in the supply chain. A common rule of thumb is that distributor markup averages around 20%, but it can range from about 5% to 40% depending on the product and market. That’s why the same gloves or composites can cost very different amounts across suppliers.

To spot markup pain fast, do this once a quarter:

Pull your top 10 most-purchased items from the last 90 days. Compare the unit price across at least 3 suppliers (include shipping). Flag anything where the “same item” is 15%+ cheaper elsewhere. Set your reorder list to default to the best-price supplier. Re-check after 30 days (prices change often).

Other Overhead Killers to Audit Right Now

Staff Costs (If Above 25%)

According to industry benchmarks, top-performing practices generate $200,000+ per team member. If you’re significantly below this benchmark, you may have too many people for your current patient volume.

Solutions:

Cross-train team members to match labor to demand

Balance retention priorities with cost control through competitive compensation packages

Track employee turnover costs (recruitment, training, lost productivity often exceed retention expenses)

Lab Fees (If Above 10%)

Laboratory fees should remain around 6-8% of revenue for general practices.

Solutions:

Negotiate with multiple laboratories for competitive pricing

Consolidate work for volume discounts

Review case mix for in-house milling opportunities

Track lab fees monthly as a percentage of collections

Some practices achieve lab cost reductions of 10-13% through systematic vendor management.

Facility Costs (If Above 7%)

While facility costs can range from 6-15% depending on practice size and location, the 7% threshold serves as a target for efficient operations in most markets.

As Overjet notes in their 2025 analysis, “high-volume practices frequently maintain overhead below 60% through operational scale advantages. Large practices distribute fixed costs across more patients while negotiating better supplier terms.”

Solutions:

Energy efficiency upgrades for older facilities

Negotiate lease renewals well in advance

Evaluate whether square footage matches operational needs

Marketing (The Goldilocks Problem)

The “just right” amount typically falls between 4-7% of annual revenue for established practices, with newer or aggressively growing practices pushing toward 8-10%.

The key distinction lies in marketing ROI rather than absolute spending. Track cost per new patient acquisition and lifetime value per patient to determine whether marketing delivers profitable growth.

Red Flags You’re Overspending

Supply Warning Signs

Supply costs above 6-7% of monthly collections

Frequent inventory stockouts requiring emergency orders

Expired materials discovered during inventory counts

Multiple staff placing orders without centralized oversight

Can’t quickly produce a list of top 10 supply expenses

Overall Practice Warning Signs

Overhead consistently exceeding 65% of collections

Production per dentist stagnating while expenses rise

Cash flow problems despite adequate production

Revenue per employee below $150,000

Real example: Miranda Moore (Lead Assistant, Beacon Dentistry) was ordering from 18 different vendors. “Each order took 2-3 hours.” After centralizing with ZenOne: “With Zen I have all my products in one place. Ordering takes 15-20 minutes (85% time reduction).”

Conclusion

The difference between operating at 55% overhead versus 70% equals $150,000 in additional profit on a practice collecting $1 million annually.

Real results from practices using ZenOne:

Dr. Brandon Johnson : $24,000/year saved through price comparison

$24,000/year saved through price comparison Dr. Nikki : 12 days/year reclaimed by delegating ordering to team

12 days/year reclaimed by delegating ordering to team Miranda Moore: 85% reduction in ordering time

Start with the categories offering the quickest wins: dental supplies through better inventory management, staff costs through productivity improvements, and facility expenses through space optimization. The practices thriving in 2026 aren’t necessarily the ones with the highest production. They’re the ones maintaining healthy overhead that preserves profitability.

Ready to see where your supply costs really stand? Visit zenone.com to discover how automated inventory management helps practices save an average of $17,000 annually through smarter ordering and real-time price comparisons.

Frequently Asked Questions About Dental Practice Overhead

What is a good overhead percentage for a dental practice?

A healthy overhead percentage typically falls between 55-65% of collections, with high-performing practices targeting 55-60%. This range provides adequate room for doctor compensation (usually 35-40% of revenue) while maintaining profitability. Anything exceeding 70% requires immediate intervention.

How much should a dental practice spend on marketing?

Marketing expenses should represent 4-7% of annual revenue for most established practices, with newer or aggressively expanding practices potentially spending 8-10%. Track your cost per new patient acquisition and lifetime patient value to ensure marketing delivers profitable growth.

What is average associate dentist production per day?

Associate dentist production typically ranges from $2,500 to $4,500 per day, with new associates at the lower end ($2,000-$3,000 daily) and experienced associates at the higher end ($3,500-$4,500 daily). High-performing associates in well-managed practices can exceed $5,000-$6,000 per day.

How often should I review my overhead benchmarks?

Review your overhead benchmarks monthly for calculations and tracking, with quarterly comprehensive comparisons against annual standards. Monthly reviews enable early detection of cost trends, particularly important given the 5% annual overhead increases many practices experience.

Do startup practices have different overhead expectations?

Yes. New practices must fund substantial upfront costs including $350,000 to over $500,000 in initial investments before generating revenue. Startups typically experience overhead ranging from 70-80% during their first 12-24 months as fixed costs spread over growing patient volumes. With efficient management, startups can move toward standard 60-65% overhead ranges within 24 months.

NEWPORT BEACH, Calif., Dec. 9, 2025 /PRNewswire/ -- Medit, a global leader in 3D intraoral scanning and digital dentistry solutions, today announced the launch of AuraVue, a next-generation visualization and consultation platform that integrates Overjet's AI technology to deliver real-time diagnostic insights and clearer patient communication. Continue Reading

Medit Launches AuraVue: A Unified 3D Intraoral Scan and X-Ray Visualization Powered by Overjet AI With AuraVue, clinicians can now view 3D intraoral scans and X-rays side by side in one interactive workspace. By combining Medit's 3D imaging with Overjet's AI-powered radiographic analysis, AuraVue transforms diagnostic data into clear, visual storytelling that helps patients understand their conditions and treatment plans. "Most patients understand best when they can see what's happening," said Michael Lee, chief technology officer of Medit. "AuraVue transforms diagnostics into a visual story—helping patients better understand their oral health in seconds and empowering clinicians to communicate with confidence." For example, a traditional bitewing can reveal decay, distance to the pulp, bone loss, and existing restorations. AuraVue brings that to life by pairing it with a corresponding 3D scan that shows soft tissue, inflammation, cracks, occlusion, discoloration, and wear—all in the same visual frame. The result is a clear, image-backed treatment plan that helps boost case acceptance and strengthen patient trust. "AuraVue is a strong example of how technology can advance patient-centered care. By combining Medit's leadership in intra-oral scanning with Overjet's clinical AI, we're giving clinicians a clearer, more complete view of oral health than ever before. When patients can see and understand their conditions in real time, trust grows, decisions become easier, and care improves. We're proud to partner with Medit to make that experience accessible to every practice," said Wardah Inam, CEO, Overjet. With AI-powered insights from Overjet, clinicians can simply highlight an area of concern and instantly view the corresponding X-ray with diagnostic information displayed side-by-side. Additionally, AuraVue can generate a one-click summary report for easy sharing, whether with patients, referring practitioners, or for insurance claim submissions. AuraVue runs entirely on the cloud, requiring no installation, local storage, or additional set-up. Users can get started immediately by importing X-rays without having to install Overjet separately. To celebrate its launch, Medit is offering a limited-time introductory promotion for AuraVue. For information on how to take advantage of this offer, visit the Medit website for more details. About Medit Medit is a global provider of 3D intraoral scanners and digital dentistry solutions based on proprietary technology. The company supports collaborative workflows between dental clinics and labs through innovative hardware and software solutions. Headquartered in Seoul, South Korea, since 2000, Medit has a strong global presence through its offices in the Americas and Europe and a distributor network spanning over 100 countries. Disclaimer: AuraVue is a patient consultation and communication application that displays diagnostic results generated by Overjet.ai (FDA approved) software. AuraVue does not analyze, interpret, or provide diagnoses. About Overjet Overjet is the world leader in dental AI. Founded by experts from MIT and Harvard University, Overjet builds artificial intelligence that helps dental organizations give patients the highest quality of care. Overjet Secures FDA Clearance for CBCT Assist AI Platform

Overjet has received FDA 510(k) clearance for its CBCT Assist tool, expanding its AI platform to support diagnostic interpretation of 3D dental imaging. Overjet has received 510(k) clearance from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for its CBCT Assist product, expanding the company’s AI platform to include diagnostic support for cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) imaging. AI Support for CBCT Imaging The new product assists dental professionals in the review and interpretation of CBCT images. It enables anatomical assessment and supports diagnostic and treatment planning by automatically identifying, labeling, segmenting, and quantifying key anatomical and restorative structures in CBCT scans. Clinically relevant measurements provided include periodontal bone levels, airway minimal cross-sectional area, distances between tooth and anatomical structures, and tooth impaction ratio. Image Enhancement and Measurement Capabilities CBCT Assist includes image enhancement tools such as brightness, contrast, and Virtual Panoramic reconstruction. It also features measurement tools for distance, area, angle, and signal intensity. Clinical Applications The product supports advanced visualization with Multi-Planar Reconstruction views and 3D Volume Rendering. It facilitates surgical planning, including third molar surgery, by generating linear measurements to nearby critical structures. It also aids in implant site evaluation by providing measurements for assessing bone availability and anatomical features. For airway assessment, it automatically reports the minimum cross-sectional area. “This FDA clearance for CBCT Assist, Overjet’s 10th FDA clearance to date, is a critical milestone that reinforces our leadership in bringing clinically validated AI to the forefront of oral healthcare,” said Dr Wardah Inam, CEO of Overjet. “As the industry standard for dental AI, we are committed to giving providers the best tools available to drive evidence-based treatment and ensure the highest quality of care for their patients.” Dr Parag Kachalia, head of clinical practice at Overjet, added, “The FDA clearance for CBCT Assist is more than just a regulatory achievement; it is validation of our foundational scientific rigor. This innovation directly supports our mission to provide unparalleled diagnostic clarity and elevate the quality of care across the entire dental ecosystem.” Photo: Overjet Overjet in the news: Medit Debuts AuraVue to Combine 3D Scans and AI Diagnostics

approvals.full_text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE SAN MATEO, CA – December 16, 2025 – Overjet, a leader in artificial intelligence (AI) for dental organizations, today announced that it has received 510(k) clearance from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for Overjet CBCT Assist. This clearance expands Overjet's AI platform to enable interactive review and support diagnostic interpretation of 3D CBCT data, further solidifying its position as one of the most comprehensive clinical intelligence AI solutions in dentistry. With this new clearance, Overjet’s clinical intelligence platform extends its AI capabilities to cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) imaging. Overjet’s CBCT Assist product will assist dental professionals in their review and interpretation of CBCT images by facilitating anatomical assessment and supporting their diagnostic and treatment planning process. The product uses AI to automatically identify, label, segment, and quantify key anatomical and restorative structures in CBCT scans, surfacing clinically relevant measurements such as periodontal bone levels, airway minimal cross-sectional area, tooth-to-maxillary sinus and tooth-to-inferior alveolar canal distances, and tooth impaction ratio (percent of crown within bone). “This FDA clearance for CBCT Assist, Overjet’s 10th FDA clearance to date, is a critical milestone that reinforces our leadership in bringing clinically validated AI to the forefront of oral healthcare,” said Dr. Wardah Inam, CEO of Overjet. “As the industry standard for dental AI, we are committed to giving providers the best tools available to drive evidence-based treatment and ensure the highest quality of care for their patients.” The CBCT Assist platform combines essential image enhancement tools such as brightness, contrast, and Virtual Panoramic reconstruction, with measurement capabilities for distance, area, angle, and signal intensity. Key clinical capabilities include: Advanced Visualization: features Multi-Planar Reconstruction (MPR) views and 3D Volume Rendering for a thorough view of patient anatomy.

Surgical Planning & Safety: Facilitates third molar surgery planning by generating linear measurement to nearby critical structures.

Implant Site Evaluation: Provides robust measurement tools to support assessment of bone availability and anatomy for optimal implant placement.

Airway Assessment: Supports airway evaluation by automatically reporting the minimum cross-sectional area. Dr. Parag Kachalia, Head of Clinical Practice at Overjet, said, “The FDA clearance for CBCT Assist is more than just a regulatory achievement; it is validation of our foundational scientific rigor. This innovation directly supports our mission to provide unparalleled diagnostic clarity and elevate the quality of care across the entire dental ecosystem.” Clinics based in the United States can sign up for early access to Overjet’s CBCT Assist.

funding_news.title: DentScribe Was Supposed to Be a Scribe
funding_news.ai_summary: DentScribe, an AI startup originally focused on clinical documentation for dental practices, pivoted in March to capture post-appointment sales conversations between treatment coordinators and patients, targeting dental service organizations (DSOs) to help standardize revenue processes. The company competes with Overjet, which took the opposite approach—moving from billing and revenue cycle management toward clinical documentation—and has raised $133 million at a $550 million valuation. DentScribe lacks public funding or disclosed metrics, raising questions about its ability to scale against a better-capitalized competitor in what the article describes as a race to control dental practice information flows.
funding_news.author: Yesterday Adam Shapiro

sic_codes.name: SERVICES-OFFICES & CLINICS OF DOCTORS OF MEDICINE

funding_news.full_text:
Aime Summary Overview The 5 Ws Opposite Sides Infobox - DentScribe shifted from clinical documentation to capturing post-appointment sales conversations, targeting dental service organizations (DSOs) to standardize revenue processes. - The AI tool digitizes treatment coordinator-patient discussions about costs and payment plans, creating structured data for DSOs to analyze conversion rates and revenue leaks. - Competitor Overjet, focused on billing and expanding into clinical documentation, contrasts DentScribe’s clinical-to-revenue approach in a race to control dental practice information flows. - DentScribe’s unproven scale and lack of public funding raise questions against Overjet’s $550M valuation and DSO partnerships, though its clinical integration offers a stronger dentist-centric wedge. - The winner will control both clinical notes and revenue discussions, dominating the workflow that connects patient care to practice profitability.

DentScribe was supposed to be a documentation tool. That was the premise: listen to dentist-patient conversations, turn them into clinical notes, save the practice time. A reasonable idea, the way AI scribing works everywhere else. Then in March they announced Treatment Coordinator Notes-an AI workflow that structures the conversations treatment coordinators have with patients after appointments. Those are not clinical notes. They are sales conversations. Treatment coordinators explain recommended procedures, discuss costs, negotiate payment plans, and try to get patients to accept treatment plans that can run into the thousands of dollars. DentScribe wants to listen to those conversations, too, and turn them into structured internal records. Ask Aime: Could the recent surge in gold prices, coupled with a downward trend in the stock market, indicate a safe-haven investment opportunity for sector diversification? The move is not obvious. Why would a clinical documentation startup go after revenue conversations? And why specifically target dental service organizations-the large multi-location groups that own dozens or hundreds of practices? Quick Backtesting Tool Symbol SPY Strategy Absolute Momentum Backtest Range Past 5 years I think the answer is that DentScribe is trying to solve a problem it couldn't solve from the clinical side alone. Ask Aime: Why is Amazon's (AMZN) stock price down today? Here's the thing about dental practices. The money lives in the gap between what a dentist recommends and what a patient accepts. A dentist sees a cavity, writes up a treatment plan, and hands it to the patient. Whether that plan becomes revenue depends on the treatment coordinator. But treatment coordinators are the least digitized role in a dental office. Their conversations happen in hallways, at front desks, over the phone. The details scatter into text messages, sticky notes, and individual memory. For a single-location practice, that's annoying. For a DSO trying to standardize operations across 200 locations, it's a structural problem. If you can't see what the treatment coordinator said to a patient in one clinic, you can't compare conversion rates, train staff, or spot where revenue is leaking. DentScribe's treatment coordinator feature turns those scattered conversations into something a DSO can actually analyze. Expressed concerns, discussed procedures, follow-up actions-structured, searchable, comparable across locations. This is not a documentation product anymore. It's an information layer for revenue operations. The founder sees it this way. Ratinder Paul Singh Ahuja, a tech visionary with over 70 patents, co-founded DentScribe. The company has patented AI technology for processing clinical interactions. And in October 2025, Dr. Mandeep S. Dhalla-a surgeon who built a large-scale retina consolidation practice-invested in DentScribe and joined as a strategic advisor. He reportedly described DentScribe's AI as turning SOAP notes into "the operating system for growth". That's a big claim. It suggests the vision extends well beyond charting. But there's a competitor already playing this game, and from the opposite direction. Overjet, the better-funded dental AI company, started with revenue cycle management-eligibility checks, claim processing, payment routing-and has been expanding toward clinical documentation. Overjet raised $53 million in March 2024, bringing total funding to roughly $133 million and a $550 million valuation. In June 2026, Dental Care Alliance, a major DSO, deployed Overjet AI across its entire patient journey, from check-in to claim. So you have two companies converging on the same territory. Overjet moves from billing toward clinical. DentScribe moves from clinical toward revenue. The one who controls both sides controls the practice's information flow. Here's what I don't know. DentScribe's funding is not public. I couldn't find user counts, revenue figures, or DSO customer names. The company clearly believes it has a path, but the evidence for scale is thin. Overjet, by contrast, has the war chest and the headline DSO deal. If this becomes a funding war, DentScribe could be outspent. But there's a reason the underdog path might work. DentScribe starts from inside the exam room. Clinical documentation is the highest-friction, most universally hated task in dentistry-every dentist experiences it daily. That's a stronger wedge than billing optimization, which mainly appeals to practice managers and finance teams. If DentScribe gets in through clinical and then expands into revenue coordination, it's adding features to a product dentists already use. Overjet has to do the reverse. The way to win this isn't to be the better scribe. It's to be the system that connects what happens in the chair to what shows up on the practice's P&L. DentScribe seems to understand that. The question is whether a private company with no visible funding can build it fast enough. If you're watching dental AI, the test is simple. Watch which company controls the full conversation-not just the clinical notes, but the treatment discussion that follows. Whoever owns both sides of that conversation owns the practice's most important workflow. The rest is features.

funding_news.ai_summary: Overjet, Inc. filed a Form D notice with the SEC on December 24, 2025, for an exempt offering of equity securities under Rule 506(b), with a first sale occurring on December 12, 2025. The total offering amount is $34,801,486, of which $24,562,699 has already been sold to 22 investors, leaving $10,238,787 remaining. The company, incorporated in Delaware and headquartered in Boston, Massachusetts, did not disclose revenue information and reported zero sales commissions or finders' fees.

product_offering.core_offering: Overjet sells an FDA-cleared, cloud-based dental AI platform that combines radiographic diagnostic AI (Vision AI, IRIS imaging, CBCT Assist), ambient clinical voice documentation (Overjet Voice), insurance eligibility and claims review automation (Insurance Verification, ReviewPASS), multi-location DSO analytics, and insurer-side Provider Network Management. It is sold primarily as multi-year enterprise subscriptions to DSOs, group dental practices, and dental insurance carriers, with a self-serve entry tier for individual practitioners.
product_offering.product_overview: Overjet offers a unified dental AI platform with a modular architecture that serves dentists, dental service organizations (DSOs), dental insurers, and dental educators. The platform centers on Vision AI (the FDA-cleared diagnostic imaging AI for radiographic analysis that evolved from the original Dental Assist product), IRIS AI-Native Imaging (AI-native dental imaging software, with a separate DSO edition that adds the LENS multi-location layer), and Overjet Voice (the ambient AI documentation suite). These clinical-intelligence products feed Insurance Verification and ReviewPASS (revenue-cycle automation with connections to 300+ payers) and DSO Analytics (the multi-location clinical intelligence dashboard), while CBCT Assist extends the imaging capability to 3D cone beam computed tomography. The Dental Clarity Network (DCN) orchestrates insurer-provider collaboration anchored by ReviewPASS, Provider Network Management handles insurer-side recruiting/data/portal workflows, and the acquired American Dental Examiners (ADE) business provides licensed dental claims review. Together, these products automate clinical decision support, imaging, documentation, and insurance workflows across the dental ecosystem.

recent_move.description: Expanded the Dental Care Alliance partnership so that DCA became the first DSO to deploy Overjet AI (Voice, IRIS, AI Revenue Cycle Management, and Vision) across all 400+ affiliated practices in 24 states, covering the entire patient journey.

Raised a $53.2 million Series C led by March Capital, with participation from the American Dental Association, Crosslink Capital, General Catalyst, Insight Partners, Harmonic Growth Partners, Liquid 2 Ventures, SpringRock Ventures, and E14 Fund.
Launched the Dental Clarity Network (DCN) anchored by the ReviewPASS real-time claims-bypass signal, with major dental providers and insurers including MetLife and Humana joining the initiative.

Received FDA 510(k) clearance for CBCT Assist, an AI product for 3D cone beam computed tomography imaging, marking Overjet's 10th FDA clearance and extending the platform from 2D radiographs into 3D surgical and implant planning.
Acquired DentalBee for an undisclosed amount, expanding the platform's footprint beyond imaging and documentation into adjacent dental software workflows.
Partnered with Spear Education to integrate Overjet's AI-assisted diagnostic tools into dental school curricula and continuing education, opening the dental educator customer segment.

expansion_highlight.description: The June 2026 expansion of the Dental Care Alliance agreement into a full-suite, enterprise-wide deployment covering Voice, IRIS, AI Revenue Cycle Management, and Vision across 400+ practices signals a meaningful land-and-expand motion that converts single-product pilots into platform-wide recurring revenue.

The January 2026 partnership with Spear Education to embed AI diagnostic tools in dental school curricula and continuing education opens the dental educator and future-practitioner segment, creating a top-of-funnel training channel and a long-cycle brand-loyalty moat.

The December 2025 acquisition of DentalBee, combined with the December 2025 $25.4M funding round, indicates both balance-sheet capacity and strategic intent to extend the platform beyond imaging, documentation, and revenue cycle into adjacent dental software categories.

The December 2025 raise (~$25.4M, following the $53.2M Series C in March 2024) shows sustained investor appetite despite a tighter 2024-2025 venture environment, signaling capital for further product expansion and likely sales build-out.

The 10th FDA 510(k) clearance for CBCT Assist in December 2025 expanded the imaging franchise from 2D dental radiographs into 3D cone beam computed tomography, unlocking use cases in implantology, periodontics, airway analysis, and surgical planning and widening the addressable clinical surface area.

Integration partnerships with Medit (AuraVue, incorporating Overjet AI in cloud-based 3D intraoral scanning) and Planet DDS (DentalOS, embedding Overjet alongside Pearl and VideaHealth) extend distribution into third-party imaging and DSO platforms, suggesting channel-led geographic and customer reach expansion without proportional sales headcount.

company_assessment.market_position: Overjet is a venture-backed, Boston-based dental AI company founded in 2018 that positions itself as a leader in clinical decision support and insurance workflow automation for the dental ecosystem. The company serves dentists, Dental Service Organizations (DSOs), dental insurers/payers, and dental schools through a multi-product SaaS platform anchored by 10 FDA clearances, the Dental Care Alliance enterprise rollout across 400+ practices in 24 states, and named customers such as MetLife and Humana on the payer side.

strengths.details: The Dental Clarity Network launched March 2025 with MetLife and Humana as flagship participants, anchored by ReviewPASS — a real-time signal that tells practices whether a claim will bypass manual clinical review. If Overjet successfully recruits additional top-10 dental insurers (the company already counts 16+ major carriers per Series B disclosure), ReviewPASS becomes a two-sided utility that no single competitor can replicate, and per-claim transaction economics could expand margins well beyond traditional SaaS. This is the clearest path to a venture-scale outcome.
strengths.headline: Dental Clarity Network creates winner-take-all utility

strengths.details: Overjet Voice claims ~5+ hours saved per provider per week and a ~25% reduction in claim denials. With ~200,000 practicing dentists in the US and ambient documentation rapidly becoming a baseline expectation (mirroring what Abridge and Nuance DAX have done in medicine), expansion from imaging AI into voice/documentation could 3-5x revenue per existing DSO customer and unlock an entirely new solo-practice and small-group segment via the "Try for free" PLG motion currently in market.
strengths.headline: Voice AI unlocks massive per-dentist TAM expansion

strengths.details: The Dental Care Alliance relationship began in 2022 and has expanded through three documented phases (initial partnership → 2024 full imaging rollout → June 2026 full patient-journey deployment). With ~5,000+ DSOs in the US operating 30%+ of dental practices, even modest penetration of the top 100 DSOs replicates DCA at scale. The acquired American Dental Examiners (June 2021) and DentalBee (December 2025) also signal an M&A roll-up strategy to consolidate claims-review and adjacent workflows.
strengths.headline: Land-and-expand model replicates across thousands of DSOs

strengths.details: CBCT Assist received FDA 510(k) clearance in December 2025 — Overjet's 10th FDA clearance — extending AI from 2D to 3D imaging for implant, surgical, and airway planning. With 3D CBCT scanners becoming standard in mid-market practices and implants representing a high-value revenue line (~$5K-$50K per case), AI-guided implant case capture via the Implant Finder feature alone could unlock a multi-hundred-million-dollar revenue category distinct from the existing subscription base.
strengths.headline: CBCT Assist and Implant Finder expand into high-value surgical revenue

strengths.details: Overjet counts 10 FDA clearances, HITRUST CSF certification, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, GDPR, and CCPA compliance — a regulatory and security posture that few dental AI competitors can match and that effectively blocks new entrants from selling into enterprise DSOs and insurers. Combined with integrations into Medit AuraVue and Planet DDS DentalOS, Overjet is positioned as the default AI layer across the dental software stack, justifying premium pricing and pricing power as the category matures.
strengths.headline: 10 FDA clearances create durable regulatory moat

weakness.details: Planet DDS's DentalOS platform lists Overjet alongside direct competitors Pearl and VideaHealth as interchangeable AI imaging vendors, signaling a commoditization risk where DSO customers can swap vendors with limited switching cost. If a competitor undercuts pricing or achieves comparable FDA-cleared accuracy, Overjet's $425M+ valuation could compress materially. The dental AI category is attracting significant capital from strategic acquirers (Henry Schein acquired VideaHealth in 2024), which may accelerate consolidation and pressure standalone players.
weakness.headline: Pearl and VideaHealth commoditize dental imaging AI

weakness.details: Overjet's marquee customer Dental Care Alliance accounts for 400+ practices across 24 states, and the June 2026 expansion makes DCA Overjet's flagship reference account. Any churn, budget cut, or strategic change at DCA would have an outsized impact on revenue, given the limited number of disclosed enterprise DSO logos (CoreDental, Jefferson Dental, The Smilist, Dental 365, North American Dental, Platinum Dental). Concentration in a handful of large DSOs leaves the revenue base vulnerable to a single relationship deteriorating.
weakness.headline: DCA customer concentration creates revenue fragility

weakness.details: Overjet's last disclosed post-money valuation was $425M in December 2021. With ~$80M raised since then across Series C ($53.2M in March 2024 led by March Capital) and a $25.36M extension in December 2025, the company has either marked up meaningfully in private rounds or faces flat/down rounds in a tighter 2024-2025 AI funding environment. The lack of disclosed current valuation is a material gap, and any IPO path is likely several years away given AI market conditions.
weakness.headline: Last valuation disclosure is 4+ years stale

weakness.details: While FDA clearance is a current moat, increasing FTC and HHS scrutiny of AI in clinical decision support, plus ongoing debates around algorithmic bias in healthcare AI, could impose new validation, monitoring, or disclosure requirements. The CBCT Assist clearance and 10 total clearances create regulatory surface area that must be maintained; any adverse event or recall could compromise market positioning and trigger costly remediation across the entire platform.
weakness.headline: Regulatory scrutiny of clinical AI is tightening

weakness.details: Overjet has expanded from a single Vision AI product in 2021 to a portfolio spanning imaging AI, ambient voice documentation, insurance verification, RCM analytics, and payer provider-network tools — five distinct product categories with different buyers, competitors, and integration requirements. Ambient documentation alone competes against well-funded players like Abridge, Suki, and Nuance DAX in healthcare AI. Execution risk across this portfolio may strain engineering and sales resources, slowing the path to profitability.
weakness.headline: Product sprawl dilutes execution focus

competitive_moat.details: Overjet holds 10 FDA 510(k) clearances across its imaging AI products, including the first FDA clearance ever granted to a dental AI company (Dental Assist, August 2021) and the more recent CBCT Assist clearance for 3D imaging. Each clearance represents a multi-year, data-intensive regulatory investment that is difficult and expensive for competitors to replicate in a clinical decision-support category.

Enterprise-scale deployments across DSOs such as Dental Care Alliance (400+ practices in 24 states), TD Dental (34 locations), and integrations with 300+ insurance payers generate a continuous, clinically labeled data flywheel that improves model accuracy on caries detection, bone loss measurement, and clinical review automation. Volume and diversity of data is structurally hard for later entrants to match.

Platform integrations with practice management systems, sensors (IRIS), 300+ payer connections, and embedded clinical workflows (chart notes, perio charts, automated referrals, revenue cycle) create high operational switching costs once a DSO or payer is deployed. Customers report 18x ROI and 25%+ case acceptance lifts that anchor multi-year contracts.

Overjet has built a defensible go-to-market by winning flagship DSO accounts (Dental Care Alliance, Core Dental, Jefferson Dental, Aligned Dental Partners, The Smilist, Dental 365, North American Dental Group, Platinum Dental Services) and major insurers (MetLife, Humana, plus 16 carriers by December 2021). Land-and-expand is reinforced by integration partnerships with Medit (AuraVue) and Planet DDS (DentalOS), extending distribution without adding direct sales headcount.

The Dental Clarity Network (DCN) and ReviewPASS create a two-sided payer-provider network effect: more payer participation increases ReviewPASS signal coverage (300+ procedures), which in turn increases the platform's value to dental practices. This network, combined with the Spear Education curriculum partnership, is converting the product from point solution into industry infrastructure.

Overjet was the first dental AI company to receive FDA clearance, has 10 cumulative clearances, and is consistently positioned as the category leader by customers and investors, supported by HITRUST, HIPAA, SOC 2 Type II, GDPR, and CCPA certifications. These compliance and brand assets lower enterprise procurement risk.

key_risks.details: Dental Care Alliance's 400+ practices across 24 states represent Overjet's most prominent reference account and the anchor of its land-and-expand DSO strategy. With only a handful of other DSO logos disclosed (CoreDental, Jefferson Dental, The Smilist, Dental 365, North American Dental, Platinum Dental), churn or budget compression at any single large DSO would have outsized impact on revenue concentration risk.
key_risks.headline: DCA customer concentration creates revenue fragility

key_risks.details: Planet DDS's DentalOS platform lists Overjet, Pearl, and VideaHealth as interchangeable AI imaging vendors, signaling commoditization risk and limited switching costs at the DSO buyer level. Henry Schein's 2024 acquisition of VideaHealth and well-funded entrants like Pearl continue to compress pricing power and could trigger a feature/price race that pressures margins.
key_risks.headline: Dental imaging AI faces accelerating competitive pressure

key_risks.details: Overjet has raised approximately $155M+ across seed ($7.85M), Series A ($27M), Series B ($42.5M), Series C ($53.2M, March 2024), and a December 2025 extension ($25.36M). The pace of funding and headcount of 101-250 employees suggest a continued reliance on external capital to fund sales, RCM, payer-side, and Voice product expansion before reaching self-sustaining cash flow.
key_risks.headline: Capital intensity remains elevated with ~$155M+ raised

key_risks.details: The Series B post-money valuation of $425M was disclosed in December 2021. No pre/post-money valuations are disclosed for the 2024 Series C or the 2025 extension, leaving current mark-to-market unclear and creating uncertainty for any secondary transactions or IPO planning in an AI-market-sensitive environment.
key_risks.headline: Last disclosed valuation is 4+ years old

key_risks.details: Overjet Voice enters the ambient clinical documentation market where competitors like Abridge (medicine), Suki, and Nuance DAX have raised billions in capital and are extending into dental. Overjet must compete for talent, integrations, and accuracy benchmarks against companies with substantially larger war chests and broader clinical footprints beyond dentistry.
key_risks.headline: Voice AI is a contested, well-funded category

key_risks.details: With 10 FDA clearances covering diagnostic interpretation across 2D radiographs and 3D CBCT scans, any misdiagnosis, algorithmic failure, or FDA post-market surveillance issue exposes Overjet to clinical liability, recall costs, and reputational damage in a category where accuracy is being actively marketed (Overjet claims >90% accuracy).
key_risks.headline: Regulatory and clinical liability risk is real

key_highlights.details: Overjet is rolling out its full AI suite (Overjet Voice, IRIS AI-Native Imaging, AI Revenue Cycle Management, and Vision) across DCA's 400+ affiliated practices in 24 states — described as one of the most ambitious AI deployments in dentistry. The relationship began in 2022 and expanded through documented phases, demonstrating a clear land-and-expand motion that scales revenue per customer materially.
key_highlights.headline: Landmark DSO deployment at Dental Care Alliance

key_highlights.details: Overjet holds 10 FDA 510(k) clearances across its platform, including the first FDA clearance ever granted to a dental AI company (Dental Assist, August 2021) and the December 2025 CBCT Assist clearance for 3D imaging. FDA-cleared status is a prerequisite for selling into enterprise DSOs and payers, and the cumulative clearance footprint is a meaningful barrier for new entrants.
key_highlights.headline: 10 FDA clearances create regulatory moat

key_highlights.details: Launched March 2025 with MetLife and Humana as flagship participants, the Dental Clarity Network — anchored by ReviewPASS — positions Overjet as a two-sided platform between payers and providers. The Series B disclosure (Dec 2021) noted 16 major insurance carriers as customers, validating payer distribution as a real wedge into revenue-cycle automation.
key_highlights.headline: Payer-side anchor: Dental Clarity Network with MetLife and Humana

key_highlights.details: Overjet is HIPAA-compliant, HITRUST CSF certified, SOC 2 Type II compliant, GDPR-compliant (with UK/EU Standard Contractual Clauses), and CCPA-compliant. This certification stack is required for enterprise DSO and payer contracts and is held by very few dental AI competitors.
key_highlights.headline: Robust enterprise security and compliance posture

key_highlights.details: The platform spans Vision AI (diagnostic imaging), IRIS (AI-native imaging software), Overjet Voice (ambient documentation), Insurance Verification (300+ payer connections), ReviewPASS (instant claim approvals), DSO Analytics, and CBCT Assist — bundling clinical intelligence, imaging, documentation, and revenue cycle into a single enterprise sale. Customers report ~25% reduction in claim denials and ~5+ hours saved per provider per week via Voice.
key_highlights.headline: Multi-product platform diversifies revenue per customer

key_highlights.details: Overjet has raised ~$155M+ across rounds, with backing from General Catalyst, Insight Partners, March Capital (Series C lead, March 2024), Crosslink Capital, and the American Dental Association. The December 2025 $25.36M extension demonstrates continued investor appetite post-Series C despite a tougher 2024-2025 AI funding environment.
key_highlights.headline: Strong investor syndicate and continued funding momentum

key_highlights.details: Overjet acquired American Dental Examiners (ADE) in June 2021 to add licensed dental claims review services to its payer offerings, and acquired DentalBee in December 2025 to bolster capabilities. A roll-up strategy around clinical and revenue-cycle AI positions Overjet to consolidate fragmented dental-services software.
key_highlights.headline: Strategic acquisitions extend platform breadth

customer_concentration.details: Customer concentration is best characterized as Moderate to High. Dental Care Alliance (400+ practices across 24 states) is by far the largest publicly named customer, and the relationship has progressed from a 2022 initial partnership to a June 2026 full-suite enterprise deployment, meaning a material share of Overjet's DSO revenue base is likely tied to a single anchor account. On the payer side, the December 2021 disclosure of 16 major insurance carriers as customers, combined with the March 2025 named commitments from MetLife and Humana to the Dental Clarity Network, diversifies revenue across at least two national carriers but also concentrates platform importance in a small number of large payers. The remaining named DSO logos (TD Dental, Core Dental, Jefferson Dental, Aligned Dental Partners, The Smilist, Dental 365, North American Dental Group, Platinum Dental Services) plus the self-serve "Try for free" funnel suggest a mid- and long-tail base exists, but the absence of disclosed revenue figures prevents a definitive split; loss of DCA or one of the top three payers would meaningfully affect revenue predictability.

launches.title: Pearl Launches Second Opinion 3D, Bringing FDA-Cleared CBCT Imaging AI to General Dentists for the First Time
launches.ai_summary: Pearl launched Second Opinion 3D, making its FDA-cleared CBCT imaging AI available to general dentists in the US and Canada. The product adds embedded specialist radiology-report requests and automatic conversion of CBCT findings into insurance claim-ready documentation. AI-powered pathology detection is available in Canada and pending approval in additional markets.
launches.full_text:
Key Takeaways:

Pearl has launched Second Opinion 3D, making its FDA-cleared 3D imaging AI available to general dentists in the US and Canada.

The commercial release of the FDA cleared technology adds two workflow features built specifically for general dentists: an embedded specialist radiology-report request, and automatic conversion of CBCT findings into insurance claim-ready documentation.

Built for chairside use rather than specialist image review, Second Opinion 3D is designed to help general dentists interpret CBCT scans and walk patients through what the AI finds in real time.



LOS ANGELES, Sept. 03, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Pearl today launched Second Opinion 3D, putting its FDA-cleared 3D imaging AI into general dentists' hands as a commercial product for the first time. General practices are adopting CBCT faster than the software built to support them: most viewers on the market were designed for specialist image review, not for a general dentist working through a normal patient appointment. Second Opinion 3D is Pearl's answer: a CBCT tool built around how general practices actually work, and integrated into the same Second Opinion interface providers already use for 2D imaging.

The launch builds on the FDA 510(k) clearance Pearl received last year , when it became the first dental AI company cleared by the FDA for both 2D and 3D radiologic image analysis. That clearance covered the underlying AI, which automatically identifies structures such as the mandible, maxillary complex, nasal space, airway, inferior alveolar nerve canal, and individual teeth in CBCT scans. Today's launch turns that clearance into a product: alongside general availability, Second Opinion 3D now lets providers request a report from a board-certified oral and maxillofacial radiologist without leaving the interface, and automatically converts 3D findings into insurance claim-ready documentation, two steps that previously required separate portals and manual staff work.

“General dentists have invested in CBCT for years, but reading these scans well has traditionally required specialist-level training most practices don’t have. Second Opinion 3D helps every dentist do more with CBCT. That matters beyond the tooth being treated: CBCT is one of the more exciting imaging modalities we have because of what it can reveal about a patient's health beyond their mouth. By making CBCT more accessible and useful for dentists, we’re advancing a technology that has a role to play in bridging the gap between dental medicine and systemic health."

— Ophir Tanz, CEO and Founder, Pearl

"What I really wanted was something that would scan every slice, flag anything worth a second look, and take me straight to it. That's exactly what it does. It's caught things I would've missed just focusing on the one area I came in to check. And when I'm sitting with a patient, I can isolate exactly what I'm looking at and show them, instead of trying to explain a blob on a screen. That changes how confident patients feel about the treatment plan we land on."

— Dr. Todd Yerondopoulos, Enamel Creations, Pleasanton, CA

What does this mean for general dentists?

CBCT has moved from a specialist tool into everyday use in general practice, but the software built to support it hasn't kept pace, and the workflow around it hasn't either. Getting a specialist's opinion on a scan typically means exporting files and going through a separate referral process, and turning a 3D finding into something a payor will accept for a claim is manual work that falls to practice staff. Both add friction to a workflow that's already asking general dentists to interpret imaging outside their usual training.







Second Opinion 3D is Pearl's answer to that gap, now available as a full product rather than just a cleared technology. The AI automatically segments key anatomy and color-codes each for easy visualization, allowing users to remove or highlight specific anatomical structures. It presents anatomical structures in an interactive viewer with 3D rendering, zoom and rotation, opacity controls, length measurement. Second Opinion 3D also supports radiology-report requests and claim-ready documentation, and the ability to easily turn CBCT scans into claim-ready 2D images features mean providers no longer have to leave the software or hand work off to staff to get a second opinion or bill for what they found.

How does this compare to existing CBCT viewers?

Most CBCT software was designed for technical image review, engineered for radiologists and specialists first, with general dentists and practice workflow as an afterthought. Second Opinion 3D is built the other way around. Where a traditional workflow requires downloading a scan and uploading it to a separate radiology portal, Second Opinion 3D keeps that request inside the same software. Where turning a 3D finding into claim documentation has meant manual rework by staff, Second Opinion 3D generates it automatically. And where most viewers assume the person reading the scan is a specialist, Second Opinion 3D is also built for the general dentist and the chairside conversation.







What happens next?

Second Opinion 3D also includes AI-powered pathology detection, covering findings such as TMD, carotid artery calcifications, impactions, periapical radiolucency, and sinus radiopacities. These capabilities are currently available in Canada and pending regulatory approval in additional markets.

For multi-location practices and DSOs, Second Opinion 3D can standardize how CBCT is reviewed, documented, and communicated across locations and providers.



About Pearl

Pearl is a dental AI company committed to enhancing how patient care is delivered. Founded in 2019 by a team with decades of experience developing successful, enterprise-grade computer vision solutions, Pearl introduced the first-ever FDA-cleared AI capable of reading and instantly identifying diseases in dental x-rays. With regulatory clearance in 120 countries, Pearl's AI assists dentists in making precise clinical decisions and effectively communicating with patients, thereby transforming the dental care experience worldwide. As dentistry's global AI leader, Pearl is committed to the ongoing innovation of robust, accessible AI tools that improve patient health outcomes and build greater trust in dental medicine. To request a demo, please visit hellopearl.com/demo .

Highest disease burden: Delaware (14.22 showing signs of decay, loss, or restoration; calculus 62.6 percent).

Highest tartar buildup: New Jersey (67.7 percent of patients). This is a 23-point spread vs. Hawaii on a single hygiene indicator.

Highest rate of extraction: Kansas, where nearly 1 in 10 affected teeth was extracted rather than restored. Article content The Dentist Lottery: A 4x gap in what two offices on the same block may diagnose

Within single zip codes, Pearl identified a 9.2 percentage-point average spread in D-Load (the share of decay left untreated) between neighboring offices, with the top 10 percent of zip codes showing spreads of 17.8 points. Pearl matched zip-code data against the National Provider Identifier (NPI) registry of 180,974 U.S. dental practices and 295,509 dentists. launches.ai_summary: Pearl, a dental AI company, released the Pearl Oral Health Index, analyzing 26 million dental x-rays across 15 million patients and 737 million teeth to produce the largest radiographic census of American oral health. The study found that U.S. cavity rates are 4.5 times worse than CDC NHANES estimates, with 94 percent of adults aged 18-24 having untreated dental disease and patients in "dental deserts" losing 40 percent more teeth than those in areas with sufficient dental coverage.
