funding_news.title: The pivot behind Snorkel AI's $3.5 billion valuation
funding_news.ai_summary: Snorkel AI raised $350 million at a $3.5 billion valuation, nearly tripling its May 2025 valuation. Its annualized revenue run-rate crossed $350 million, up from about $20 million a year earlier, after pivoting to data-as-a-service. The company expects to reach profitability this year, but renewal risk remains.
funding_news.author: Anders Mirofollow
funding_news.full_text:
The headline number hides the one that matters. Snorkel AI, a Redwood City data startup spun out of the Stanford AI lab, raised $350 million in fresh funding at a $3.5 billion valuation, nearly triple the $1.3 billion valuation investors set in May 2025. But the figure underneath is the striking one: its annualized revenue run-rate crossed $350 million this year, up from roughly $20 million a year earlier. A company does not grow like that by doing more of the same. It grew like that by changing what it sells.

For most of its life, Snorkel sold software861053--. Its programmatic labeling tools — which let a data team turn an expert's rules into training data instead of hand-annotating every example — built a respectable enterprise business and, in May 2025, a $100 million round led by Addition. Then, in September 2025, it added a "data-as-a-service" offering: finished datasets and reinforcement-learning environments, sold as products rather than as a tool to build them. That pivot is the entire story of the tripling. What changed is not just the growth rate but what the revenue line measures and who pays for it.

The new customers are the most concentrated, best-capitalized buyers in technology: frontier AI labs, hyperscalers, enterprises, and the U.S. federal government. Demand has centered on coding data, with law and medicine behind it. To produce it, Snorkel draws on a network of tens of thousands of specialists in those fields, working alongside a fleet of specialized AI agents.

Here is where a careful reader should slow down, because one accounting choice does real work. Snorkel does not charge customers for human labor. It sells the finished data, and payments to its experts sit in cost of goods sold — below the revenue line. Its $350 million run-rate is therefore a top-line figure: that largest cost is recorded as an expense below the revenue line, not subtracted from the headline number. Not every rival reports it that way: the pass-through competitors in this space hand 60% to 70% of their top-line income to outside specialists, so a same-sized gross number from one of them overstates how much value it keeps. This is part of why Snorkel expects to reach profitability this year even while growing this fast.

The catch is that it is still a services business, and a services business captures value only as long as the customer keeps buying. The cleanliness of the accounting does not tell you whether a frontier lab will renew at these prices a year from now — whether Snorkel's data measurably improves its models, or whether a customer worth tens of billions decides it would rather own the capability. That last risk is live. Meta's June 2025 purchase of a 49% stake in Scale AI for $14.3 billion shows how high the data bottleneck has risen, and how willing the biggest AI spenders are to buy their way into it. The concentration that makes Snorkel's customers rich enough to pay also makes them powerful enough to internalize the work or fund a competitor.

Work through the arithmetic and the round looks ordinary for the category. A $3.5 billion valuation against a $350 million run-rate is roughly ten times revenue, unremarkable for a hypergrowth AI infrastructureAIIA-- name. The valuation tripled not because ten times became extraordinary but because the revenue in the denominator grew about seventeenfold in a year. An investor's honest question is not whether the multiple is rich. It is whether the revenue is real and repeatable. It is real in that customers pay for finished data. Its repeatability is unproved, because a year-old services run-rate sold to a handful of hyperconcentrated buyers has not yet been tested through a single renewal cycle.

The round is a signal about the AI stack even for investors who will never own a share of Snorkel. Value has been sliding from raw compute toward the data that decides how good a model actually is, and a company that spent years as a modest labeling tool just converted that position into more than $350 million of annualized revenue in a year. The bullish case is a flywheel — human expertise training specialized agents that make the next dataset cheaper and better, so each renewal gets harder to walk away from. The case that fails it is a services business whose revenue rests on a few laboratories that could, at sufficient scale, build the capability themselves. What separates the two is not the tripled valuation but the one thing nine months of new revenue cannot yet show: whether the customers come back.

funding_news.title: Snorkel AI's $3.5 Billion Round Looked Like a Re-Rating — It Was Actually a Discount
funding_news.ai_summary: Snorkel AI raised $350 million at a $3.5 billion valuation, co-led by Insight Partners and S32. The company's annualized revenue crossed $350 million, down from $20 million a year prior, making the round a discount on sales. It expects to reach profitability this year.
funding_news.author: Julian Cruzfollow
funding_news.full_text:
After the close on Monday, private AI data company Snorkel AI said it had raised $350 million in fresh funding at a $3.5 billion valuation, in a round co-led by Insight Partners and S32, with existing investors Addition, Greylock and Wells Fargo participating.

On its face that reads like a startup in escape velocity — nearly three times the $1.3 billion Snorkel fetched in its May 2025 round. But the more revealing math sits underneath, because on a sales basis the company actually got cheaper.

Here is the ledger. Annualized revenue has crossed $350 million, up from approximately $20 million a year prior. Divide today's $3.5 billion valuation by that roughly $350 million run-rate and you get about 10 times sales. Run the same divide on the May 2025 round — $1.3 billion on roughly $20 million of revenue — and you're at about 65 times. In absolute dollars the company nearly tripled in value; on revenue it de-rated by a factor of more than six. That is not the shape of a bubble round. It's the shape of a company that grew into its number.

The reason the number moved so fast is that the business itself changed. Snorkel was founded in 2019 by Stanford AI lab researchers and built its name on software861053-- — Snorkel Flow, a programmatic data-labeling platform. For years that software model produced only modest revenue. Then, in September 2025, the company launched a data-as-a-service business: instead of selling tools, it began selling finished datasets and reinforcement-learning environments, and it sells the resulting data products rather than charging for human labor.

The pivot was a genuine break, not a cosmetic one. Right around that same launch, Snorkel cut 31 of about 240 employees — roughly 13% of the workforce — with software engineers hit hardest, as the company said it was deprioritizing legacy areas. You don't lay off your software engineers the month after launching the product you were built around unless the old model wasn't scaling. The layoff and the launch describe the same event from two directions.

All of which points at the question that matters for anyone sizing the AI data theme: is this data-as-a-service a product, or a services business in disguise? The bull case is that it leans toward product. Snorkel combines teams of human experts in coding, law and medicine with specialized AI models and agents for quality control, then sells the finished data; it does not bill for headcount. Cost it favorably and that could carry software-like margins, and Reuters reports the company expects to reach profitability this year.

The bear case is that any business built around expert humans carries heavier costs than a pure software license, and the public AI complex makes that tension visible. PalantirPLTR--, the closest big public AI software name, trades at roughly 72 times trailing sales with a gross margin near 85%, as of Monday's close. Against that, Snorkel at about 10 times forward run-rate looks cheap — but Palantir sells software and Snorkel sells data with a human-expert layer inside it. A discount to 72 times sales doesn't automatically mean fair value if the cost structure never reaches software margins. The whole gap between Snorkel's single-digit multiple and Palantir's 70-plus is a wager on how productized, and how margin-rich, "expert data" can actually get.

For an ordinary retail reader, the honest caveat is that you cannot buy Snorkel — it is privately held, and none of this re-rating is capturable in a brokerage account. What the round is, then, is a live data point on the AI supply chain: the market increasingly treats high-quality training and evaluation data as the binding constraint on frontier models, and it is willing to pay for the companies that produce it. The public way to express that bet runs through the AI software names, which already carry far richer multiples — so a private raise at about 10 times run-rate either validates the theme or is a reminder of how extended the public AI complex has become. It can be both.

When I rank the live issues here, valuation is not the one that worries me. At roughly 10 times a growing, near-breakeven run-rate, the price looks defensible even if the dollar figure in the headline is big. The larger question is the durability and the margins of the data-as-a-service model, which is barely a year old and, by the company's own accounting, only just approaching profitability. I'd take the round as real evidence that the AI data layer is a competitive bottleneck worth watching, but I'd want to see proof that a human-expert data business can hold software-like margins across a few more quarters of scale before giving it the benefit of the doubt. Profitability is expected this year, not yet delivered.

A company that priced itself at $1.3 billion a year ago just raised $350 million at a $3.5 billion valuation in a round led by InsightNSIT-- and S32, roughly tripling the $1.3 billion valuation it set in May 2025. Read like every other frothy AI headline, this looks like a data-labeling startup re-rating on narrative momentum. The math underneath says otherwise: Snorkel AI grew its revenue base faster than it grew its valuation, so the tripling actually made each dollar of its sales cheaper to own. At the May 2025 round, Snorkel carried a $1.3 billion valuation on about $20 million in revenue — a 65x multiple on a company that sold software861053--. Twelve months later, annualized revenue has crossed $350 million, up from roughly $20 million a year earlier, a step the company describes as growth of more than 18x. Try the division yourself: take the new $3.5 billion valuation and divide by roughly $350 million of revenue, and the multiple lands near 10x. The price tag tripled while the multiple fell by more than 80 percent, because revenue compounded far faster than the number on the term sheet changed. What produced that step-change is a change in what the company sells. Instead of licensing data-labeling software, Snorkel now supplies the finished datasets and reinforcement-learning environments that frontier models are actually trained on, a data-as-a-service offering launched in September 2025. The structure matters to returns: it sells data products rather than billing for human hours, so it can pay specialists well while machines handle the repetitive quality-control work. That a service launched less than a year ago now anchors a $350 million-plus annualized run rate is usage and real capital, not attention. The read-through for a retail investor needs one explicit warning: this is not a stock you can buy. The $3.5 billion figure is a private, negotiated price set by professional investors, not a public-market quote. What the round does hand an outsider is a map of where institutional money believes the AI bottleneck has moved — from compute toward the specialized data that trains, evaluates, and keeps models aligned. It is the difference between selling a labeling tool once and supplying the scarce data itself on a recurring basis, which is why funds pay a venture multiple for the second. Two limits should temper how far that logic carries. Every number above is company-reported from a private firm with no audited public disclosure, so a retail investor cannot verify the run rate. And the customer base is concentrated among frontier labs, hyperscalers, and the federal government, which makes a lab deciding to build data work in-house the single largest threat to the model. The company says it expects to reach profitability within the current year — that is the condition worth watching. If the run rate keeps compounding at these margins, a roughly 10x multiple has organic support; if growth decelerates sharply or a major customer pulls the work inside, there is no public bid standing by to catch the price. The honest judgment to take from the round is that the tripling is real, because it is carried by a revenue jump of roughly 17x rather than by a higher multiple. The open question is not whether Snorkel deserves more per dollar of sales than it did a year ago — it clearly does — but whether the data-as-a-service compound can keep clearing past $350 million and, eventually, at what price a public market chooses to value it. funding_news.ai_summary: Ten venture rounds totaling about $1.379 billion were announced on September 22, 2026, with Cyera, Snorkel AI, and Heidi Health leading. The headline capital includes $240 million non-dilutive financing from Heidi, leaving roughly $1.139 billion in equity. Investors are concentrating capital on companies controlling strategic bottlenecks in AI infrastructure.
funding_news.author: Nickie Louise
funding_news.full_text:
0 Shares

Venture capital today is clustering around a surprisingly consistent idea: the next layer of AI value is shifting away from the model itself and toward the systems that make AI usable, governable, trustworthy, and economically productive. Cybersecurity company Cyera pulled in another $400 million. Snorkel AI raised $350 million to supply increasingly specialized training data and reinforcement-learning environments. Heidi Health paired a $100 million equity round with a $240 million non-dilutive facility as clinical AI moves from transcription into healthcare workflows. That pattern continues further down the funding stack. Go.AI is putting private AI infrastructure inside regulated institutions. Firecrawl is building the data-access layer agents need to interact with the web. Baselayer is attacking financial fraud. Sela is applying voice agents specifically to mortgage sales, while Teal Health and Ramona Optics show that investors are still willing to finance differentiated healthcare and life-science infrastructure outside the generative-AI rush. Axios’ deal reporting captures the unusually dense cluster of enterprise AI, security, fintech and healthcare rounds announced Tuesday. Across the ten rounds selected below, the headline capital committed totals about $1.379 billion. That figure needs one qualification: $240 million of Heidi’s package is non-dilutive financing rather than equity, leaving roughly $1.139 billion of equity or equity-like venture/growth funding in the selected set. The three largest transactions, Cyera, Snorkel AI, and Heidi, account for about 79% of headline capital, or roughly three-quarters of the equity component. That concentration is the day’s clearest market signal: investors are writing very large checks where companies can demonstrate strategic control points, customer adoption or both. The Macro Environment: Capital Is Paying for Control, Not Just Intelligence The backdrop is not one of cheap money. The Federal Reserve raised its target range by 25 basis points on September 16 to 3.75%–4.00%, meaning venture investors are still competing against a meaningful cost of capital. That makes today’s nine-figure private rounds more revealing than they would be in a zero-rate environment: investors are reserving large checks for businesses they believe can either dominate a category or become infrastructure other businesses cannot easily remove. Cyera is a good example of the first category. Goldman Sachs is putting $400 million into a company already valued at more than $12 billion, shortly after Cyera completed its $1 billion acquisition of non-human-identity specialist Oasis Security. The investment is less about financing basic product development than giving Cyera enough balance-sheet latitude to broaden its platform, pursue federal and overseas customers, make acquisitions, and choose its own timing for a future public offering. The Wall Street Journal reports that Cyera has raised $1.94 billion since June 2025 alone and has now landed its first customer spending more than $10 million annually. Snorkel represents the second category: infrastructure underneath increasingly capable models. Its annualized revenue run-rate has risen from roughly $20 million a year ago to more than $350 million, according to Reuters, as frontier labs need harder training tasks, specialist-generated datasets and reinforcement-learning environments rather than commodity labeling. At a $3.5 billion valuation, the round prices Snorkel at roughly ten times its reported annualized revenue — a valuation that looks aggressive in ordinary software but much less unusual for a company growing at this speed and positioning itself directly in the frontier-model supply chain. We calculated that multiple from Reuters’ reported valuation and revenue figures. Private and public capital are also beginning to meet around AI infrastructure. On the same day these venture rounds surfaced, data-center infrastructure provider Accelevation set U.S. IPO terms at $20 to $24 per share, implying a market capitalization of around $4.9 billion at the midpoint. That does not mean the public market is broadly open to every venture-backed software company. It suggests something narrower: businesses connected to AI’s physical, security, and operational requirements have a more credible path toward institutional-scale financing than undifferentiated application companies. The implication for founders is important. Calling a product “AI-native” is not enough to command premium capital. Today’s stronger financings sit at specific bottlenecks: who can access sensitive data, where models run, how training data is generated, how clinical work is documented, how agents retrieve information, and how regulated transactions are verified. Investors appear increasingly willing to fund the companies that own those bottlenecks rather than another thin interface sitting on top of somebody else’s model. The Top Funding Rounds Cyera raises $400M to secure data and AI-agent access across the enterprise Cyera’s $400 million investment from Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives extends the company’s Series G and comes only months after a $600 million Series G valued the New York cybersecurity company at $12 billion. Cyera says the new investment will support its AI-security roadmap, federal-market expansion and continued growth across Europe, the Middle East, Africa and Asia-Pacific. The strategic premise has broadened substantially from classic data-security posture management. Enterprises deploying AI agents now have software identities that can call tools, query databases, and act on corporate information without constant human involvement. Cyera’s acquisition of Oasis Security brought non-human identity management into the same platform as data security, allowing the company to address both sides of the permission problem: where sensitive information sits and which human, machine or agent can reach it. That is also why Goldman entering at this stage is notable. This is late-stage capital going into a company that already has the scale to contemplate an IPO, not a speculative bet on whether a category will exist. The Wall Street Journal reports that Cyera’s newest financing gives it additional freedom to invest in products and M&A while delaying a listing if private capital remains attractive. For competing data-security and identity vendors, that creates a well-funded consolidator with both an acquisition currency and a $12 billion-plus valuation benchmark. Funding Details

Sector: Cybersecurity, data security, AI-agent security, identity security Snorkel AI raises $350M to become the data infrastructure behind frontier AI Snorkel AI raised $350 million at a $3.5 billion valuation, co-led by Insight Partners and S32, with participation from Greylock and Wells Fargo. The valuation is almost three times the $1.3 billion figure attached to Snorkel’s $100 million financing in May 2025. More striking is the operating trajectory: Reuters reports annualized revenue above $350 million, versus roughly $20 million a year earlier. The change is tied to a strategic pivot. Snorkel began as software for programmatic data labeling but has increasingly become a supplier of finished datasets and reinforcement-learning environments. Its network includes specialists in coding, law and medicine, while AI systems automate portions of quality assurance and data production. CEO Alex Ratner argues that increasingly capable models require data that is harder to source and judge, creating demand for human expertise combined with automated production rather than conventional annotation labor. That places Snorkel in a market reshaped by Scale AI, Mercor, Surge AI and the frontier labs’ appetite for difficult training and evaluation data. Reuters notes that investor interest intensified after Meta’s 2025 purchase of a 49% stake in Scale AI for $14.3 billion. Snorkel’s answer is to sell the data product rather than bill customers for hours of human work — potentially giving it better operating leverage if it can preserve quality as volumes rise. The company says it expects to reach profitability this year, an unusually consequential detail for a company growing this quickly. Funding Details

Sector: AI training data, reinforcement learning, model evaluation infrastructure Heidi Health raises $100M in equity and secures a $240M growth facility for clinical AI Heidi Health’s financing is best understood as $100 million of Series C equity plus a $240 million non-dilutive growth facility, not a conventional $340 million venture round. Blackbird led the equity financing, with Phoenix Court and, according to Axios, Point72 Private Investments and Headline participating; General Catalyst led the $240 million financing component. The Melbourne healthtech startup started with an AI medical scribe but is pushing toward a broader clinical-workflow platform. The Times reports that Heidi handles about 2.8 million patient interactions each week in 110 languages and has won a major NHS clinical documentation deployment spanning 15 trusts and integrated-care organizations, as well as more than 1,200 GP practices in England’s Midlands. That moves the thesis beyond whether clinicians will use an ambient scribe: the harder question is whether one vendor can become part of the operating layer of large health systems. Valuation reporting differs slightly by outlet. The Times puts the latest valuation at about $900 million, while Australian coverage describes Heidi as reaching roughly the $1 billion or unicorn threshold. The discrepancy likely reflects rounding and reporting conventions, not two separate financings. The more important signal is the financing structure itself. Using $240 million of non-dilutive capital lets Heidi finance expansion without selling the same amount of ownership at today’s valuation — a playbook increasingly relevant to rapidly growing software companies with enough revenue visibility to support structured capital. The financing puts the company’s total capital raised at roughly $90 million. Go.AI sells AI hardware appliances aimed particularly at banks and other regulated organizations that cannot casually move confidential data or sensitive workloads into external AI services. That makes this an infrastructure bet rather than another model-company wager. Banks increasingly want access to generative AI while preserving control over data residency, audit trails, security, and deployment architecture. Go.AI is trying to occupy the gap between public AI APIs and a fully bespoke internal stack by packaging compute and software into systems that institutions can run under their own governance. Competitive pressure will come from both directions: hyperscalers can offer private-cloud configurations, while server, chip, and enterprise-software companies can assemble their own on-premises AI stacks. Go.AI therefore has to win on deployment speed, regulatory fit, and operating simplicity rather than raw model capability. The size of the Series A suggests investors believe regulated AI deployment itself can become a meaningful product category. Funding Details

Axios describes the company as providing data infrastructure for AI agents — the layer that turns information on the open web into material software agents can retrieve and use programmatically. That may sound like plumbing, but plumbing becomes more valuable as agents move beyond chat interfaces. An AI system asked to research companies, monitor competitors, source products, qualify leads, or execute workflows needs fresh external data in a predictable structure. Model vendors can improve reasoning, but they do not automatically solve crawling, extraction, website changes, access reliability or data preparation. This is the deeper reason infrastructure investors continue financing companies around the model layer. As foundation models become easier to substitute, the differentiated asset can move to the systems that supply them with current information and connect them to real-world workflows. Firecrawl still faces a crowded field spanning web search, crawling, browser automation, and structured-data extraction, so its long-term position will depend on whether developers treat it as a default component rather than one interchangeable API among many. Baselayer’s challenge is that fraud, KYC, and identity verification already contain well-funded incumbents. Its opportunity is to build for a world in which the entity on the other side of a workflow may increasingly be software rather than a person. The company builds voice agents designed specifically to automate mortgage sales calls rather than offering a horizontal voice-AI platform for every industry. That focus is strategically significant. Voice generation is becoming cheaper and more widely available, so merely producing natural-sounding speech is unlikely to remain defensible. Vertical products instead need to understand industry terminology, connect with existing systems, handle escalation, operate within compliance requirements, and improve measurable conversion or labor economics. Mortgages are an attractive but demanding proving ground: high customer value supports meaningful software pricing, while the regulated nature of lending raises the cost of inaccurate or uncontrolled automation. Sector: Voice AI, mortgage technology, financial-services automation What Today’s Funding Activity Reveals The first pattern is capital concentration. Roughly four-fifths of the $1.379 billion in headline financing represented here went into Cyera, Snorkel, and Heidi. On an equity-only basis after stripping out Heidi’s $240 million non-dilutive facility, those three still account for roughly 75% of the selected capital. Investors are not spreading money evenly across the AI economy. They are concentrating it around companies with evidence of category leadership, unusually high growth, or strategically scarce infrastructure. The second pattern is that AI infrastructure has expanded beyond GPUs and data centers. Today’s deals define infrastructure much more broadly: Snorkel supplies the training and evaluation data; Firecrawl supplies external information to agents; Go.AI supplies controlled deployment environments; Cyera controls sensitive-data access; Baselayer addresses trust and fraud. Taken together, these financings suggest the investable AI stack is moving outward from compute into governance, context, verification and deployment. Third, vertical AI is being held to a different standard than it was two years ago. Heidi, Chamelio and Sela are not being financed merely because they insert a language model into healthcare, legal or lending workflows. Their investment cases increasingly depend on owning the surrounding process. In healthcare, that means integration with clinical systems and institutional deployment; in legal, it means privileged organizational context and workflow; in mortgages, it means compliance and conversion economics. Fourth, cybersecurity is becoming a direct beneficiary of agent adoption rather than a separate technology category. Cyera’s strategy of combining data governance with non-human identity management reflects a broader issue: autonomous software can only become more useful by receiving more permissions. Every additional permission creates another security decision. The value of the agent and the value of controlling the agent may therefore rise together. Cyera’s $12 billion-plus valuation is one of the strongest private-market expressions of that thesis so far. Finally, geography is more concentrated than the word “global” might imply in this particular 12-hour slice. The United States dominates the selected rounds, with Australia represented by Heidi and cross-border capital visible throughout the investor syndicates. That should not be read as evidence that European or emerging-market funding disappeared Tuesday: several sizable European and international deals surfaced in September 22 newsletters but traced back to September 21 or outside the strict cutoff and were therefore removed from this edition. Comparative Funding Table Startup Amount Raised Sector Funding Stage Lead Investors Country Cyera $400M Cybersecurity / AI security Series G extension Goldman Sachs Alternatives U.S. Snorkel AI $350M AI data / RL infrastructure Growth round Insight Partners, S32 U.S. Heidi Health $340M package ($100M equity + $240M facility) Clinical AI Series C + non-dilutive financing Blackbird; General Catalyst on facility Australia Go.AI $85M Private AI infrastructure Series A Updata Partners U.S. Firecrawl $75M AI-agent / web-data infrastructure Series B Smash Capital U.S. Baselayer $35M Fraud / financial infrastructure Series A M13 U.S. Chamelio $26M Legal AI Series A Entrée Capital U.S./Israel Ramona Optics $25M Life-science tools Series A ARCH Venture Partners U.S. Teal Health $22M Women’s health/diagnostics Series A .406 Ventures U.S. Sela $21M Voice AI/mortgage tech Seed + Series A Emergence Capital, Costanoa U.S. The table also shows why round size alone can mislead. Heidi’s headline $340 million is not economically equivalent to Snorkel’s $350 million financing because $240 million of Heidi’s package is non-dilutive. Likewise, Cyera’s $400 million arrives at a $12 billion-plus valuation and late-stage scale, while a $21 million check into Sela carries far more ownership and company-building significance at an earlier stage. Comparing venture rounds requires looking at capital structure, stage and strategic intent, not only the number in the headline. Strategic Takeaways for Founders and Investors For founders, the bar for “AI differentiation” is moving up quickly. Access to a capable model is becoming less persuasive as a fundraising story. Today’s financings reward companies that can explain what they control around the model: proprietary data production, regulated distribution, embedded workflow, identity and permissions, deployment architecture, physical instrumentation, or institutional relationships. Firecrawl, Snorkel, and Go.AI occupy different layers, but all three sell something the underlying model does not provide on its own. The best vertical-AI businesses are becoming workflow businesses. Founders should therefore measure outcomes that buyers actually budget for: clinician hours returned, mortgage conversion rates, legal work brought in-house, fraud losses reduced or deployment time shortened. A company whose value proposition collapses when inference prices fall faces commoditization. A company whose product gets more valuable as models get cheaper has a much stronger economic position. Treat security and governance as product surfaces, not compliance afterthoughts. Cyera’s financing shows how large the market can become when AI adoption creates a new class of access-control problem. For enterprise founders, the ability to explain what an agent can see, which tools it can call, and how its actions are audited may become part of the sales proposition rather than a box checked after deployment. Capital structure is becoming part of competitive strategy. Heidi’s combination of $100 million in equity with a $240 million non-dilutive facility is especially instructive. Companies with substantial revenue and predictable expansion requirements do not always need to fund every growth dollar by selling shares. Debt, structured facilities and other non-dilutive instruments can preserve founder and employee ownership — provided the business has the cash-generation profile to carry the obligation. Late-stage investors are paying for option value. Goldman Sachs’ investment in Cyera gives the company additional time before an IPO, more acquisition capacity and greater flexibility in deciding when to access public markets. For mature private companies, a strong balance sheet can therefore become competitive weaponry: it reduces pressure to list at an inconvenient moment and can turn the company into an acquirer while weaker competitors are still conserving cash. Investors, meanwhile, need to distinguish real infrastructure from temporary abstraction layers. Some AI tooling categories will be absorbed by model providers, cloud platforms or larger enterprise-software vendors. The stronger bets are likely to be products whose value grows with AI usage but whose function is difficult for a model provider to internalize: access governance, specialized proprietary data, regulated deployment, physical data generation and deeply integrated industry workflows. The biggest pricing risk is at the application layer. If two products use similar foundation models, operate on the same customer data and connect to the same systems, switching costs can deteriorate quickly. The financing environment is therefore increasingly rewarding companies that can answer a hard question with specificity: what becomes harder for a customer to replace as your company gets bigger? Conclusion September 22’s funding activity is not simply another day in which “AI got most of the money.” The more useful interpretation is that venture capital is becoming more discriminating about which parts of the AI economy deserve durable margins. Cyera is being financed because autonomous software makes data and identity control harder. Snorkel is being financed because better models require harder-to-produce training and evaluation data. Go.AI is addressing institutions that cannot simply push sensitive workloads into public AI services. Firecrawl addresses the problem of giving agents dependable external information. Heidi, Chamelio and Sela are attempting to turn general AI capability into industry-specific operating systems. Meanwhile, Ramona Optics and Teal Health show that differentiated physical and healthcare products can still draw serious institutional capital without competing in the foundation-model race. The day’s capital concentration matters just as much as the sector mix. With close to four-fifths of headline commitments going to three companies, the market is not behaving like an indiscriminate technology boom. It is behaving like a market willing to pay extraordinary prices for a small number of perceived control points while forcing everyone else to prove the economics at Series A and Series B. That is the signal founders and investors should carry forward. As model intelligence becomes more abundant, scarcity migrates elsewhere: toward trusted data, permissioning, distribution, regulated deployment, specialized workflows, and physical systems that generate information the digital world cannot manufacture by itself. The next valuable startup may still use the same models as everyone else. What matters is whether it owns something around those models that everyone else still needs. 0 Shares

funding_news.full_text:
#United States #San Francisco #Insight Partners #Snorkel AI #Data Factory Snorkel AI Secures $350 Million to Advance Frontiers in AI Data Development On September 22, 2026, Snorkel AI, a pivotal player in frontier AI development, announced a significant funding milestone of $350 million, which elevates its valuation to $3.5 billion. This funding round was co-led by Insight Partners and S32, with noteworthy participation from various existing and new investors, including Addition, March Capital, Blumberg Capital, Allegis Capital, and several others. The capital raise underscores Snorkel’s trajectory toward expanding its agentic data factory, which is responsible for producing the underlying data and environments that fuel advanced AI labs globally.



The broader landscape of AI data is witnessing a fundamental shift. In prior eras, developing AI was largely about managing labeling tasks with a workforce-driven approach. However, today’s complex frontier systems demand far more sophisticated capabilities—termed Data 2.0—which entail handling expert tasks that often take skilled human workers days to accomplish. Designing effective solutions in this context has become a research-intensive endeavor, where quality and complexity are critical determinants of value.



To rise to this challenge, Snorkel has established a fresh paradigm for data creation and management. Since launching its Data-as-a-Service platform in September 2025, the company has demonstrated significant growth and relevance in the industry. Partnering with leading AI labs and major enterprises, Snorkel focuses on delivering high-quality data solutions that underpin frontier model evaluation and training processes.



Rooted in the prestigious Stanford AI Lab, which birthed the company nearly a decade ago, Snorkel was founded by a team known for its pioneering work in data-centric AI. This legacy is exemplified by a substantial body of research, including over 250 peer-reviewed papers that collectively have gained more than 25,000 citations.



“The frontier of AI needs research partners who are at the cutting edge of data science,” stated Alex Ratner, co-founder and CEO of Snorkel AI. “Snorkel was designed to be that partner—drawing on over ten years of research and development to be the leading lab for agentic data.”



Lonne Jaffe, Managing Director at Insight Partners, noted, “Snorkel’s rigorous approach to AI data and environments becomes an increasingly critical factor in developing capable and trustworthy AI systems. Their remarkable growth at scale is a testament to the value they deliver.”



According to Andy Harrison, CEO and General Partner at S32, “Snorkel’s unique expert-agentic environments create a synergistic relationship between human skills and AI, offering quality data at unprecedented speeds. This capability enables a new era of efficiency and precision in model development.”



With the fresh funding, Snorkel AI plans to greatly enhance its agentic data factory's capacity to keep pace with demand, strategically invest in vertical and enterprise-level AI solutions, and further its research in new domains and modalities. The company has also committed to enriching its open research initiatives, including the establishment of programs like its Open Benchmarks Grants.



In summary, Snorkel AI’s recent funding round captures the company’s aggressive pursuit of innovation and leadership within the AI landscape, paving the way for its continued contributions to high-performing AI systems for various industries, including healthcare, law, and software engineering.

company_assessment.market_position: Snorkel AI is a privately held frontier AI data lab founded in 2019 out of Stanford AI Lab and headquartered in Palo Alto, California. It positions itself as a research-led partner to frontier AI labs and large enterprises, supplying expert-curated training data, evaluation systems, and runnable environments for frontier models and agents. The company achieved unicorn status in 2021 at a $1 billion valuation and a $1.3 billion valuation in its May 2025 Series D, with ARR growing from $36.8M in 2024 to $148M in 2025. Customers and partners include Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, BNY, Harvey, Apple, Intel, and Stanford Medicine, and the company serves 30+ Fortune 500 attendees at its SnorkelCon user conference.

strengths.details: As foundation models saturate general web data, performance gains shift to high-quality, expert-curated domain data and RL environments. Snorkel's positioning as a 'frontier AI data lab' with products like GDPval+ (100+ occupations) and Terminal-Bench 2.0 puts it at the center of the next training-data cycle, where budgets are large and alternatives are scarce.
strengths.headline: Specialized data is the bottleneck for frontier AI

strengths.details: Snorkel publishes and maintains category-defining benchmarks (Terminal-Bench, SWE-Bench+, BigLaw Bench, Continual Learning Bench, Agents' Last Exam). Owning the yardsticks for evaluating frontier models creates credibility and inbound demand from labs and enterprises that need to be measured against them, funneling prospects into the Snorkel Flow and DaaS offerings.
strengths.headline: Benchmark authority compounds into commercial pull

strengths.details: The Expert Data-as-a-Service platform pays domain experts (top earners $3,000+/week) and feeds them into a growing project pipeline. As more experts join, Snorkel can take on more concurrent enterprise engagements across more verticals, increasing delivery capacity without proportionally scaling internal headcount.
strengths.headline: Expert network creates flywheel and moat

strengths.details: Strategic distribution via AWS Marketplace, Microsoft for Startups Pegasus, Azure integration, and Accenture Ventures' Project Spotlight gives Snorkel a low-cost channel into Fortune 500 regulated buyers. Each partnership compounds the existing enterprise sales motion and supports land-and-expand into financial services, healthcare, and legal verticals.
strengths.headline: Hyperscaler and SI partnerships unlock distribution

weakness.details: Customers like OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, and Microsoft are aggressively building internal data curation and evaluation teams as they scale. As these labs mature their internal tooling, the reliance on third-party data labs like Snorkel could decline, threatening the core revenue base that drove the 4x ARR jump to $148M.
weakness.headline: Frontier labs could internalize data capabilities

weakness.details: A large portion of revenue (Expert DaaS, custom data development, custom agent builds) is delivered via human-expert labor and forward-deployed engineering rather than pure software. This services-heavy mix typically caps gross margins well below pure SaaS peers and makes the business harder to scale efficiently as headcount grows.
weakness.headline: Services-heavy model limits margin scalability

weakness.details: Headcount expanded from 352 (2024) to ~776 (2026) before a 13% reduction in September 2025. This whipsaw in workforce planning, coinciding with the Series D raise, suggests capital efficiency and unit economics may be weaker than headline ARR growth implies, increasing execution risk on the path to profitability.
weakness.headline: Layoffs after rapid hiring reveal miscalibrated growth

weakness.details: Revenue depends heavily on a small set of frontier AI labs and large enterprises (Apple, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, BNY). Any pullback in frontier-model training budgets or enterprise AI spend could create disproportionate revenue shocks, especially given multi-year contract structures that may face renewal pressure.
weakness.headline: Concentrated customer base in volatile frontier AI

competitive_moat.details: Snorkel has accumulated a catalog of expert-curated, rubric-validated benchmark-grade datasets (Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-Bench+, CUA-Bench+, GDPval+, BigLaw Bench) and proprietary quality-control methodologies (calibrated expert signal, multi-layer verification). These assets are co-developed with frontier labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft) and are refreshed quarterly, creating a compounding lead that generic crowdsourced data pipelines cannot easily replicate.

Founded out of Stanford AI Lab with co-founders Alexander Ratner, Chris Re, Braden Hancock, Henry Ehrenberg, Paroma Varma, and Vincent Sunn Chen, plus Chief Scientist Fred Sala (PhD CS, UW-Madison, DARPA Young Faculty Award recipient 2024). The team carries deep relationships across frontier AI labs and academic institutions (Stanford, Berkeley, UW-Madison), and runs an Expert Community platform funneling thousands of paid domain experts into its pipeline.

Proprietary methodology combining programmatic labeling, calibrated expert review, rubric-based evaluation, and programmatic verification. Active publication record across arXiv (Agents' Last Exam, RIFT taxonomy, RLVR, JudgmentBench, insurance underwriting benchmarking) builds thought leadership and shapes evaluation standards adopted by frontier labs.

Embedded distribution through Microsoft Azure (Microsoft for Startups Pegasus Program, Snorkel Flow integration), AWS Marketplace (ISV Accelerate Program), and Accenture Ventures' Project Spotlight providing access to enterprise client networks. Hyperscaler co-sell motions materially reduce customer acquisition friction in the enterprise tier.

The Harbor open-source framework for RL environments and OpenEnv's transition to community governance (June 2026, with Meta-PyTorch, Nvidia, Microsoft, Hugging Face on the coordination committee) positions Snorkel as a standards-setter. Once third-party agents and labs build on these environments and benchmarks, switching costs rise.

The Expert Community platform pays domain experts (top contributors earning over $3,000 weekly) and supplies both customer engagements and Snorkel's own benchmark catalog. The SARG reading group and SnorkelCon (30+ Fortune 500 attendees in 2024) compound researcher mindshare, but network effects are still maturing relative to mature two-sided platforms.

key_risks.details: Snorkel cut 13% of headcount in September 2025 to focus on the Data-as-a-Service model, after roughly doubling the workforce from 352 to ~776 within roughly a year. Combined with the recent Series D raise, the layoff suggests prior hiring outpaced sustainable revenue scaling and that the operating model is being retooled mid-flight.
key_risks.headline: 13% workforce reduction signals operational recalibration

key_risks.details: Headline customers include OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, Apple, Intel, and BNY. Concentration among a small number of frontier-model developers creates revenue cliff risk if any major customer reduces external data spend or builds equivalent internal capabilities.
key_risks.headline: Heavy reliance on frontier AI labs as customers

key_risks.details: Scale AI is explicitly identified as a competitor with comparable frontier-lab offerings, and Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth plus Microsoft Azure tooling provide commoditized alternatives. Snorkel's premium positioning on expert-curated data must continually justify higher pricing against well-funded competitors.
key_risks.headline: Competition from Scale AI and hyperscalers is intense

key_risks.details: Major revenue streams (Expert DaaS, custom data development, custom agent builds) are delivered through expert labor and forward-deployed engineering rather than pure self-serve software. This mix typically caps gross margins, limits operating leverage as the business scales, and slows the path to durable profitability.
key_risks.headline: Services-heavy revenue mix constrains software economics

key_risks.details: Snorkel sells through discovery phases, pilots, and staged rollouts with custom scoping per customer, rather than a self-serve product. While this supports high-ACV enterprise deals, it caps how quickly revenue can scale without proportionally adding sales and delivery headcount.
key_risks.headline: Custom enterprise sales motion limits scalability

key_risks.details: The leadership team is anchored by Stanford AI Lab alumni (CEO Alexander Ratner, co-founders Chris Re, Braden Hancock, Henry Ehrenberg, Paroma Varma, Chief Scientist Fred Sala). Departures of a few founders or senior researchers could weaken both research credibility and enterprise relationships that depend on the Stanford pedigree.
key_risks.headline: Key-person and Stanford talent concentration risk

key_highlights.details: Revenue grew from $36.8M ARR in 2024 to $148M ARR in 2025, indicating strong product-market fit in enterprise and frontier AI data services.
key_highlights.headline: ARR quadrupled year-over-year to $148M

key_highlights.details: Customers include OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, Apple, Intel, Stanford Medicine, BNY, and Harvey, spanning frontier labs, regulated enterprises, and vertical AI specialists.

key_highlights.details: Founded in 2019 out of Stanford AI Lab by Alexander Ratner, Chris Re, Braden Hancock, Henry Ehrenberg, and Paroma Varma, with Chief Scientist Fred Sala holding a 2024 DARPA Young Faculty Award.

customer_concentration.details: Named enterprise customers span multiple industries and geographies — Apple, Intel, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, Stanford Medicine, BNY, Harvey, and an unnamed global bank — indicating that no single customer dominates disclosed logos. However, the dual-segment focus on a small number of frontier AI labs (Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft) plus a handful of marquee enterprise anchors (BNY, Harvey) creates meaningful concentration at the top of the customer pyramid even though revenue is not formally disclosed by customer. Engagement economics point to multi-year enterprise contracts and high-stakes specialized-agent work, which raises switching costs but also magnifies the revenue impact of any single anchor churn event. The DaaS catalog (Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-Bench+, GDPval+, BigLaw Bench) is sold across many buyers and broadens the long-tail base, partially offsetting lab-segment concentration.

launches.full_text: Thrilled to see Meta — Thomas Scialom, PhD, Grégoire Mialon, and the brilliant Meta Agents team — launch 𝗚𝗮𝗶𝗮𝟮, built within their new 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗥𝗟 𝗘𝗻𝘃𝗶𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 platform! Gaia2 sets a new bar for agent evaluation by testing models in dynamic, real-world conditions, where APIs timeout, priorities shift, and unexpected friction derails even the smartest systems. The ARE RL Environment framework is designed to 𝗿𝘂𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 in environments that look and feel like the real world. (After all, in this day and age, winning IMO medals is a challenge of the past. It’s deploying models into the rich, long tail messiness of the real world that’s the golden frontier.) Two years ago, Meta pioneered this vision with 𝗚𝗔𝗜𝗔, a benchmark we were proud to help build. Since then, we’ve had the privilege of collaborating again on 𝗚𝗮𝗶𝗮𝟮 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗔𝗥𝗘, creating the diverse scenarios and data that helped bring these ideas to life — with a team at Meta that recognized the importance of RL environments long before they became the hot new kid on the block. We’ve always believed that training models is only half the story. Measuring them — with the right objectives, in the right environments — is just as critical. industries.name: Synthetic Data & Data Augmentation for Foundation Models

launches.full_text:
Surge AI: The $24B Data Engine Teaching AGI Real Human Taste 🤖 Meet Edwin Chen: the 37-year-old who bootstrapped a $24B AI startup with $0 in VC

In partnership with

(5 minutes)

Hi 👋, this is the Today in AI Newsletter: The weekly newsletter bringing you one step closer to building your own startup.

We analyze a cool, industry-shaping AI startup every week, with a full breakdown of what they do, how they make money, how much they’ve raised, and the opportunity ahead.

Let’s get to the good stuff in this email:

💡 This startup is the human-data engine behind frontier labs like OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral AI & more.

📈 They’ve bootstrapped to $1B+ in revenue , stayed profitable from day one , and now manage a core team of about 250 people .

🚀 They are now preparing their first-ever external raise of up to $1B, targeting a ~$24B valuation - founder Edwin Chen owns ~75% of the company and sits on an estimated $18B net worth as the youngest member of the Forbes 400 (#55).

So what’s the startup and who are the founders behind it? Here’s the story of Surge AI 📈

Surge AI was founded by Edwin Chen in 2020 to build high-quality human data that trains and evaluates the most advanced AI models.

Instead of cheap crowd work that tags cat photos, Surge runs a curated marketplace of elite annotators who handle things like RLHF, safety, reasoning, taste, and multi-step agent behavior. 🤖

Their mission is to raise AGI like you would raise a child so it grows up curious, imaginative, and aligned with rich human values, not just optimized for leaderboard scores & clickbait.

On the product side, that looks like:

Humans and models working together, with models generating and self-labeling, then Surgers reviewing, correcting, and adversarially testing them.

Complex RL environments that feel like video game worlds filled with tools like Slack, Gmail, GitHub, spreadsheets, and CRM systems, where agents learn to handle real productivity tasks across long timelines.

Surge’s key idea: the ceiling of your model is set by the quality of your human data.

You can’t train a master chef by giving them a million recipes for boiling water.

You train them on rare, expert recipes, subtle flavor calls, and detailed feedback.

Surge gives that level of training signal to AI.

Backstory 👀

Edwin Chen grew up in Crystal River, Florida, in the back of his parents’ Chinese-Thai-American restaurant, Peking Garden.

He did homework near the cash register while his parents worked shifts, and he fell in love with math in the eighth grade, when calculus made the world feel legible.

That curiosity took him to Choate, then to MIT at 17, where he studied math, linguistics, and computer science and even worked on decoding an Incan knot language.

He was obsessed with how humans encode meaning into patterns, whether it was language, symbols, or data.

After MIT, Edwin went deep into applied math and ML.

He did algorithmic work at Peter Thiel’s Clarium Capital, then held ML roles at Google, Facebook, Twitter, and Dropbox, shipped recommendation systems, search, and content moderation.

This is where the frustration started.

At Facebook and Twitter, he watched outside vendors deliver datasets that were slow, and off-target.

Basic tasks like distinguishing a coffee shop from a hospital would come back with ridiculous errors.

The teams were spending millions on data that made models worse. Edwin saw a huge waste of human potential.

Smart people inside big tech were building powerful models, while outsourced annotators with weak tooling and low pay were tagging data with almost no context.

Around 2020, right after GPT-3 landed, Edwin snapped.

He realized the entire industry treated data labeling as a commodity cost center, when it should be a core R&D function.

So he quit, moved to Manhattan, and decided to build the opposite of the standard playbook.

High-end human data, top talent, premium pricing, and no VCs telling him to chase vanity metrics.

The Hustle 🤑

Edwin wrote the first version of Surge AI’s MVP in about one month, mostly solo, in a small San Francisco apartment.

The product was simple at first. A platform where ML teams could define rich labeling tasks, and route them to a hand-picked pool of annotators.

He used savings from his decade in big tech, a "couple million" by his own count, and set three strict rules for the company:

No external financing. No burning cash. No low-value, simple orders.

If a task looked like commodity tagging for pennies, Surge would decline it.

Edwin then used one of his most underrated assets. His blog.

He had built a reputation in the data science community through long technical posts, like the famous "Pop vs. Soda" map that went viral from his Twitter days.

He turned that distribution into a GTM channel.

Early Surge customers came through deep content aimed at serious data scientists.

He wrote about data quality, annotation philosophy, and AGI alignment.

From there, the team focused on building the highest-quality data annotation workforce on the planet.

To join Surge Force, annotators had to pass a brutal funnel.

Strong professional background. Five trial writing tasks. Review and approval by senior annotators.

They pulled in professors from Stanford, Princeton, and Harvard, lawyers, finance pros, and native speakers across 50+ languages and dialects.

For many roles, the acceptance bar is described as harder than getting into an Ivy League. Surge paid accordingly.

Contractors earn $20–$40+ per hour, with some tasks paying 30–40 cents per working minute, far above other gig platforms.

Inside the platform, Surge’s own ML models track keystrokes, speed, accuracy, and agreement patterns, constantly updating per-annotator trust scores.

Bad or lazy work is detected and removed.

Surge also leaned into adversarial work.

They run AI red teams, including projects with groups like Redwood Research, where experts try to trick models into sneaky behavior, then label and fix the failure modes.

Quality is the product.

That contrarian take turned into a huge advantage when Meta invested heavily in rival Scale AI and took a huge stake.

Labs like Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI did not want their most sensitive data and roadmaps flowing through a vendor effectively tied to a competitor.

They needed a neutral, independent supplier.

Surge was sitting there, profitable, battle-tested, and fully independent.

Stats 📊

From a cold start in 2020, Surge AI scaled to about $1.2B in revenue in 2024, beating Scale AI’s ~$870M over the same period.

The company has roughly 250 people including part-time and consultants, which means close to $9M+ in revenue per person.

On top of that, Surge coordinates a global workforce of over 1M contractors, with about 50,000 considered expert, high-skill Surgers.

Surge has been profitable almost from day one, growing into what many consider the most capital-efficient AI infrastructure company in Silicon Valley.

It has done this with $0 in outside funding so far. Edwin still owns roughly 75% of the company.

At a current estimated valuation of ~$24B, that gives him a personal net worth of ~$18B. In 2025, he entered the Forbes 400 at #55, as the youngest person on the list.

Customer spend shows how central Surge has become.

Meta reportedly spends over $150M per year with Surge.

Google spends over $100M per year.

Other major labs, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, and xAI, rely on Surge for RLHF, model evaluation, and safety-critical pipelines.

Surge often charges 50% to 10x more than other providers.

They’re so good because their data improves model performance in ways you cannot reach with cheap labeling.

Before you go 👋

Thank you for reading. Know someone who'd love this newsletter? Share the love. 🌟

launches.full_text:
Deadline: Ongoing Applications are open for the Surge AI Research Fellowship Program 2026. The Surge AI Fellowship is founded on a singular conviction: progress in artificial intelligence must be grounded in quality at the highest level. In recent years, AI systems have achieved remarkable breakthroughs, yet they continue to reveal critical limitations when applied to academic research. To address this, Surge AI is convening leading scholars and practitioners, PhD-level experts across disciplines, to guide the development of models capable of performing at the frontier of human knowledge. Their initial efforts are concentrated in the STEM fields, where rigor, precision, and depth of understanding are indispensable. Their vision is a future where AI is both safe and accurate—advancing human knowledge while meeting the most exacting standards of scholarship. To realize this, they are committed to ensuring that the world’s brightest minds are the ones leading this initiative. Responsibilities Fellows are entrusted with advancing the frontier of evaluating model development. They focus on systematically identifying the limitations and failure modes of current AI systems, designing rigorous challenges to probe their boundaries, and collaborating with Surge AI leadership to propose and refine strategies for improvement. This program complements, rather than replaces, ongoing scholarly or professional commitments. Fellows retain full autonomy in setting their schedules, with compensation provided on an hourly basis. Benefits You’ll gain access to some of the most highly sought-after projects on the Surge platform and contribute to high-profile, deeply impactful work that is exclusive to their select team. In this role, you’ll collaborate closely with the Surge leadership team, where your feedback is not only welcomed but essential. They offer competitive pay, the flexibility to set your own schedule, and they do not require exclusivity, allowing you to balance other commitments alongside your work with them. Eligibility They welcome leading scholars and practitioners, PhD-level experts across disciplines to apply.

Applications may be from anywhere in the world. Application If you’re interested in learning more about the opportunity, email researchfellows@surgehq.ai with a CV or any relevant work samples. For more information, visit Surge AI Fellowship Program.
