Best Practices, Challenges, and Limitations Managing human data labeling effectively is as crucial as the modeling itself. This section looks at what AI teams have learned about ensuring quality, where human labeling works best (and where it can falter), and the limitations and pitfalls to watch out for. Quality Assurance is King: A recurring theme is that quality matters far more than quantity in labeling. Successful AI projects implement multiple layers of QA to make sure labels are accurate and consistent. Some best practices include inserting gold standard examples (with known correct labels) into the task stream to monitor annotator accuracy, performing spot checks on a sample of the work by expert reviewers, and using consensus (having multiple people label the same item and resolving differences). For instance, Appen’s platform requires workers to pass a quiz and continues testing them on hidden questions as they work, removing those who fall below accuracy thresholds. Many vendors will also do a “calibration phase” at a project’s start: the client and labeler team go over a batch of data together to align on how it should be labeled, refining guidelines until everyone is on the same page (Sama and CloudFactory often do this). The lesson is that you can’t just hand data to humans and expect perfection – you need a process to continuously verify and improve their output. Selecting and Training Labelers: Not everyone is suited to be a labeler for a given task. Effective projects use careful screening and training to get the right people. This might mean giving applicants a test (e.g., ask a series of sample labeling questions and see how well they do), or only selecting annotators with certain backgrounds (like only biology majors to label medical text). For long-term projects, labelers often have to go through training modules or even formal certification. A classic example: search engine evaluation projects (like those run via Appen or Google’s Rater program) require labelers to read a 100+ page guideline and pass an exam before they can rate queries. In 2025, companies are investing even more in screening – some use AI to evaluate labeler candidates’ skill sets, some do trial tasks with detailed feedback. The goal is to filter in the best, filter out the rest early on. And once on the job, providing ongoing feedback to labelers (like “you missed this detail, here’s the correct approach”) helps them improve. Treating labelers as a genuine part of the team and communicating with them can dramatically raise quality and consistency. Proven Methods for Consistency: One challenge is keeping labeling consistent across a large group. If 50 people are working on the same dataset, you want them all to apply labels the same way. Techniques to ensure this include: very clear and detailed written guidelines with examples for every rule; regular team meetings or updates if new ambiguities are discovered (so everyone hears the resolution); and overlap and review, where a fraction of tasks are labeled by two people and any disagreement is reconciled, thereby catching divergent interpretations early. Many providers have a notion of an “annotation ontology” or taxonomy that is carefully defined and version-controlled, so labelers are always referring to the source of truth. Some platforms like Labelbox allow embedding these instructions into the interface for easy reference. The best projects also encourage labelers to ask questions – e.g., via Slack or an online forum – when unsure, and have a lead analyst or project manager provide prompt clarifications. In effect, managing a labeling project can be like managing a distributed team of junior employees: it needs coordination, communication, and supervision. Costs and Throughput: Labeling can be surprisingly expensive and time-consuming. We’ve seen that certain high-end tasks (like expert RLHF feedback) can cost dozens of dollars per example. Even simpler annotation, when multiplied by millions of data points, adds up quickly. One best practice is to do a pilot project – label a small sample of data first to get a sense of cost, speed, and quality – before committing to labeling an entire huge dataset. This pilot can surface any issues in guidelines or estimator whether the vendor can meet your quality bar. It’s also wise to compare pricing models: some providers charge per label, others per hour. Depending on your task, one or the other may be more cost-effective. For example, if tasks vary in complexity, an hourly model might be better (so you’re not overpaying for easy ones or underpaying for hard ones). Keep in mind that LLM-related tasks are on the high end of the cost spectrum. Expert networks bill by the hour and the published bands are steep: micro1 lists $100 to $200+ per hour for frontier expert projects against $15 to $40 for general annotation, and that is what the contractor sees before the vendor adds its own margin. Simpler annotation still costs cents per item, so the same dataset can differ in price by three orders of magnitude depending on who has to look at it. The key is that budgeting for labeling should be an integral part of your AI development plan, not an afterthought. Many AI projects have learned the hard way that getting the data ready can eat a large chunk of the project budget and timeline. Where Human Labeling Shines: Humans excel at tasks that require understanding context, nuance, or subjective judgment. For instance, determining the sentiment of a sentence, or whether a joke is funny, or if an image is appealing – these are things people can do instinctively that are still tricky for AI. Humans are also great at dealing with novelty and edge cases: if something totally unexpected appears in the data, a person can adapt on the fly and handle it, whereas an AI might be completely confused. Human labelers can learn and apply complex criteria (like multi-factor rubrics) and can notice subtle patterns. They are also the gold standard for evaluating AI output quality – an AI might be able to generate an answer, but only a human can truly judge if that answer would please another human or if it’s written in a naturally good style. Moreover, humans bring ethical and common-sense considerations; they can tell if content is inappropriate or if a translation, while literal, doesn’t make sense culturally. Where It Can Fail: On the flip side, human labeling is prone to certain failure modes. Human error and bias are big ones. Labelers might misunderstand instructions or have personal biases that skew their labels. For example, studies have shown that crowdsourced labelers can exhibit biases (cultural, gender, etc.) that then get baked into the AI. If not caught, these errors propagate. There’s also the issue of inconsistency – two people might label the same item differently. Without proper consensus or adjudication, the dataset can become noisy. Another issue is scalability under tight timelines: if you suddenly need 1 million labels in a week, rushing can lead to corners being cut (either by labelers or by using too many new, untested workers). Task difficulty is a limitation too; some tasks might simply be beyond the capability of non-specialist labelers. For instance, asking crowd workers to label complex legal documents for accuracy is likely to fail – you’d need actual lawyers, which are harder to source in large numbers. One subtle pitfall is “reward gaming” or instruction gaming: if your labeling instructions or reward model have loopholes, labelers (or even AI agents trying to maximize a reward) might exploit them. For example, if labelers are told their performance is measured by agreement with a certain heuristic, they might focus on that metric at the expense of true quality. In RLHF, if the reward model is poorly aligned, the AI might learn to give answers that score high but aren’t genuinely useful – essentially hacking the feedback signal. To mitigate this, companies rotate labelers, periodically update instructions, and use checks like inter-rater agreement measures to detect when something is off-kilter. Ethical and Logistical Challenges: The human side of AI development raises ethical questions. Are labelers being paid fairly? Are their working conditions good? Do they face psychological harm from reviewing traumatic content? These concerns became public after the Sama reporting above put real payslips on the record. Leading providers are now moving toward fair labor practices, not just for morality but because it correlates with better quality (a well-treated, well-trained workforce is more motivated and accurate). In fact, clients are beginning to ask vendors about how they treat workers. It’s plausible that in the future, AI companies will choose “ethically sourced” data annotation as a selling point. On the logistical side, privacy is a big challenge – if labelers are seeing private or proprietary data, measures must be in place to prevent leaks. Best practices include having labelers sign strong NDAs, using secure annotation platforms (no downloading data locally), perhaps even having work done on-premises or in a VPC for ultra-sensitive data. For example, Scale AI achieved FedRAMP Moderate accreditation to handle US government data securely. Some projects will require that labelers are in specific jurisdictions (for legal compliance). Ensuring all these boxes are ticked adds complexity. Active Learning and Efficiency: To address cost and time, many teams use active learning strategies – essentially, let the model help decide what needs labeling. Rather than labeling everything blindly, you can run a model on your dataset first and have it predict labels or scores, then have humans focus on the cases where the model is least confident or likely wrong. This way, you spend human effort only where it adds the most value. This approach was highlighted in a 2025 case study for scaling LLM output review: OpenAI was generating thousands of outputs, then using a reward model and other heuristics to filter out the majority of low-quality ones, so that humans only had to rank the top ~20% of candidate responses. They even trained a classifier to detect when the AI was trying to game the reward (reward hacking) so those instances could be caught. Such model-in-the-loop approaches drastically reduce the number of human labels needed while maintaining training efficacy. The labeled data you do get is higher-quality too, because humans spent more time on the tough cases instead of wasting time on easy ones. Utilizing techniques like this – auto-labeling plus human correction, uncertainty sampling, etc. – is increasingly seen as a best practice. It’s a collaboration: let AI handle the first pass, then have humans polish the results. The outcome is a more efficient pipeline where each human label carries more weight in improving the model. Continuous Monitoring: Even after a dataset is labeled and a model is trained, the job isn’t done. Model performance needs to be continuously monitored, and new labeling tasks often emerge (e.g., labeling errors the model makes in production, handling new types of input data, or updating the dataset as real-world conditions change). One challenge is label drift – over time, the definition of labels or the distribution of data might shift, making old labels less relevant. For instance, in a few years the standard for what content is considered “hate speech” might evolve, or a model might start seeing new slang that wasn’t in the original data. Having a process to regularly review and refresh labels (a “human in the loop” maintenance cycle) is important to keep models on track. Many top AI firms now have permanent labeling or data curation teams for this reason, as part of their ML operations. In short, human data labeling is powerful but not plug-and-play. It requires thoughtful management: picking the right people, giving them good instructions and tools, maintaining quality aggressively, respecting their well-being, and integrating their work tightly into the model development loop. When done right, it’s an enormous competitive advantage – enabling models to reach levels of performance and safety they never could with raw data alone. When done poorly, it can lead to wasted effort, biased models, or even PR nightmares. As the industry matures, we’re seeing a convergence on best practices and higher standards, which is a win-win for AI companies and the humans behind the AI. 6. Future Outlook: AI Agents, Automation, and Evolving Roles Looking ahead to the next few years (2026 and beyond), the AI data labeling industry is poised to both grow and transform. The consensus is that humans will remain an indispensable part of the AI training loop, but how they contribute will evolve significantly. Several key trends are shaping the future of this field: Increased Automation and “AI Agents” in Labeling: Ironically, AI is starting to assist in the task of labeling data for AI. We’ve already discussed model-assisted labeling where AI pre-labels a large portion of the data. The next step is more autonomous AI agents that can handle parts of the annotation workflow end-to-end. For example, an AI system might automatically detect which data points are easy and label them without human input, only forwarding the tricky ones to humans. We can imagine an AI agent that monitors an annotation project and dynamically assigns work: it might say “I’m 99% sure about these 1000 images – I’ll mark them as done; these 50 need a human to double-check.” In fact, some modern pipelines are getting close to this, with AI models in a sort of managerial role for labeling. As one report noted, the goal is for AI to handle the repetitive 80% of cases and leave only the edge 20% to people. We also see AI agents helping with quality control – for instance, an LLM judge model can be used to evaluate model outputs at scale, mimicking human evaluators. OpenAI has found that GPT-4-based judges agree with human raters about 80% of the time on which outputs are better, at a fraction of the cost. This doesn’t eliminate humans (because that remaining 20% and calibration still need humans), but it points to a more efficient future. Another angle is using AI agents for real-time human-in-the-loop systems. Imagine a deployed AI that knows when to ask for help: e.g., a self-driving car’s vision AI might flag a frame and query a remote human “Is there a pedestrian in this image? I’m not confident.” The human answers, and the AI proceeds. This kind of setup is already being prototyped – essentially turning the labeling process into an on-demand service during model operation. It blurs the line between training and inference. For data labeling companies, it means they may offer 24/7 on-demand human backup for AI agents. Some are building capabilities for very low-latency responses, so that an AI can seamlessly pull a human for help when needed (say, under a second for certain applications). Evolution of Labeler Roles – From Labelers to AI Auditors: As AI takes over the easy parts of annotation, the role of humans will shift towards the highest value parts. Repetitive, mindless labeling (like drawing 10,000 boxes around cars) is gradually diminishing (those are being automated by things like SAM). Instead, humans will be focusing on quality control, edge cases, and providing expertise. The term “data labeler” might broaden into roles like AI auditor, AI evaluator, or AI safety specialist. These people won’t just blindly label data; they will critically assess model behavior, devise new tests, and ensure the AI is aligned with human values. We already see this with some providers offering red-teaming services (expert labelers who try to break the model and then label those failure modes for retraining). In the future, a typical human-in-the-loop might spend more time analyzing model outputs and giving high-level feedback than doing simple annotations. It’s a move from “assembly line worker” to “craftsman” or “inspector” in a sense. The volume of data per project might decrease, but the value of each labeled data point will be higher because it’s targeting a specific weakness or fine-tuning a model on something subtle. For data labeling companies, this means upskilling their workforce. Many are already investing in training labelers to have basic ML understanding, better critical thinking, and domain knowledge, so they can effectively collaborate with AI tools and spot issues. Domain Specialization and Consulting: As noted, the trend is toward quality over quantity, which also means domain-specific data is king. A few years ago, having millions of generic labeled examples was a selling point. Now, AI labs want smaller but expertly-curated datasets. That means labeling providers are becoming more like consultants or partners in designing the data strategy. They might advise a client on what data would most improve their model, not just provide the labels. Some firms now offer “data curation” or “model evaluation as a service” in addition to labeling. For example, a provider might analyze a model’s errors and then help collect a targeted dataset to address those errors. We can expect this high-level involvement to grow. The best providers in 2026 might be those who have built pools of specialized talent (like Surge’s mathematicians or iMerit’s medical coders) and can deploy them with a mix of automation to produce very insightful training data, not just raw labels. Continuous Labeling and Active Learning Loops: The workflow of the future is continuous and integrated. Rather than a one-off labeling project that outputs a dataset, we’ll have ongoing loops where models in production continuously send back data to be labeled or reviewed by humans, and then updated models are rolled out – an active learning cycle. Data labeling platforms are merging with ML ops platforms; providers like Scale AI and Labelbox already provide model testing, embeddings-based data selection, etc., along with labeling. This integration will deepen. For AI practitioners, it means your relationship with labelers/providers becomes long-term and iterative. You might always have a trickle of data being labeled each day to keep your model sharp, rather than a big dump of labels upfront. Ethical and Regulatory Factors: Looking forward, there will likely be more oversight and standards around data labeling. The EU AI Act, for instance, may require transparency about how training data was annotated and ensure that it was done in a lawful, ethical manner. We could see the emergence of certifications for fair labor or data handling in the annotation industry. Providers that have been proactive about worker welfare (like Sama or iMerit) could set the bar, as mentioned. Also, data privacy laws might force data to be labeled within certain jurisdictions (e.g., European data labeled by EU-based workers to comply with GDPR). This could lead to more localization – providers setting up teams in specific countries to meet data residency requirements. Governments themselves are now buying labeling at industrial scale. The U.S. National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency awarded a data labeling contract worth up to $708 million over seven years to the startup Enabled Intelligence in November 2025, to train computer vision models on satellite and airborne imagery - Breaking Defense. This might create “approved vendor” lists or security-clearance requirements for labelers on sensitive projects. All this points to an industry maturing and professionalizing, with more formal structures. Consolidation and New Entrants: The market will likely continue to evolve through mergers and new startups. We’ve already seen consolidation: Appen acquiring Figure Eight, Telus acquiring Lionbridge AI, LXT acquiring Clickworker. Large tech or consulting firms might even acquire data labeling companies to have that capability in-house (some speculate a big cloud provider or a consulting giant like Accenture could buy one of the major players). On the flip side, new startups will keep emerging to address new needs – for example, platforms for synthetic data generation (to complement human-labeled real data), or services for specialized domains like quantum computing or highly technical data. The barrier to entry can be low (anyone can start a small managed crowd), but scaling with quality is hard, so successful newcomers usually have a unique angle (like an AI recruiting agent in Micro1’s case, or a focus on a new modality, etc.). It’s an exciting space that attracts entrepreneurs because the TAM (total addressable market) keeps expanding as AI reaches more industries. Will AI Replace Human Labelers? It’s a natural question: as AI gets more powerful, won’t it eventually learn to teach itself or require far less human input? The consensus among experts is not fully, and not yet. In the near term, humans are still very much needed. AI models, no matter how advanced, can’t completely escape the need for human grounding. Unstructured real-world data is messy – new slang, new events, subtle ethical dilemmas – and AI can’t perfectly grasp all that without guidance. Even when models auto-label data, we still need humans to verify and correct those labels. And when it comes to aligning AI with human values and complex intents, human judgement is the gold standard. What will happen is that the nature of human involvement will shift (as discussed): fewer humans doing rote tasks, more humans doing high-level oversight. The volume of raw labeling work per model might decrease (because models will do more of it), but paradoxically the importance of the human-provided data may increase (because it will be the critical edge cases and alignment data). An analogy is often made: data is the new oil, and humans are needed to refine that oil. In the future, AI might do the initial refining, but humans will be checking the quality of the fuel. To put it succinctly: by 2026, we expect to see smaller but more skilled human teams working hand-in-hand with AI agents to curate datasets. Labelers will be more like “AI teachers” or “AI auditors” than assembly line workers, evaluating models on an ongoing basis. Data labeling companies are already adapting, upskilling their workforce and developing hybrid human-AI pipelines to stay relevant. Those that succeed will be key players in AI development for years to come. The human data labeling industry, far from fading, is evolving into a more specialized, value-driven service. As AI becomes ubiquitous – in healthcare, finance, government, you name it – the need for high-quality, human-curated data will only grow (albeit in different forms). Organizations will continue to rely on external human-in-the-loop providers to ensure their AI models are accurate, fair, and safe. The methods and tools will get more advanced, the work will become less menial and more insightful, and the collaboration between humans and AI will deepen. But at its core, the principle remains: your model is only as good as the human feedback and data it's trained on. In 2026 and beyond, human expertise will remain a critical ingredient in the AI recipe – the quiet force that shapes how AI systems learn, adapt, and ultimately, how they perform in the real world. As one industry guide put it, if “data is the new oil,” then these human data providers are the ones drilling, refining, and ensuring that fuel is high-octane for the AI engines of the future. They will continue to be indispensable partners in the AI journey, even as their own industry rapidly innovates and adapts. He works on the same problem this industry is built on: using AI to find and vet the specific humans a task actually needs, at a scale manual sourcing cannot reach. This overview reflects the AI data labeling landscape as of early 2026. funding_news.title: Meet the newly minted AI billionaires of 2025
funding_news.ai_summary: In 2025, more than 50 individuals became paper billionaires from AI infrastructure, models, and applications as investors poured over $200 billion into AI startups, capturing roughly half of all global venture funding. Notable new AI billionaires include Edwin Chen ($18 billion from data labeling firm Surge AI), Bret Taylor and Clay Bavor ($2.5 billion each from customer service AI startup Sierra), and three founders of Mercor who at age 22 became the youngest self-made billionaires. Big Tech executives also saw massive gains, with Elon Musk's net worth reaching $645 billion and the top 10 wealthiest U.S. tech founders adding $550 billion to their combined net worth.
funding_news.author: Niamh Rowe

industries.name: Enterprise Foundation Model Integration & APIs (Connectors, Governance, Deployment)
Documentation & Reporting Automation (Model Cards, Datasheets, Impact Assessments)

funding_news.full_text:
Getty Images / Bloomberg



In 2025, artificial intelligence became a billionaire-making machine. Suggested Reading AI wants a place in your holiday traditions The 7 car brands with the most recalls in 2025 Gold caps off a monster year with another record breakthrough Investors poured more than $200 billion into AI startups during the year, capturing roughly half of all global venture funding — up from a 34% share in 2024 — according to startup data firm Crunchbase. Related Content AI wants a place in your holiday traditions Sen. Mark Kelly on taxing AI companies that kill jobs, data center revolts, and working with Republicans As a result, more than 50 individuals building the infrastructure, models, and applications bringing AI to market became billionaires on paper, Forbes reports. The geography of this wealth creation was global: While many new billionaires emerged from established U.S. hubs, Chinese AI firms — particularly those with competitive open-source models trained with far less compute — also catapulted founders into the billionaire club. Here's who topped the list. Edwin Chen, CEO Surge AI With an estimated net worth of $18 billion, Edwin Chen, CEO of data labelling firm Surge AI, is the wealthiest of the new AI billionaires. In less than five years, Surge AI has grown to a $24 billion valuation, with clients such as Google, Meta, Microsoft, Anthropic, and Mistral. Chen, a U.S.-based CEO, is estimated to have a 75% stake, making him the wealthiest newcomer on this year’s Forbes 400 list, and at 37, he was also the youngest person listed. Bret Taylor and Clay Bavor, cofounders of Sierra Next up are Bret Taylor and Clay Bavor, the U.S.-based cofounders of Sierra; the startup aims to replace human customer service with AI agents for large companies like The North Face and electric vehicle maker Rivian. The duo are worth an estimated $2.5 billion each, joining the billionaire club in September when Sierra raised $350 million in a round that valued the company at $10 billion. Brendan Foody, Adarsh Hiremath, and Surya Midh, cofounders of Mercor Following them are U.S. founders Brendan Foody, Adarsh Hiremath and Surya Midha of Mercor, worth $2.2 billion each. Age 22, the trio became the youngest self-made billionaires of all time when Mercor, founded in 2023, raised $350 million, valuing the company at $10 billion. Mercor recruits experts and PhDs to evaluate and label data on behalf of AI companies like Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic, as they train their models. Anton Osika and Fabian Hedin, cofounders of Lovable Behind them: Anton Osika and Fabian Hedin, cofounders of Swedish startup Lovable, worth an estimated $1.6 billion each. Lovable, a so-called 'vibe coding' startup, allows users with no software experience to create websites and apps via prompts. The pair became billionaires in December after raising $330 million at a $6.6 billion valuation. Lucy Guo, cofounder of Scale AI Closely following them is Scale AI's cofounder Lucy Guo, from the U.S. Age 31, Guo became the world’s youngest self-made woman billionaire this year — usurping Taylor Swift — when Meta acquired around half of the data labeling behemoth. Big Tech executives also raked in AI wealth The top 10 wealthiest U.S. tech founders and CEOs added more than $550 billion to their combined net worth this year, the Financial Times reported, taking their net worth to $2.5 trillion in cash, equity, and other investments, according to Bloomberg data, with the S&P 500 climbing more than 18% this year. Topping the list is Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, defending his status as the world's richest person. His net worth soared nearly 50% in 2025, to $645 billion. This year, Musk secured a $1 trillion pay deal with Tesla shareholders — the largest remuneration package in history — while the valuation of his rocket company SpaceX soared to $800 billion. 📬 Sign up for the Daily Brief Our free, fast and fun briefing on the global economy, delivered every weekday morning. funding_news.title: Data scraped from the web for AI is out — specialized human-made data is in
funding_news.ai_summary: While major AI companies continue to operate at a loss, specialized data providers such as Mercor and Surge AI are experiencing rapid growth by supplying human-generated training data. This trend highlights a shift in the AI supply chain where firms facilitating high-quality data collection are achieving significant financial success compared to model developers.
funding_news.author: Technologykimberly Adams
funding_news.full_text:
Despite the billions and billions of dollars flowing into AI companies, most are not making a profit just yet. On the flip side, companies like Mercor or Surge AI, which are in the business of supplying AI companies with highly specialized data from human workers, are among the fastest-growing companies of all time.

Josh Dzieza is the investigations editor at The Verge, where he co-wrote a piece with Hayden Field about what it takes to feed the beast that is AI models. Dzieza joined “Marketplace” host Kimberly Adams to talk about who these workers are and what the future of the industry looks like.

Click the media player above to hear the conversation.

funding_news.full_text:
Surge AI: The $24B Data Engine Teaching AGI Real Human Taste 🤖 Meet Edwin Chen: the 37-year-old who bootstrapped a $24B AI startup with $0 in VC

In partnership with

(5 minutes)

Hi 👋, this is the Today in AI Newsletter: The weekly newsletter bringing you one step closer to building your own startup.

We analyze a cool, industry-shaping AI startup every week, with a full breakdown of what they do, how they make money, how much they’ve raised, and the opportunity ahead.

Let’s get to the good stuff in this email:

💡 This startup is the human-data engine behind frontier labs like OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral AI & more.

📈 They’ve bootstrapped to $1B+ in revenue , stayed profitable from day one , and now manage a core team of about 250 people .

🚀 They are now preparing their first-ever external raise of up to $1B, targeting a ~$24B valuation - founder Edwin Chen owns ~75% of the company and sits on an estimated $18B net worth as the youngest member of the Forbes 400 (#55).

So what’s the startup and who are the founders behind it? Here’s the story of Surge AI 📈

Surge AI was founded by Edwin Chen in 2020 to build high-quality human data that trains and evaluates the most advanced AI models.

Instead of cheap crowd work that tags cat photos, Surge runs a curated marketplace of elite annotators who handle things like RLHF, safety, reasoning, taste, and multi-step agent behavior. 🤖

Their mission is to raise AGI like you would raise a child so it grows up curious, imaginative, and aligned with rich human values, not just optimized for leaderboard scores & clickbait.

On the product side, that looks like:

Humans and models working together, with models generating and self-labeling, then Surgers reviewing, correcting, and adversarially testing them.

Complex RL environments that feel like video game worlds filled with tools like Slack, Gmail, GitHub, spreadsheets, and CRM systems, where agents learn to handle real productivity tasks across long timelines.

Surge’s key idea: the ceiling of your model is set by the quality of your human data.

You can’t train a master chef by giving them a million recipes for boiling water.

You train them on rare, expert recipes, subtle flavor calls, and detailed feedback.

Surge gives that level of training signal to AI.

Backstory 👀

Edwin Chen grew up in Crystal River, Florida, in the back of his parents’ Chinese-Thai-American restaurant, Peking Garden.

He did homework near the cash register while his parents worked shifts, and he fell in love with math in the eighth grade, when calculus made the world feel legible.

That curiosity took him to Choate, then to MIT at 17, where he studied math, linguistics, and computer science and even worked on decoding an Incan knot language.

He was obsessed with how humans encode meaning into patterns, whether it was language, symbols, or data.

After MIT, Edwin went deep into applied math and ML.

He did algorithmic work at Peter Thiel’s Clarium Capital, then held ML roles at Google, Facebook, Twitter, and Dropbox, shipped recommendation systems, search, and content moderation.

This is where the frustration started.

At Facebook and Twitter, he watched outside vendors deliver datasets that were slow, and off-target.

Basic tasks like distinguishing a coffee shop from a hospital would come back with ridiculous errors.

The teams were spending millions on data that made models worse. Edwin saw a huge waste of human potential.

Smart people inside big tech were building powerful models, while outsourced annotators with weak tooling and low pay were tagging data with almost no context.

Around 2020, right after GPT-3 landed, Edwin snapped.

He realized the entire industry treated data labeling as a commodity cost center, when it should be a core R&D function.

So he quit, moved to Manhattan, and decided to build the opposite of the standard playbook.

High-end human data, top talent, premium pricing, and no VCs telling him to chase vanity metrics.

The Hustle 🤑

Edwin wrote the first version of Surge AI’s MVP in about one month, mostly solo, in a small San Francisco apartment.

The product was simple at first. A platform where ML teams could define rich labeling tasks, and route them to a hand-picked pool of annotators.

He used savings from his decade in big tech, a "couple million" by his own count, and set three strict rules for the company:

No external financing. No burning cash. No low-value, simple orders.

If a task looked like commodity tagging for pennies, Surge would decline it.

Edwin then used one of his most underrated assets. His blog.

He had built a reputation in the data science community through long technical posts, like the famous "Pop vs. Soda" map that went viral from his Twitter days.

He turned that distribution into a GTM channel.

Early Surge customers came through deep content aimed at serious data scientists.

He wrote about data quality, annotation philosophy, and AGI alignment.

From there, the team focused on building the highest-quality data annotation workforce on the planet.

To join Surge Force, annotators had to pass a brutal funnel.

Strong professional background. Five trial writing tasks. Review and approval by senior annotators.

They pulled in professors from Stanford, Princeton, and Harvard, lawyers, finance pros, and native speakers across 50+ languages and dialects.

For many roles, the acceptance bar is described as harder than getting into an Ivy League. Surge paid accordingly.

Contractors earn $20–$40+ per hour, with some tasks paying 30–40 cents per working minute, far above other gig platforms.

Inside the platform, Surge’s own ML models track keystrokes, speed, accuracy, and agreement patterns, constantly updating per-annotator trust scores.

Bad or lazy work is detected and removed.

Surge also leaned into adversarial work.

They run AI red teams, including projects with groups like Redwood Research, where experts try to trick models into sneaky behavior, then label and fix the failure modes.

Quality is the product.

That contrarian take turned into a huge advantage when Meta invested heavily in rival Scale AI and took a huge stake.

Labs like Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI did not want their most sensitive data and roadmaps flowing through a vendor effectively tied to a competitor.

They needed a neutral, independent supplier.

Surge was sitting there, profitable, battle-tested, and fully independent.

Stats 📊

From a cold start in 2020, Surge AI scaled to about $1.2B in revenue in 2024, beating Scale AI’s ~$870M over the same period.

The company has roughly 250 people including part-time and consultants, which means close to $9M+ in revenue per person.

On top of that, Surge coordinates a global workforce of over 1M contractors, with about 50,000 considered expert, high-skill Surgers.

Surge has been profitable almost from day one, growing into what many consider the most capital-efficient AI infrastructure company in Silicon Valley.

It has done this with $0 in outside funding so far. Edwin still owns roughly 75% of the company.

At a current estimated valuation of ~$24B, that gives him a personal net worth of ~$18B. In 2025, he entered the Forbes 400 at #55, as the youngest person on the list.

Customer spend shows how central Surge has become.

Meta reportedly spends over $150M per year with Surge.

Google spends over $100M per year.

Other major labs, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, and xAI, rely on Surge for RLHF, model evaluation, and safety-critical pipelines.

Surge often charges 50% to 10x more than other providers.

They’re so good because their data improves model performance in ways you cannot reach with cheap labeling.

product_offering.core_offering: Surge AI provides human intelligence services for training and evaluating advanced AI models through a platform that combines RL environments, expert-curated rubrics, RLHF data, SFT demonstrations, human evaluation, and access to a global network of 200,000+ PhD-level experts. The platform supports multimodal annotation across text, image, video, and audio, and serves frontier AI labs with usage-based pricing tied to expert hourly rates ranging from $150 to $1,000 per hour.
product_offering.differentiator: Surge AI differentiates through an elite expert network of 200,000+ PhDs across 500+ disciplines who provide nuanced human judgment for AI training. The company focuses on complex AI agent behavior rather than simple data labeling, offering RL environments, expert-curated rubrics, and sophisticated evaluation frameworks. Their talent-matching algorithm assigns experts based on measured skills rather than credentials, and they've built proprietary benchmarks like EnterpriseBench, Hemingway-bench, and AdvancedIF.
product_offering.functional_benefit: Provides high-quality human-generated datasets essential for training AI systems that can function reliably in real-world applications. Offers RL environments for agent training, expert rubrics for evaluation, and access to domain specialists (doctors, lawyers, professors, etc.) who can shape AI models through both theory and real-world judgment.
product_offering.problem_solved: AI companies face a critical bottleneck where training data quality—not quantity—constrains AI advancement. Frontier AI labs exhaust publicly available text and increasingly rely on highly skilled human experts to train models. Surge AI solves the need for high-quality, nuanced human data that reflects intelligence, taste, creativity, and real-world judgment.

product_offering.product_overview: Surge AI is a data platform providing comprehensive human intelligence services for training and evaluating advanced AI models. The offering consists of nine integrated service modules: RL Environments and Agents (for agentic AI training), Rubrics and Verifiers (for evaluation), RLHF (preference/reward data), SFT (demonstration data), Human Evaluation (expert assessment), Expert Professional Domains (specialist contributors), Internationalization (multi-language data), Multimodal (image/audio/video), and Off-The-Shelf Data (pre-built datasets). These services work together to provide the complete data pipeline needed for frontier AI development, from initial training through evaluation and iteration.

company_assessment.market_position: Surge AI is the world's most powerful data labeling platform for NLP, founded in 2020 by Edwin Chen and headquartered in San Francisco. The company generated $1.2 billion in revenue in 2024 without any external venture capital, surpassing Scale AI's $870 million and likely making it the highest-grossing data labeling company globally. It is valued at approximately $24 billion and serves frontier AI labs including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and Microsoft.

strengths.details: As frontier labs exhaust public web data and synthetic approaches plateau, demand for elite human-generated training and evaluation data should accelerate rather than fade. Surge AI's 200,000+ PhD network and RL environments position it to capture disproportionate share of this next wave of spend, with $1.2B in 2024 revenue already demonstrating scaling.
strengths.headline: Expert human data becomes the binding AI constraint

strengths.details: AI capabilities are shifting from general text to specialized domains (law, medicine, finance, science). Surge AI's credentialed expert pool — Supreme Court lawyers at $500–1000/hr, board-certified physicians, McKinsey partners, Fields Medalists — is uniquely positioned to monetize this verticalization trend as customers pay premiums for verifiably expert judgment.
strengths.headline: Talent moat deepens as labs demand domain specialists

strengths.details: Move beyond raw data labeling into RL environments (EnterpriseBench), expert rubrics, and verifiers creates higher-value, stickier products that compound with the talent network. Co-developed benchmarks with Meta (AdvancedIF) and OpenAI (GSM8K) embed Surge IP inside frontier model release pipelines, raising switching costs over time.
strengths.headline: Platform expansion from labels to RL environments and verifiers

strengths.details: Surge AI's day-one profitability without venture capital is rare in AI infrastructure and supports a premium valuation thesis. With a planned round at $25–35B post-money and $1.2B revenue already in hand, continued bootstrapped-style capital efficiency could let the company capture outsized equity value creation for founder and incoming investors.
strengths.headline: Bootstrapped profitability underwrites premium valuation narrative

strengths.details: Research collaborations today (Constitutional AI, AdvancedIF, scaling instruction finetuning) should convert into broader commercial relationships as labs standardize evaluation on Surge benchmarks. Embedding Surge rubrics in model release gating creates the conditions for recurring, expanding spend per customer rather than transactional project work.
strengths.headline: Anchor relationships evolve into multi-product, multi-year platform deals

weakness.details: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and Microsoft collectively control the majority of Surge AI's customer base and have both the capital and incentive to build internal human-data operations. Any meaningful insourcing decision by one anchor customer would compress revenue and undermine the premium pricing commanded by Surge AI's expert network.
weakness.headline: Frontier labs insource data labeling at scale

weakness.details: Frontier model performance improvements from synthetic data, self-play, and AI-generated evaluations are accelerating rapidly. If even a portion of Surge AI's use cases shift to synthetic alternatives, the company faces a multi-year revenue headwind as total addressable spend on human data contracts rather than expands.
weakness.headline: Synthetic data and model-written evals erode human-label demand

weakness.details: Surge AI's pricing (e.g., $500–1000/hr for top legal/finance experts) is roughly 5–10x typical data labeling rates. Scale AI, Mercor, and emerging players with deeper capital or lower-cost workforces can compress this premium over time, especially as customers push back on rising labeling bills.
weakness.headline: Premium pricing becomes unsustainable under competitive pressure

weakness.details: Increasing regulatory scrutiny of AI training data (copyright, consent, labor classification of contractors) directly threatens Surge AI's business model. New disclosure or licensing requirements could force expensive dataset rework, restrict use of certain contractor pools, or expose the company to litigation tied to its customers' downstream model behavior.
weakness.headline: AI regulation targets human training-data provenance

weakness.details: Edwin Chen retains majority ownership and personal brand equity with no evidence of a deep operating bench. As the company scales past $1B revenue and into a $25B+ valuation tier, gaps in executive depth, governance, and capital allocation discipline could translate into execution missteps or governance disputes that constrain growth.
weakness.headline: Founder dependency limits institutional scaling

competitive_moat.details: A curated global network of 200,000+ PhDs spanning 500+ disciplines and 80+ languages—including Ivy League professors, Nobel laureates, NASA engineers, Supreme Court litigators, and Olympic athletes—accessed via a proprietary talent-matching algorithm that assigns by measured skill rather than credentials, resulting in low turnover.

Proprietary training and evaluation assets not available elsewhere: the EnterpriseBench suite (including CoreCraft, a customer support simulation with 2,500+ entities), Hemingway-bench writing leaderboard, AdvancedIF benchmark co-developed with Meta, and bespoke rubrics/verifiers for agentic RL. These datasets and environments compound with each engagement.

Deep, multi-year research and data partnerships with OpenAI (GSM8K, PALMS), Anthropic (Constitutional AI, scalable oversight), Google (instruction finetuning scaling), and Meta (AdvancedIF), plus academic collaborations with Stanford, NYU, UC Berkeley, and Princeton create co-developed outputs and switching friction.

Bootstrapped to $1.2 billion in 2024 revenue without any external venture capital while remaining profitable from day one, indicating highly capital-efficient unit economics that competitors funded with billions have not matched on revenue per dollar raised.

The expert contractor network grows more valuable as additional frontier labs join, since the same PhD pool can serve multiple customers and the talent-matching data improves with scale; the network also functions as a marketing channel recruiting further experts.

key_risks.details: Revenue depends on a small handful of AI labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft). Loss or insourcing decision by any single customer would have an outsized impact on top-line revenue and on the company's ability to retain elite contractors.
key_risks.headline: Extreme customer concentration in five frontier AI labs

key_risks.details: The company was bootstrapped by Chen, who retains majority ownership and personal brand equity. There is no evidence of a deep executive bench or institutional governance, creating succession and concentration risk if Chen departs or reduces involvement.
key_risks.headline: Key-person dependency on founder/CEO Edwin Chen

key_risks.details: Scale AI (largest incumbent, $870M revenue), Mercor ($10B valuation), and other well-capitalized data labeling entrants are competing for the same frontier-lab relationships. Surge AI must continuously defend share through quality and exclusivity of its expert network.
key_risks.headline: Intense competitive pressure from Scale AI, Mercor, and well-funded entrants

key_risks.details: Frontier labs are actively investing in synthetic data, model-written evaluations, and self-play to reduce reliance on human-generated labels. If these approaches mature, Surge AI's human-in-the-loop model could face structural demand erosion in 3–5+ years.
key_risks.headline: Long-term displacement risk from synthetic and AI-generated training data

key_risks.details: Quality, throughput, and IP exposure depend on coordinating 200,000+ PhD-level contractors across 80+ countries. Wage inflation, regulatory shifts (e.g., contractor reclassification), or competitor poaching of top-tier experts could compress margins or degrade output quality.
key_risks.headline: Heavy operational reliance on a 200,000+ global contractor workforce

key_risks.details: Surge AI's data is used to train commercial LLMs that are subject to increasing copyright, consent, and data-source scrutiny. Any future regulation on training-data provenance or licensing could force repricing, rework, or removal of key datasets.
key_risks.headline: Regulatory and IP exposure from frontier AI training pipelines

key_highlights.details: Active data labeling and RLHF engagements with OpenAI (GSM8K, PALMS), Anthropic (Constitutional AI, Claude training), Google (instruction finetuning), Meta (AdvancedIF, GAIA), and Microsoft.

launches.title: 新 PayPal 黑帮：10 个实习生，1000 亿美元
launches.ai_summary: Ten interns from Hudson River Trading's 2015 program now lead companies valued over $100 billion, including Scale AI, Hyperliquid, and Cognition. Their combined valuations exceed $100 billion, with Wang, Yan, and Wu among the founders.
launches.author: 深潮Techflow
launches.full_text:
撰文：小饼

2026 年 10 月 19 日，Meta 首席 AI 官 Alexandr Wang 在 X 上发了一张自拍，配文只有七个单词：got the HRT gang back together！ 评论区炸了。 这张看起来随意至极的合影，藏着当今科技世界最离谱的一个事实：照片里的三个人，加上他们不在场的几位老同学，在 2015 年冬天共同参加了华尔街量化交易巨头 Hudson River Trading 的首届实习生项目，那个项目一共只招了 10 个人。 十年后，这 10 个实习生创办或执掌的公司，合计估值超过 1000 亿美元。 照片右边是 Wang 本人，29 岁，Scale AI 创始人，去年被扎克伯格以 143 亿美元的代价挖去 Meta，出任首席 AI 官，掌舵 Meta 超级智能实验室。 左边是 Jeff Yan，Hyperliquid 创始人，一个零融资、11 人团队打造的去中心化交易所，去年利润 9 亿美元，项目市值高达 760 亿美元。 中间是 Scott Wu，Cognition 创始人兼 CEO，他的 AI 编程智能体 Devin 正在以每月 50%的速度增长企业客户，公司最新估值 480 亿美元。 三个人上一次同时出现在一个房间，可能还是 2015 年那个冬天，在哈德逊河边的交易公司办公室里。 哈德逊河畔的冬天 这群天才的缘分在高中时代就已经开始了。 Jeff Yan 和 Scott Wu 都在国际信息学奥林匹克竞赛（IOI）上拿过金牌，Wu 更是三次夺金，2014 年以满分登顶。Alexandr Wang 是美国计算机奥林匹克和数学奥林匹克的常客，他们在各种夏令营和集训队里反复碰面，那个圈子小到几乎所有人都互相认识。 2015 年冬天，这些散落在哈佛、MIT 各处的竞赛少年，被一个共同的名字聚到了一起：Hudson River Trading。 HRT 是全球最顶尖的量化交易公司之一，总部在纽约，日均交易量一度占到美国股市的 15%以上。 2015 年冬天，HRT 第一次尝试招收实习生。名额极少，总共只有 10 人。Jeff Yan 当时是哈佛大三学生，Scott Wu 是大一新生，Alexandr Wang 在 MIT 读大一。 这个实习项目的设计本身就很「量化」：为期三周，以竞赛形式进行，每一轮都会排名。据 Jeff Yan 后来回忆，每一轮的前两名，永远是他和 Scott Wu。 但这段实习最具历史意义的时刻，可能不是交易竞赛本身。据 Colossus 杂志对 Jeff Yan 的深度访谈，Yan 正是在 HRT 实习期间，从两位前合伙人的推介中第一次听说了比特币。虽然他当时并未立即行动，但很快就找到了以太坊的黄皮书，读到了一个描述：一台全世界共同运行、无人能关闭的计算机，那颗种子，在几年后长成了 Hyperliquid。 同样是在那个冬天，年仅 19 岁的 Alexandr Wang 在自己的生日聚会上，对围坐在桌旁的哈佛和 MIT 同学们说了一句话，后来被反复引用： 「为什么不能是我们？」 三条道路，一个原点 从 HRT 的办公室走出来之后，这些年轻人选择了完全不同的赛道。但他们身上有一个共同的底层逻辑：用算法思维重构一个传统行业。 Alexandr Wang：从数据标注到扎克伯格的 AI 大脑 离开 HRT 后，Wang 做了一个让所有人意外的决定：从 MIT 辍学。 2016 年，19 岁的他和 Lucy Guo 联合创立了 Scale AI，做的事情听起来一点都不性感，就是给 AI 训练数据做标注。但 Wang 的判断极其精准：他跳过了具体的 AI 应用，直接押注整个 AI 产业的「铲子」。 随着 AI 浪潮席卷全球，Scale AI 成了 OpenAI、Meta、美国国防部等巨头的核心供应商。2021 年，公司估值飙升至 73 亿美元，24 岁的 Wang 成了全球最年轻的白手起家亿万富翁。2024 年的融资中，Scale AI 估值达到 138 亿美元，背后站着英伟达、亚马逊和 Meta。 然后是 2025 年 6 月那笔震动硅谷的交易。Meta 以 143 亿美元收购了 Scale AI 49%的股权，整体估值 290 亿美元。作为交易的核心条件，扎克伯格要求 Wang 本人加入 Meta，出任首席 AI 官，领导新成立的「Meta 超级智能实验室」。 一个 28 岁的年轻人，成了全球最大社交媒体帝国 AI 战略的总指挥。 Jeff Yan：从量化交易员到链上金融基础设施的建造者 如果说 Wang 选择了 AI 的「铲子生意」，Jeff Yan 选择的则是加密世界里最硬核的那条路：重建交易基础设施。 Yan 在哈佛毕业后并没有急着创业。他先后在 Google 和一家自动驾驶公司工作，同时对加密世界的观察从未停止。2020 年，他创立了 Chameleon Trading，一家加密货币做市商。这段经历让他深刻理解了中心化交易所的结构性缺陷，FTX 的崩塌给了他决定性的一推。 2022 年，Yan 解散了 Chameleon 的团队，开始用自有资金搭建 Hyperliquid，一个运行在区块链上的去中心化永续合约交易所。没有 VC 投资，没有代币预售，11 个人的团队，从零开始。 这种「反 VC」的路径在加密行业几乎闻所未闻。Yan 的底气来自 Chameleon 积累的交易利润，更来自量化交易员对产品的极致追求：延迟要低，吞吐要高，用户体验要逼近甚至超越中心化交易所。 ICE 的 CEO Jeffrey Sprecher 曾称 Hyperliquid 的交易活跃度「超过了纳斯达克」。 如今，Hyperliquid 是全球人均盈利能力最高的企业之一。去年，这家公司仅有的 11 名员工创造了超过 9 亿美元的利润。公司成立仅四年，市值已达到 760 亿美元。 Scott Wu：让 AI 自己写代码的人 Scott Wu 是这群人里竞赛成绩最恐怖的一个。三枚 IOI 金牌，2014 年以满分夺冠，MathCounts 全美冠军，Google Code Jam 第三名。在哈佛读了两年书后辍学，与人联合创立了 AI 社交网络平台 Lunchclub。 但真正让他名震硅谷的，是 2023 年底与 Steven Hao、Walden Yan（三人合计持有 5 枚 IOI 金牌）联合创立的 Cognition。2024 年 3 月，Cognition 发布了 Devin，号称「全球第一个 AI 软件工程师」的产品，能够独立规划、编写、测试和部署代码。 Devin 引发了科技界的巨大争议，但市场给出了自己的回答：Cognition 的估值从 2024 年初的 3.5 亿美元一路飙升到 2025 年 9 月的 102 亿美元，再到 2026 年 5 月的 260 亿美元（融资 10 亿美元），年化收入从 2024 年年中的 540 万美元暴涨到 2026 年年中的近 5 亿美元。 到 2026 年 9 月，年化收入已逼近 10 亿美元，最新估值据报道已达 480 亿美元。Wu 本人说，Cognition 超过 90%的内部代码现在由 Devin 自己编写。 一个三岁的创业公司，估值从 3.5 亿到 480 亿，涨了 130 多倍。 不止三个人 今天那张自拍里只有三个人，但这个圈子远比一张照片能容纳的更大。 据 Scott Wu 本人补充，HRT 实习项目并不是这群人友谊的起点。早在高中时代，他们中的许多人就已经因为各种奥林匹克竞赛结识。而那个小圈子延伸出去的名字，每一个都在今天的科技版图上占据一席之地。 Jesse Zhang，同批 HRT 实习生之一。他此前创办的社交游戏公司 Lowkey 被 Niantic（《Pokémon Go》的开发商）收购。2023 年，他创立了 AI 客服智能体公司 Decagon，专注于用 AI 替代企业客户服务。公司成立不到三年，估值已达 45 亿美元，客户包括 Duolingo、赫兹租车等巨头，2026 年入选福布斯 30 Under 30。 Johnny Ho，三枚 IOI 金牌得主，哈佛校友。高中时就与 Scott Wu、Jeff Yan 相识。2013 年的美国 IOI 代表队合影中，他和 Steven Hao、Scott Wu 并肩站在一起。 离开竞赛圈后，Ho 在 Tower Research Capital 做量化交易员，随后加入 Quora 做工程师。2022 年，他与 Aravind Srinivas 等人联合创立了 AI 搜索引擎 Perplexity，目前担任联合创始人兼首席战略官。Perplexity 最新一轮融资的估值据报道已达约 300 亿美元，正在重新定义搜索引擎这个万亿级市场。 Demi Guo（郭文景），来自杭州的「天才少女」，2015 年 IOI 银牌得主。哈佛数学学士加计算机硕士，曾是 Meta AI Research 最年轻的全职研究员。2023 年，她从斯坦福博士项目辍学，与同学 Chenlin Meng 联合创立了 AI 视频生成平台 Pika，估值达到 4.7 亿美元，用户超过 1600 万。她曾在 HRT 和 Quora 实习，又是同一个圈子。 Steven Hao，2014 年 IOI 金牌得主，MIT 数学系毕业。他曾是 Alexandr Wang 在 Scale AI 时期的早期核心工程师，后来加入 Scott Wu 的 Cognition 担任联合创始人兼 CTO。根据福布斯的估算，30 岁的 Hao 个人净资产已达约 13 亿美元，是 2026 年福布斯 400 富豪榜上最年轻的美国人。 从 Hao 的轨迹可以清晰地看到这个圈子内部的「人才流动」：他把在 Scale AI 积累的工程经验和对 AI 数据的理解，带进了 Cognition。而 Cognition 三位创始人 Wu、Hao、Walden Yan 合计持有 5 枚 IOI 金牌，他们把竞赛中锤炼出的算法思维，直接灌注到了 AI 编程智能体的核心架构中。 量化交易公司为何成了创始人摇篮？ 这不是巧合。 当 Wang 在今年 10 月初转发那张 2015 年实习生合影时，他给它加了一句注释：「HRT 2015 intern class is the new-gen PayPal Mafia。」 PayPal 黑帮的故事人尽皆知。Elon Musk、Peter Thiel、Reid Hoffman、David Sacks 等人从同一家公司走出来，分别创建了 Tesla、Palantir、LinkedIn、Yammer 等公司，定义了上一个十年的科技格局。 但 HRT 这批人和 PayPal 黑帮有一个根本性的不同。PayPal 黑帮的纽带是一家公司和一段共同的创业经历。HRT 这群人的纽带更早、更深，他们共享的是一种思维方式。 竞赛选手出身意味着什么？ 意味着他们从十几岁起就被训练用最优解思维处理问题，对效率有近乎偏执的追求，对复杂系统有直觉性的理解。量化交易公司是这种思维方式的天然放大器：在 HRT，他们学会了如何在海量噪音中提取信号，如何在毫秒级的时间窗口内做出决策，如何搭建能够自我优化的系统。 Jesse Zhang 在一篇文章中写道：「做数学、编程和科学竞赛长大的这一代人，在今天的创始人中占了不成比例的高份额。」 量化交易公司正是这群人从竞赛圈到创业圈之间的关键跳板。Jane Street、Citadel、DE Shaw、Two Sigma，这些名字背后都站着类似的故事，但 HRT 2015 届的浓度，确实异常之高。 10 个实习生，至少 4 位成为独角兽创始人，公司合计估值超过千亿美元，这个「人才转化率」超过了 Google、Meta 等以盛产 AI 人才著称的科技巨头。 更深层的原因或许在于：这些量化交易公司提供的不仅是技术训练，还有一种对市场结构的本能理解。Wang 把这种理解用在了 AI 数据基础设施上，Yan 用在了链上金融基础设施上，Wu 用在了软件工程的自动化上，Zhang 用在了客户服务的重构上，Ho 用在了搜索引擎的颠覆上。 他们解决的问题不同，但拆解问题的方式如出一辙：找到一个低效的系统，用算法和工程能力重建它。 天才总是早早相遇。但这个故事真正动人的地方，不在于他们有多聪明。竞赛金牌早就证明了聪明。动人的地方在于时代终于翻到了属于他们的那一页。 十年前，这群人的画像是什么？数学竞赛冠军，编程极客，社交场上的隐形人。在任何一所美国高中的鄙视链里，他们都被归入同一个词：nerd。那个词在很长一段时间里不是褒义，它意味着古怪、无趣、与主流格格不入。 但 2024 年之后的世界，给了 nerd 们一个前所未有的舞台。 当 AI 成为所有产业的底层操作系统，当代码本身开始书写代码，能够驾驭这一切的人，恰恰是那些从小就活在算法和公式里的人。 Wang、Yan、Wu、Zhang、Ho、Guo、Hao，这些白人念起来拗口的华人姓氏，从奥赛赛场走向了时代的舞台中央。 曾经被鄙夷的 nerd，终于迎来了属于他们的黄金时代。

launches.title: ALIF: Building AI Fluency, One Cohort at a Time
launches.ai_summary: Scale AI launched ALIF, a government AI training program, in Qatar in December 2025. Between January and June 2026, it delivered 15 cohorts, upskilling 240 professionals, with average assessment scores rising from 57% to 77%. Advanced modules and a self-paced LMS are planned for 2026.

industries.name: Data Science, Machine Learning & AI (Modeling, MLOps, GenAI)

company_mentions.name: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology

launches.full_text: AI adoption is growing quickly. Organization-wide impact is not. Most organizations now use AI in at least one business function. Yet the majority remain in the experimentation or piloting stages and have not begun scaling AI across the enterprise. Only a small fraction have reached the point where AI is thoroughly integrated across most of their functions. Everyone else is somewhere behind them. What distinguished these organizations was not technology alone. It was the workforce. These organizations invested early in the workforce and operating foundations surrounding AI, including training, change management, workflow redesign, and leadership sponsorship. In government, where the workflows in question govern tax administration, healthcare delivery, and national security, that dependency only sharpens. The systems only work if the people responsible for them know how to evaluate, apply, and govern them. From Theory to Operational Playbook ALIF, Scale AI's flagship Generative AI Foundations program for government professionals across technical and non-technical roles, draws its name from Alif, the first letter of the Arabic alphabet, and the related Arabic verb meaning "to become familiar with." Both meanings reflect the program's purpose: to provide a starting point and build familiarity with AI from the ground up. Developed by Scale AI for the region, ALIF integrates Arabic, regional use cases, and public-sector context into the curriculum from the outset, rather than treating localization as a translation step. ALIF was first launched in Qatar in December 2025 by the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT), in partnership with Scale AI, and is delivered through Qatar Digital Academy (QDA). ALIF is built on the principle that effective AI learning must be applied, hands-on, and contextually relevant. It helps government professionals move beyond general awareness and build the practical foundations for operational fluency. Rather than stopping at concepts, ALIF connects foundational understanding with practice grounded in the work of government. The curriculum is inspired by the playbook Scale's delivery teams use on live engagements, distilled into a structured, accredited program and informed by Scale's experience building and deploying production AI systems. Those lessons are translated into structured exercises and scenarios adapted to the realities of government work. Its core teaching objective is to move learners from awareness of AI to the ability to think through where AI can support their own workflow, and how to use it confidently and responsibly. In Qatar, ALIF directly contributes to the country’s broader digital capability ambitions. It aligns with the Digital Agenda 2030 objective of increasing professional staff digital competencies by 10%, as well as the Third National Development Strategy’s target for more than 46% of the workforce to hold skilled or highly skilled roles. Through this alignment, ALIF supports MCIT’s wider efforts to strengthen government services and accelerate digital transformation across the state. Designed with an Arabic-first focus while remaining fully accessible in English, the program split into two distinct tracks: ALIF Core is a one-day, hands-on, instructor-led workshop built for business and policy professionals. It covers AI foundations, safe output evaluation, and practical use-case identification. Every participant leaves with an AI Opportunity Canvas: a concrete, public sector-specific proposal they can bring back to their team. ALIF Tech is a two-day, hands-on, instructor-led workshop designed for ICT professionals. It covers technical foundations, multimodal generative AI, model training, retrieval-augmented generation, and the architecture, risks, and governance considerations associated with AI agents. What ALIF Has Delivered Between January and June 2026, ALIF delivered 15 cohorts and upskilled 240 government professionals from more than 40 entities, including MCIT, the General Tax Authority, the Qatar Armed Forces, the Amiri Diwan, the Prime Minister's Office, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Hamad Medical Corporation, ADLSA, and Qatar Rail. Learning assessments demonstrated measurable progress. Average scores increased from 57% before the program to 77% afterward, a gain of 20 percentage points. Nearly 8 in 10 participants improved their results, and a similar proportion met the requirements for the program's Digital Competence certificate. These results demonstrate ALIF’s reach and its ability to strengthen foundational AI capability. The program’s next measure of impact is workplace application: whether participants advance viable use cases, apply responsible AI practices, and transfer their learning into day-to-day government work. Why It Works The curriculum is grounded in production reality. Every lab, scenario, and discussion in ALIF is drawn from the public sector work Scale's teams do on live engagements, whether that is drafting a policy memo with strict safety guardrails or delegating workflows to an AI agent. Learners encounter the same tradeoffs Scale's engineers face on live deployments, in the same order they face them. It is built for the audience. ALIF was designed from the ground up for public sector professionals: their workflows, their data sensitivities, their accountability structures. Generic AI training retooled for government does not carry that specificity, and specificity is what makes training transfer to the job rather than stopping at comprehension. What's Next The ALIF roadmap for 2026 is expanding across two fronts. Advanced modules are rolling out deeper dives into production-grade prompting, safe RAG pipelines, and multi-step agentic workflows. The goal is to push graduates from foundational fluency into applied expertise. A new self-paced LMS is being built alongside the live cohorts. It features live playgrounds where learners can build, break, and refine real prompts and agents in a safe, self-directed environment. The LMS is designed to extend the cohort experience and compound it over time. The model is deliberate. Instructor-led cohorts establish the conceptual frame. The LMS converts that frame into a practiced reflex. Together, they move graduates from understanding how Generative AI works to building and deploying real tools inside their ministries. That is what turns an educational initiative into measurable public sector productivity: shorter document turnarounds, fewer rote tasks consuming senior officers' time, and a workforce that can spot and de-risk AI opportunities before they stall. Build Your Team's AI Fluency By structuring training directly around the practical day-to-day responsibilities of government professionals, ALIF offers a proven framework for public sector entities aiming to intentionally accelerate their AI adoption. To learn more about how Scale partners with governments to deploy AI in operational environments, whether by joining an upcoming cohort, commissioning a dedicated program for your organization, or piloting our LMS, visit scale.com.

launches.title: The ‘IMDb for Athletes’ Is Here — And Its Founders Built It Without Spending a Dime on Marketing
launches.ai_summary: Athlete Agent, co-founded by Ryan Rottman, Sean O’Brien, and Aaron Rodgers, launched a database connecting brands directly to over 30,000 athletes across 20 leagues without spending on traditional marketing. The platform has secured clients such as Coca-Cola, Netflix, and Goldman Sachs, while also receiving a half-million-dollar investment from Google through its Scale AI program to build custom Gemini integration.
launches.author: Dan Bova

industries.name: Full-Service Athlete Talent Agencies (Contract Negotiation & Career Management)

launches.full_text:
Listen to this post Entrepreneur Ventures is an early-stage venture capital firm partnered with Entrepreneur Media that is dedicated to backing passionate and innovative founders as early as day one. In this series, we are profiling the amazing entrepreneurs Entrepreneur Ventures is working with to share their insights on building and growing a thriving business. Ryan Rottman spent more than two decades as an actor and producer, appearing on shows like 90210 and starring in nearly a dozen Hallmark films. Sean O’Brien invented a portable beach chair in his 20s that led to an eight-figure exit, then went on to co-found Autio, an audio-storytelling app, with actor Kevin Costner. Together, alongside quarterback Aaron Rodgers as co-founder, they built Athlete Agent — a database connecting brands directly to more than 30,000 athletes across 20 leagues — with its eye on 280 more across the globe. Their client list already includes Coca-Cola, Netflix and Goldman Sachs, and they built it almost entirely without spending a penny on marketing budget. I spoke with Rottman and O’Brien to talk about how it happened. Dan Bova: So where did the idea for Athlete Agent even come from?

Ryan Rottman: As an actor, IMDb was my business card. Every time I walked into an audition room, casting directors were asking about my filmography — past, present, future projects. Producers from Hallmark saw me on “90210,” looked at my IMDb Pro account, where they list your representation information, saw who my agent was, and reached out. Because that information was correct, I’ve since done around eight Hallmark films. Had it not been correct, they would’ve gone down the next guy on the list. I’ve also been fortunate to call Aaron Rodgers a good friend for over 17 years. We went to dinner in LA, and I said, “I’m so confused. I know all the athletes through you — why is there not an IMDb for athletes?” He said, “Who have you told?” I said, “A couple buddies.” He said, “Don’t tell anyone else. There’s white space for this. Let’s do it.” How did you first hook up with Aaron?

Ryan Rottman: We played in a golf tournament, and that’s one of the things I love about golf — where else can you just spend four hours with someone, sitting in a cart, understanding who they are as a person? Do they get angry when they hit the ball out of bounds? How do they handle adversity? It was such an amazing time, and we bonded over “The Big Lebowski,” one of our favorite movies. We just forged a friendship after that. Sean, how did you end up joining as CEO?

Sean O’Brien: My whole career started with an invention — my friends and I built a portable chair for the beach, we got a cover story in Entrepreneur magazine, and someone from Swimways Corp read it and approached us. We sold the company for eight figures shortly after — that was my liquidity event at age 27. More recently, I co-founded Autio, an audio-storytelling app, with Kevin Costner — we raised $20 million and were on “Shark Tank.” I was going to retire after that, and then this came across my desk. The first thing I did was buy an IMDb Pro subscription and look up Costner’s team, and I thought, “This is crazy that sports doesn’t have this.” That’s why I joined — started as CTO and got bumped up to CEO. How do you actually gather and fact-check all this data?

Sean O’Brien: We spent $3 million building the initial database for the first 10 leagues. There’s nowhere to scrape this stuff from, so it’s mostly manual effort — even AI tools aren’t great at it, which is why Google partnered with us. We’re the only people in the world who have this data. It’s relationship-driven; we have a whole research team, and we update rosters around events like trade deadlines. Agents will also notify us of changes — they’ll email us and say, “Pull that endorsement off a profile, that deal just ended.” Photo credit: Athlete Agent What’s the business model?

Sean O’Brien: It’s $99 a month or $999 a year, per seat license. A company might have five accounts with us, paying roughly $5,000 a year. In the long run, we intend to do the IMDb model, where agents pay us to manage their athletes’ pages too. Ryan Rottman: What we didn’t realize going in is that 90% of an agent’s job is outbound. Now we’re creating inbound for them, and they love us for that. We don’t take any piece of the deal flow — we’re simply connectors. The brands pay us to get the information, and they go do the deal. What does a profile actually look like when you pull one up?

Sean O’Brien: Say you’re a real customer like Netflix, and you want to put Travis Kelce in a new film you’re developing. You come to his page, and the vitals aren’t paywalled, but everything else is. You get Travis’ whole team — right in the middle, you’ll see his theatrical agents, and you can copy the email and go direct to the right person, rather than emailing the famous agent or the league agent, which is what people used to do. We’ve got the contract values, so you can see how much money they make, plus a full endorsement list — most sites only list four or five endorsements for someone like Travis, but we have all of them, linked. We’ve got all their startup investments, anything business-related that’s not an endorsement, and finally, the charity work. You haven’t spent a dollar on marketing, yet you’ve signed Coca-Cola, Netflix and Hugo Boss. How?

Sean O’Brien: They’re finding us in the press, but also through AI applications — ChatGPT recommends us, Gemini recommends us. I took that data to Google, and they’re now backing us through the Scale AI program, a half-million-dollar investment, and we’re building a custom version of Gemini together. Out of the box, an LLM knows Red Bull and Monster are energy drink companies. What it doesn’t know is whether a specific athlete has a deal in that space. We do. So a CMO could ask, “Find me all the WNBA players who don’t have an energy drink deal,” and it pulls the profiles and contact information in one swoop. What’s a lesson you’ve each learned building this?

Ryan Rottman: A big thing for me was coming from the acting world, where 90% of the job is getting told no. You get a thick skin to understand it’s not personal. On the fundraising side, when someone tells you no, it doesn’t mean it’s not a great idea — it just means it’s not right for them. A lot of founders get told no enough times that they start thinking maybe they don’t have a great idea. You just have to keep moving forward. And having Aaron is amazing — but at the end of the day, this isn’t the Aaron Rodgers business. This is a standalone business. What do you want entrepreneurs to know about Athlete Agent?

Sean O’Brien: I want them to know that the wall has come down. If you’ve got $99 a month, you can basically access any athlete. Keep the email short, and make sure what you’re pitching is relevant to the person. A lot of people assume a top athlete’s agent is never going to read their email — but if you have a great idea that’s relevant to something that athlete cares about, you might just get a Zoom. We set those up all the time, and founders can’t believe it.
