The agreement gives Scale AI a much closer role in how the DOE may eventually connect AI systems with scientific data and national lab research environments.The company could play an important role in how advanced computing environments integrate with national lab research workflows, while strengthening its position inside large scale government backed AI infrastructure initiatives.

Scale AI shared “Signing this MOU is an important step in getting the data layer right in this mission. It allows Scale to engage more directly with DOE, align on shared priorities, and discuss how AI is applied across some of the most important scientific challenges facing the country.”

Partnerships with companies, such as Scale AI, that are focused on operational AI infrastructure helps the initiative move beyond isolated AI experiments toward larger scale integration across scientific computing and research environments.

The bigger problem is not the AI models themselves, but connecting them with existing research systems and scientific workflows. That aligns with the direction of the Genesis Mission itself.

Scientific AI systems face a different set of constraints than traditional enterprise AI deployments – reproducibility, traceability, and domain specific validation within simulation based workflows. All this makes data orchestration and operational reliability increasingly important layers of the stack.

The Genesis Mission itself is also evolving. Much of the early attention surrounding AI for science focused heavily on compute scale and frontier models. However, now the attention is shifting toward the infrastructure required to operationalize AI across complex scientific environments.

Last year Wang departed for Meta’s superintelligence initiative. Former Uber Eats executive Jason Droege later took over as CEO. Despite change in leadership, Scale AI has continued expanding further into operational AI infrastructure. Meta has become a major backer of Scale AI.

In recent times, Scale AI has focused more on getting data into a usable state for real world AI deployments. That positioning fits naturally with many of the challenges emerging inside scientific computing environments.

Scale AI was founded in 2016 by Alexandr Wang and Lucy Guo as a data labeling company. The early focus was to help ML teams prepare training data for AI systems. However, demand for LLMs and operational AI systems accelerated. To meet that demand, the company expanded into broader AI infrastructure solutions.

These moves underscore Scale AI’s growing role in operational AI infrastructure beyond its original data labeling business.

Scale AI is also involved in the Defense Innovation Unit’s Thunderforge program, which focuses on bringing AI into military planning and operational decisions. This is part of President Trump’s Golden Dome homeland defense initiative.

The partnership comes at a time when Scale AI continues expanding its footprint. Earlier this week, Pentagon’s Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office (CDAO) reportedly expanded its agreement with Scale AI from $100M to $500M.

The Scale AI team aims to change this. They shared in a blog that “the massive amounts of data generated across America’s 17 National Labs represents a strategic resource that, if utilized properly, can unlock transformative advances in U.S. scientific leadership…This is the “data bottleneck,” not a lack of data, but the gap between data that exists and data that is actually usable for AI-driven discovery.”

Most of the attention in AI for science went toward bigger models and more compute. The data itself is becoming a greater part of the problem. A lot of scientific data still sits across disconnected systems and highly specialized research environments that modern AI systems were never really designed to navigate. The goal now is to make large scientific datasets usable inside operational AI systems.

The DOE national labs generate enormous amounts of data but often struggle to derive full value from it. That’s where Scale AI’s core expertise of data labeling and annotation could be useful in helping operationalize scientific data.

In its announcement, Scale AI framed fragmented and difficult to operationalize research data as one of the biggest obstacles in allowing AI systems to be fully integrated into scientific discovery workflows.

Much of messaging by Scale AI is based around the challenges surrounding scientific data infrastructure. There is greater emphasis on “unlocking the right data”. That is not surprising as industry trends and reports show data has emerged as the critical element in the success of AI systems.

Public details for the Scale AI and DOE agreement are not available. No specific projects or deployment timelines have been announced. At this stage, it remains more of a collaborative framework rather than a fully defined operational initiative.

The move adds another commercial AI infrastructure player to an ecosystem that is increasingly centered around integrating AI models with scientific datasets and high performance computing systems. Some of the big tech players that are already connected to the initiative including Nvidia.

How Investors Can Position Themselves in the AI Sector Despite Scale AI Not Yet Being Public

Although the initial frenzy of AI investing may have somewhat subsided, investor enthusiasm for this transformative technology remains high. Scale AI, a company that provides high-quality data and full-stack technology, offers its Scale GenAI platform to help customers develop customized generative AI applications using their own data based on large language models (LLMs). In short, Scale helps customers build better AI tools.

For most investors, Scale AI came into the public spotlight in June 2025—when the company announced that Meta Platforms was investing $14.3 billion in it. Meta’s investment, totaling over $29 billion, provided Scale with the capital to “accelerate innovation and strengthen strategic partnerships with customers.” As a result, Meta acquired a 49% stake in the AI startup, though without voting rights.

Is Scale AI Public Yet?

As of May 2026, Scale is not yet a public company, and Scale has not indicated any plans for an IPO. Generative AI and large language models are rapidly becoming everyday tools for both individuals and businesses. Being at the forefront of AI technology, Scale AI naturally attracts strong investor interest. However, for most investors, Scale is currently unavailable for investment, and they must wait for it to go public. Although Scale stock is not available, investors still have various AI investment options, including Palantir, Meta Platforms, Nvidia, and AI-related ETFs.

Because Scale is not subject to the regulatory standards of public companies, its financial data is not accessible to the outside world. Although the company does generate revenue—with new business revenue exceeding $1 billion in 2025—it is impossible to determine whether it is profitable. If Scale pursues an IPO in the future, it will be required to file regulatory documents, at which point investors will gain a clearer understanding of its profitability.

Alternatives to Scale AI Stock

For most investors, Scale stock is not available for purchase. Accredited investors may be able to access pre-IPO investment opportunities through platforms such as Forge Global (FRGE).

Here are several alternatives worth considering:

1. Palantir (PLTR): Similar to Scale, Palantir Technologies provides leading enterprise AI solutions. A major commonality between the two companies is that both conduct substantial business with the U.S. government. In the first quarter of 2026, Palantir’s U.S. government business grew to $687 million. Palantir expects to be profitable in every quarter of 2026 and forecasts adjusted free cash flow of $4.2 billion to $4.4 billion.

2. Meta Platforms (META): With its multibillion-dollar investment in Scale (holding a 49% stake), Meta is an obvious choice for indirect investment in Scale. Meta owns social media apps such as Instagram and WhatsApp, all of which integrate its large language model, Llama.

3. Nvidia (NVDA): Nvidia not only provides indirect exposure through its participation in Scale’s Series F funding round but is also highly favored for the critical role its graphics processing units (GPUs) play in training AI models.

As a result of the investment, Meta gained a 49% equity stake in the AI startup, though it doesn't have voting power. Disappointed as investors may be to find that Scale isn't on the 2026 IPO calendar, they may be happy to learn that a variety of other companies are planning IPOs in 2026. Is Scale AI profitable? Since Scale isn't subject to the same regulatory standards as publicly traded companies, investors aren't privy to the company's financials. While Scale is generating sales -- it reported more than $1 billion in new business in 2025 -- there's no insight into whether it's posting a profit. Should it proceed with an IPO, Scale will be required to submit regulatory filings that provide insight into its financials. At that point, investors will have a better sense of the company's profitability, or lack thereof. Alternatives to Scale AI stock While Scale is unavailable to most investors, accredited investors may be able to gain exposure to Scale before an IPO through platforms like Forge Global (NYSE:FRGE), which offer opportunities to invest in private companies. Those who aren't accredited investors but whose interests are piqued at the prospect of buying Scale stock may be unhappy to learn that the investment option is unavailable. Still, there are other opportunities they may find appealing. Here are a few alternatives to consider. 1. Palantir Like Scale, Palantir Technologies (PLTR -0.41%) provides leading enterprise AI solutions, making it a logical choice for those unable to scratch their itch for AI exposure with an investment in Scale. In the first quarter of 2026, for example, Palantir reported U.S. government business grew to $687 million. Palantir projects it will be profitable in every quarter of 2026, and it also forecasts adjusted free cash flow of $4.2 billion to $4.4 billion, making it a great opportunity for those seeking an AI growth stock with moderate risk. 2. Meta Platforms With the multi-billion investment -- totaling a 49% equity stake -- that it has made in Scale, Meta Platforms represents an obvious choice for gaining indirect exposure to Scale. Speaking to the merits of the partnership with Scale, Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg stated: "We partnered with Scale AI to work with Enterprises to adopt Llama and train custom models with their own data. We are excited to collectively make Llama the industry standard and bring the benefits of AI to everyone." Long gone are the days when Facebook was Zuckerberg's sole property. After a string of acquisitions, Meta has a portfolio that includes some of the most popular social media apps like Instagram and WhatsApp -- both of which are embedded with Llama, Meta's large language model. A pioneer in social media, Meta has emerged as a viable way to gain exposure to AI, and analysts have high expectations for Meta stock to flourish in 2026 and beyond. 3. Nvidia Primarily, Nvidia stock is an alluring alternative to Scale stock because Nvidia provides indirect exposure to Scale through its equity position from its participation in Scale's Series F funding round. But that's hardly the only reason. More broadly speaking, Nvidia is a usual suspect for any investor seeking AI exposure. Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs) are in high demand due to their valuable role in training AI models. In fact, Alexandr Wang, Scale's CEO, has spoken to the significant advantage that Nvidia chips provide for AI computing. During a January 2025 interview with CNBC, Wang speculated that the acceleration of Chinese LLM DeepSeek stems from the company's acquisition of Nvidia's H100 GPUs, which are specialized for AI and LLM computing. funding_news.full_text: Topline The Pentagon awarded Scale AI—which Meta owns 49% of—a $500 million contract to help analyze data and support decision-making, marking a fivefold increase from the $100 million deal the startup signed in September 2025, the company announced Wednesday. WASHINGTON, DC - JULY 18: (L-R) CEO of Scale A.I. Alexandr Wang, American Enterprise Institute fellow Klon Kitchen and Global A.I. ethicist at DataRobot Dr. Haniyeh Mahmoudian testify during a hearing about artificial intelligence on Capitol Hill. (Photo by Drew Angerer/Getty Images) Getty Images Key Facts The new contract is with the Pentagon’s Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office and ranks among the larger deals the Pentagon has signed with an AI startup, according to Bloomberg, which first reported the contract. The startup, founded by 29-year-old billionaire Alexandr Wang, is also reportedly working on the Defense Innovation Unit's program to integrate AI into military planning and operations along with Anduril and Microsoft, as well as on President Donald Trump's proposed missile defense shield Golden Dome. In May, the Pentagon announced agreements with OpenAI, Alphabet, Nvidia, SpaceX, Microsoft, Amazon and Reflection for expanded use of advanced AI tools in military operations. Meta took a 49% stake in Scale AI last year and brought on Wang as the chief AI officer. Key Background The Scale AI deal is the latest in Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's push to fast-track AI adoption across the department. In a January strategy memo, Hegseth laid out plans to expand the use of AI tools and strip away what he described as bureaucratic barriers slowing the adoption of new technology. Scale AI, founded in 2016, built its business on data labeling—paying contract workers to label images and text used to train AI models—for customers including OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Meta, before pivoting more aggressively into defense work. Meta's $14.3 billion investment last year for a 49% stake brought Wang into Meta's superintelligence efforts and gave the social media giant significant exposure to the federal AI contracting boom. Big Number $29 billion. That’s Scale AI’s valuation after raising $14.3 billion from Meta last June. Forbes estimates Wang, who in 2022 held the title of world’s youngest self-made billionaire, is now worth $3.2 billion. Scale AI cofounder Lucy Guo, who left the company in 2018, took the title of world’s youngest self-made woman billionaire last April, unseating Taylor Swift, thanks to her 3% stake in the startup. Kalshi cofounder Luana Lopes Lara took the title in December 2025. Crucial Quote “As the era of small-scale AI pilots gives way to enterprise-wide deployment, the infrastructure decisions the Department makes known – which platforms to trust, which data operations to invest in, which partners to build for the long term – will shape the operational AI capabilities of the U.S. military for the decade ahead,” said Kathryn Harris, head of defense at Scale AI, in Wednesday’s press release.

Despite the pandemic, an exodus of tech companies, and a feared "doom loop," a one-two punch of return-to-office mandates and the explosion of AI startups has shifted San Francisco's tech center into smaller neighborhoods.

Loading audio narration...

Together AI is one of those startups, housed in the Design District, where office space costs around $59.53 per square foot, according to a fourth-quarter 2025 report from Cresa, a commercial real estate company. That is comparably more affordable than the cost of commercial space, which has hit $70 per square foot or more in the Financial District and Mission Bay, where OpenAI's office is located.

CEO Vipul Ved Prakash told Business Insider that due to the neighborhood's creative vibe and convenient parking, more AI companies moved within a one-mile radius, and many of Together AI's customers relocated right next to the company.

"We will debug problems together or even think about partnerships and doing other stuff together," said Prakash. "It's just easier to do that in person, and I think this is how these network effects work eventually, once you have a critical mass of companies."

Companies focused on AI, such as Virtual AI, Applied Compute, Rox AI, and Curai Health, are all located in the same building as Together AI. Other AI companies with a three-block radius include Scale AI, Resolve AI, and Gamma. Together AI is currently in talks to raise a new round of funding at a $7.5 billion valuation. Altogether, these companies have a valuation of more than $40 billion.

"It all happened very organically," Prakash added.

The current startup wave isn't the first to push into smaller neighborhoods like the Design District, which was traditionally an industrial hub for material supply warehouses, furniture manufacturing, and repair shops. A previous wave of tech and innovation already showed an inclination to reimagining where the office needs to be. Airbnb, for example, established its headquarters in the Design District in 2013 and renewed its ten-year lease in 2024.

Startup employees have different needs

Richard Florida, an urban studies theorist and professor at the University of Toronto, told Business Insider that traditional office districts like the Financial District were built for a time when companies stacked knowledge workers in vertical towers, but AI startups are quickly changing the landscape.

"An office district isn't an office district anymore — it's a mixed-use area," said Florida. "Startups and interesting creative companies need cheap, reconfigurable space, and space that they can add to quickly, and that's not in the office tower."

"What we're also learning in AI is that people are working much longer hours," Florida added. "So people are in the office like 9 a.m. to 11 p.m., and they need stuff around them that keeps them energized, like going out for a break, going for a walk, and doing something outside to recharge. The streets can't be dead after 5 p.m."

Geetha Rajan, director of strategy and business operations at Freshworks, specializing in AI strategy, told Business Insider she believes that the shift in startup culture will drive significant economic activity into pockets of San Francisco.

"A couple of years ago, the big bragging rights for a company was, 'I need to hire 10,000, 20,000 more people, or 50,000 more people.'" said Rajan. "But if you think about it now, it's a 10-person startup making millions of dollars already."

"Even though AI helps us be remote, the people who are building or the companies still very much like to be in person, whiteboarding, brainstorming," Rajan added, "Because at the pace at which these companies are moving, Zoom is not going to hold up to that."

Potential beneficiaries

Rajan said that the food delivery and catering scene, as well as local coffee shops, are perhaps the biggest winners as startup workers stay late at the office and come in on the weekends with little option but to order food to their workplaces.

DoorDash, for instance, wrote in its annual report that weekday lunch deliveries to San Francisco commercial addresses, such as offices, increased 15.7% from 2024 to 2025.

Rajan also said that many hackathon events and meet-and-greet-style activities for builders are now being held in quieter bars in small neighborhoods, often not far from some startup offices, bringing vibrancy to places people may have forgotten during the pandemic lockdown.

Between the Mission District and the Castro, several up-and-coming AI companies have also quietly set up offices along the main street, including Comp AI and Ace AI, just a few blocks away from the AI Start Academy.

Many startups, like Together AI, are occupying previously vacant spaces in areas that are not heavily residential. Thinking Machines Lab, the former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati's startup, notably occupies a 72,000-square-foot, three-story building in the Northeast Mission that was once an old factory.

"I often find myself at one of these events in some bar in the Mission, and I say 'oh, I haven't been here in quite some time,'" said Rajan.

Previous startup waves were different

Some economic experts, however, are skeptical that the AI boom will directly translate into real economic growth for small neighborhoods or for the city at large.

Ted Egan, the chief economist of the city of San Francisco, told Business Insider that while a new company opening up is theoretically almost always good for service-based businesses immediately next to it, this new class of startups looks very different from previous waves.

Compared with the last tech boom in the Mid-Market neighborhood, which generated increased economic activity when the former Twitter moved there and brought a lineup of heavyweights like Uber and Square with it, AI startups won't leave the same economic footprint.

"I'm not sure we're seeing the same local economic impact that we've seen from tech booms in the past," said Egan. "It's not to say they're not hiring anybody, but our tech job listings in the city are about half of what they were before the pandemic."

Egan pointed to city data showing that proceeds from sales tax in the Mission grew by 8% in 2025, but he is not confident it is driven by AI start-ups.

"I think that there is a clustering effect for these companies," Egan added, "But it's just that the spending profile of the companies that are getting VCs these days is very different than in the past because AI is so compute-intensive."

funding_news.full_text:
What is Alexandr Wang's net worth? Alexandr Wang is an American technology entrepreneur and billionaire who has a net worth of $3.2 billion. Alexandr Wang is best known as the co-founder and CEO of the artificial intelligence company Scale AI. He became one of the youngest self-made billionaires in the world after building a company that provides the data infrastructure used to train many of the most advanced AI systems. Scale AI supplies labeled data and tools that help companies develop machine learning models used in industries such as autonomous vehicles, defense technology, robotics, and generative artificial intelligence. In 2025, Meta made a massive $14.3 billion investment in Scale AI and recruited Wang to lead its artificial intelligence efforts, placing him at the center of the company's push to compete with rivals such as OpenAI and Google in the race to develop advanced AI systems. Wang founded Scale AI in 2016 while still a teenager, quickly attracting major Silicon Valley investors and establishing the company as a key supplier of AI training data for both technology firms and government agencies. Early Life Alexandr Wang was born in 1997 in Los Alamos, New Mexico. He grew up in a household deeply connected to science and technology. Both of his parents were physicists who worked at Los Alamos National Laboratory, one of the United States' most important research facilities. Growing up in an environment centered on scientific research had a significant influence on Wang's interests. As a student, he excelled in mathematics and computer science competitions and developed a strong passion for programming and engineering. During high school, he also gained early industry experience through internships and programming jobs at technology companies. After graduating from Los Alamos High School, Wang enrolled at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology to study mathematics and computer science. However, his time at MIT was short. He left school after being accepted into the Y Combinator startup accelerator program in order to pursue a technology startup full-time. Founding Scale AI In 2016, Alexandr Wang co-founded Scale AI with entrepreneur Lucy Guo. The company was created to address one of the most pressing challenges in the artificial intelligence industry: the need for massive quantities of accurately labeled data used to train machine learning models. Artificial intelligence systems require large datasets in order to recognize images, understand language, and make predictions. Much of this data must be labeled and organized before it can be used to train algorithms. Scale AI built tools and services designed to automate and streamline that process for companies developing AI technology. The startup quickly attracted attention from major venture capital firms including Accel and Founders Fund. As funding increased, Scale AI began working with many of the world's leading technology companies and AI developers. Scale's services became particularly valuable to industries that rely heavily on machine learning systems, including autonomous vehicles, robotics, e-commerce, and natural language processing. Growth and Industry Influence As the artificial intelligence industry expanded, Scale AI grew rapidly and positioned itself as a key infrastructure provider for AI development. The company developed tools that help organizations build high-quality training datasets for machine learning models, allowing companies to accelerate the development of AI systems. Scale AI's clients have included major technology firms, startups, and government agencies working on advanced artificial intelligence applications. The company's role in providing training data infrastructure made it a critical component of the broader AI ecosystem. Because of the increasing demand for AI tools and infrastructure, Scale AI achieved multi-billion-dollar valuations through successive funding rounds. Wang remained CEO throughout the company's growth, becoming one of the most prominent young leaders in the artificial intelligence sector. Meta Investment and AI Leadership A major turning point in Alexandr Wang's career came in 2025 when Meta made a massive $14.3 billion investment in Scale AI as part of its effort to accelerate development of advanced artificial intelligence systems. The investment significantly increased Scale AI's valuation and further established Wang as one of the most influential entrepreneurs in the AI industry. As part of the deal, Wang joined Meta in a senior leadership role overseeing the company's artificial intelligence initiatives. Mark Zuckerberg recruited him to help restructure Meta's AI strategy and build a team capable of competing with advanced AI models developed by companies such as OpenAI and Google. Wang was placed in charge of a newly formed research unit focused on developing next-generation artificial intelligence systems. Internally known as TBD Lab, the group was tasked with building powerful frontier AI models that could compete at the highest level of the rapidly evolving generative AI race. Meta also launched an aggressive recruitment effort to attract top researchers from leading AI organizations. The company offered large compensation packages in order to lure talent from rival firms and accelerate the development of its AI capabilities. Zuckerberg simultaneously announced plans to invest hundreds of billions of dollars in new data centers designed to support large-scale artificial intelligence training. Wang's leadership role placed him at the center of Meta's long-term ambition to build advanced AI systems that could rival the most powerful models in the world. Who's Richer? Alexandr

funding_news.full_text: AI wealth creation is astonishing. In the latest release of the "Hurun Global Rich List", Lucy Guo has entered the list with a net worth of 9 billion yuan, becoming the world's youngest self-made female billionaire born in the 90s. Her story is a microcosm of this wave of AI: ten years ago, she co-founded Scale AI, and even though she has long since left, she has entered the top 1% of the world's wealthy due to her rapidly expanding equity. Looking further, a grander picture of wealth is unfolding: more and more female entrepreneurs are rising strongly in the AI sector, becoming the new protagonists under the spotlight. Beyond the light and shadow, another path to financial freedom has also been opened. A group of young engineers, researchers, and even interns in AI companies have completed a leap in their fortunes in just a few years. At 31, she is the youngest female billionaire in the world. The growth story of a girl born in the 90s unfolds slowly. In 1994, Lucy Guo was born into a Chinese family in San Francisco, where her parents were electronic engineers. Like most Chinese parents, they believed that studying hard was the right path and were very strict with her education. Tutoring, competitions, and abacus practice were all part of her upbringing. She also showed her geeky talent early on. In her teens, she taught herself programming and sold virtual items online, earning her first money. Later, she successfully entered Carnegie Mellon University to study computer science. But fate soon opened another door for her—after receiving the Thiel Fellowship, she made a bold decision: to drop out and start a business. In 2016, she co-founded the artificial intelligence company Scale AI with Alexandr Wang. This company later became one of the most notable unicorns in the AI infrastructure sector. However, as the company was thriving, Lucy Guo chose to leave. The reason is not complicated. The two founders gradually had differences in the company's development direction: Alexandr Wang focused more on sales and customer expansion, hoping to quickly scale the business; while Lucy Guo believed that the company should invest more energy into the product and the team itself. The differences were hard to reconcile, and she eventually withdrew from daily operations. Fortunately, she did one crucial thing right: she firmly retained about 6% of her shares. With subsequent financing diluting this proportion to below 5%. Until 2025, when Meta acquired about 49% of Scale AI's shares, Lucy Guo's shareholding valuation once soared to about 1.25 billion USD, placing her in the top 1% of the world's wealthy. After leaving Scale, Lucy first ventured into VC, founding a venture capital firm called Backend Capital, focusing on early-stage startup investments. One of the firm's most successful investments was a six-figure bet on the financial software company Ramp in 2020, which is now valued at 32 billion USD. Subsequently, she personally founded the creator economy platform Passes and quickly secured over 65 million USD in financing. Faced with the sudden influx of wealth and attention, this young entrepreneur appeared quite calm: "To be honest, I still feel like that little girl; my life hasn't changed much after becoming wealthy." They are rising. Lucy Guo is by no means an isolated case. Broadening our view, more and more female founders are emerging. Turning to the Hurun list, another name of a Chinese woman born in the 90s is equally eye-catching—Shuo Wang from Northeast China. Her trajectory has a subtle overlap with Lucy Guo's; she also dropped out of MIT and returned to China to try her hand at entrepreneurship in Beijing. In early 2019, with keen insight into the trend of remote work, she founded the HR tech company Deel. In the following years of changing circumstances, this company hit the pain points of global hiring, with its valuation climbing to 17.3 billion USD (approximately 120 billion yuan). Now, 36-year-old Shuo Wang stands alongside Lucy Guo on the "Hurun Global Rich List". The momentum of post-00s women is equally fierce. A few months ago, an AI startup called Axiom Math caused a stir in Silicon Valley. The founder is 24-year-old Carina Hong from Guangzhou. This post-00s girl, who carries the aura of a "genius girl", has an impressive resume: she was a frequent winner in math competitions during high school, entered MIT at 17, and won honors such as the Morgan Prize; she then became a Rhodes Scholar, going to Oxford University to pursue a master's in neuroscience; and is now simultaneously pursuing dual PhDs in mathematics and law at Stanford University. However, just when her academic path seemed bright, Carina made a surprising decision: to drop out of Stanford and start a business full-time. (Image source: MIT) The Axiom Math she founded aims to use AI to solve extremely complex mathematical problems. In just a few months since its establishment, while the product is still in its early stages, Axiom Math has already achieved a valuation of over 300 million USD and completed a 64 million USD seed round financing. More dramatically, Carina successfully persuaded top international mathematician and Emory University professor Ken Ono to resign from his tenured position and join her team full-time. Carina Hong's journey may just be beginning, but this wave of deep technology led by Chinese women has already converged into a sea within a broader commercial landscape. A set of data is quite meaningful: the "2026 Hurun Global Rich List" features 285 self-made women, with China dominating with a 75% share. Behind this is a clear and profound commercial context. Over the past thirty years, the previous generation of female entrepreneurs in China has completed the initial accumulation of wealth in traditional industries. From the leadership of Luxshare Precision by Wang Lichun, to the creation of Lens Technology by Zhou Qunfei, and the founding of Longfor Group by Wu Yajun, they have laid down half of the territory in traditional fields such as manufacturing and real estate with their incredible resilience and execution, writing the wealth legend of Chinese women. Now, the baton has quietly passed. The new generation of female entrepreneurs often has top academic backgrounds and is familiar with cutting-edge science. They hold codes and computing power, entering the core battleground of global hard technology. AI produces young billionaires. One cannot help but marvel that the wave of AI wealth creation is more aggressive than ever before. Looking back at this wave of large model trends, the wealth paths of workers are also being rewritten. Compared to internet companies, these AI firms generally allocate a larger proportion of equity to ordinary employees. A typical example is Zhizhu. According to its prospectus, as of the end of June 2025, the company had 883 employees, of which 452 held shares, accounting for 51.2%. In other words, in Zhizhu, one in every two people is a shareholder. As early as 2021, the company established two employee stock ownership platforms, "Huihui" and "Zhideng", which collectively hold 16.55% of the company's shares. Among them, "Huihui" covers 426 current and former employees; "Zhideng" includes some employees and 16 full-time interns serving as algorithm consultants. The wide coverage of equity incentives is quite rare. Based on Zhizhu's current market value, if we exclude two executives from "Huihui", the average book value of shares held by the remaining 424 employees is about 35 million yuan. Similar stories have also occurred at MiniMax. This AI newcomer, established for less than five years, currently has about 385 full-time employees, with nearly all technical, product, market, and functional positions achieving employee shareholding. According to its prospectus, the average age of employees is only 29, with over 70% being R&D personnel; among them, 363 ordinary employees collectively hold about 3.41% of the total share capital after the IPO. Financial reports show that in the 2025 fiscal year, MiniMax's employee compensation expenditure reached 84.3 million USD (approximately 580 million yuan), while the total number of employees that year was 428, resulting in an average salary of nearly 1.35 million yuan. Looking back at the mobile internet era, ordinary employees often needed to accompany the company through a long cycle of 8 to 10 years to achieve wealth leaps through options, experiencing multiple rounds of reshuffling and waiting for the moment the IPO bell rings. But in the AI sector, this cycle has been significantly compressed. The rapid gathering of capital, technology, and talent has caused the value of equity held by early employees to multiply in just two to three years. The wave is sweeping in, and those who are part of it have become the lucky ones. AI has not only changed the world but has also reopened the wealth imagination space for ordinary people at an unprecedented speed. funding_news.title: Venture funding for female founders in 2025 was driven by AI firms like Anthropic and Scale AI
funding_news.ai_summary: Startups with at least one female founder raised a record $73.6 billion in 2025, double the $44.7 billion raised two years ago, according to PitchBook data analyzed by Fortune. However, the milestone is heavily skewed by mega-rounds from AI firms—Anthropic, cofounded by Daniela Amodei, and Scale AI, cofounded by Lucy Guo, together attracted more than $30 billion—while overall deal counts fell for the fourth consecutive year and all-female founding teams saw steeper declines.
funding_news.author: Emma Hinchliffe

industries.name: Gender Lens / Diversity, Equity & Inclusion (DEI) Funds

funding_news.full_text:
Let’s check in on venture funding and female founders. PitchBook’s latest report on funding to the cohort is out, and my colleague Lily Mae Lazarus has a new analysis for Fortune.

Recommended Video

The good: Startups with at least one female founder raised a record $73.6 billion in 2025, doubled from $44.7 billion two years ago. The bad: Deal count fell for the fourth year in a row. Fewer female-founded companies are closing deals. And worse: All-female founding teams—those without any male cofounders—saw a steeper drop in deal value and deal count. So what’s going on? Mega-rounds of AI firms with female co-founders are skewing the data. Anthropic, cofounded by Daniela Amodei, and Scale AI, cofounded by Lucy Guo, together brought in more than $30 billion in funding in 2025. For the first time ever, companies with at least one female cofounder accounted for more than one-quarter of total U.S. deal value in 2025—an “unprecedented” 27.7%. But that record depends entirely on Anthropic and Scale AI’s $183 billion and $74.1 billion valuations, respectively. Without these outlier companies, female-founded firms aren’t getting anywhere close to breaking that record. As influential AI companies build the future of the tech industry, it’s a positive that women are involved in these teams. Understanding what “skewing” the data means requires some nuance. At Anthropic, Daniela Amodei is a critical part of the team, leading alongside her brother Dario. At Scale AI, Guo no longer holds an active role, but because she was initially a cofounder its raises are counted in this dataset. And let’s not forget Mira Murati’s $2 billion fundraise for Thinking Machines Lab, a record size for a seed round; at that company, Murati also has male cofounders but is in the driver’s seat as CEO. Yet overall, it’s clear venture needs some sort of reset to get fully female-founded companies, outside of the flashiest AI startups, back in the game. P.S. funding_news.full_text:
[Report] Investments in big data startups jump 130.9% to $133.2b YoY

Artificial intelligence may have dominated headlines in 2025, but big data startups quietly delivered the fastest investment growth of the year. Funding into big data companies surged 130.9% year-over-year (YoY) to reach $133.2 billion, outpacing even the rapid expansion of AI financing and underscoring investors’ growing appetite for data-driven infrastructure.

While AI continued to command the largest overall share of venture capital, the explosive rise in big data investment highlights a parallel conviction among investors: the future of artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and digital services depends on scalable data architecture.

To better understand how this transition unfolded, the team at BestBrokers analysed venture capital activity using data from PitchBook, CB Insights, and LIQUiDITY. The analysis examined quarterly deal activity, long-term investment trends, regional distributions, and exit outcomes to provide a comprehensive recap of how AI investment evolved over the course of 2025 and how it compared with previous years.

AI captures the majority of global venture capital

In 2025, global venture capital investment in artificial intelligence startups climbed to $270.2 billion, representing 52.7% of the $512.6 billion deployed worldwide. For the first time on record, AI and machine learning companies accounted for more than half of total global VC deal value, overtaking all other sectors combined.

Despite a continued slowdown in overall deal activity, AI funding proved resilient. Quarterly venture deal counts fell to 9,844 in Q4 2025 - the lowest level since early 2020 - yet AI-focused deal volumes remained comparatively stable. Investors are writing fewer cheques, but increasingly concentrating capital in AI companies with proven technology, enterprise traction, and infrastructure relevance.

The transition to AI dominance unfolded gradually. In 2023, AI represented 27.5% of global VC deal value, rising to 40% in 2024 before surpassing the 50% threshold in late 2024. By 2025, artificial intelligence had firmly established itself as the primary destination for venture capital worldwide.

Fewer deals, larger cheques

Venture capital firms have shifted from the aggressive, broad-based investment approach of 2021–2022 to a more selective strategy focused on established leaders and infrastructure providers.

Quarterly AI funding rose from $38.9 billion in Q1 2022 to more than $70 billion per quarter by the end of 2025. The inflection point came in Q4 2024, when AI investment reached $66.7 billion and, for the first time, accounted for more than half of total venture capital deployed.

Momentum continued through 2025:

Q1: $75.5 billion

$75.5 billion Q2: $56.9 billion

$56.9 billion Q3: $65.4 billion

$65.4 billion Q4: $72.4 billion

By comparison, all other sectors combined raised between $56 billion and $66 billion per quarter during the year.

AI deal activity remained steady at roughly 2,700 to 3,300 transactions per quarter, reflecting structural resilience even as broader venture markets cooled. Early-stage activity held firm, but average deal sizes increased significantly, concentrating capital in a smaller number of companies.

Record-breaking funding rounds

Several landmark deals defined 2025’s investment landscape.

SoftBank set a new record in Q1 with a $40 billion investment in OpenAI, marking one of the largest private technology investments in history.

In September, Anthropic raised $13 billion in a Series F round led by ICONIQ Capital, tripling its valuation to $183 billion and solidifying its position as the second-most valuable private AI company globally at the time.

Meta made the second-largest investment of the year, committing $14.3 billion to Scale AI in exchange for a 49% stake.

Meanwhile, xAI secured $10 billion in debt and equity financing, lifting its estimated valuation to $200 billion. The company also acquired X in a $33 billion all-stock transaction, integrating social media distribution with AI development capabilities.

Elsewhere, Thinking Machines Lab raised a record-breaking $2 billion seed round - the largest of its kind - highlighting investor willingness to back elite AI teams even before product launch.

Regional investment trends

North America

North America maintained overwhelming dominance in 2025, attracting $214.5 billion - 79.3% of global AI venture capital. Within the region, AI accounted for 63.8% of all VC funding, demonstrating the sector’s outsized role in shaping investment flows.

The United States remains the epicentre of AI infrastructure development, from high-performance chipmakers to cloud-based inference platforms. A notable example includes Groq, which raised $750 million to expand its cloud and hardware deployments.

Europe

European AI startups secured $36.7 billion, accounting for 13.6% of global AI investment. AI represented 43.4% of total European VC activity.

French firm Mistral AI and UK-based Nscale led several multi-billion-dollar funding rounds, underscoring the continent’s selective but growing AI ecosystem.

Asia and emerging markets

Asian AI startups raised $15.3 billion, representing 5.7% of global AI funding. Regional AI investment accounted for just under one-fifth of total VC capital, constrained by regulatory pressures and slower exit markets.

Latin America attracted $1.6 billion in AI funding - 25.9% of the region’s total venture capital - while the rest of the world accounted for $2.3 billion combined.

Deal volumes reflected similar patterns: North America recorded 6,075 AI transactions, Europe 2,857, Asia 2,232, Latin America 217, and other regions 456.

Big data’s explosive growth

While AI secured the largest absolute share of capital, big data startups experienced the most dramatic year-over-year acceleration. Investment jumped 130.9% to $133.2 billion, signalling investor recognition that AI’s expansion depends fundamentally on scalable data infrastructure, analytics platforms, and enterprise-grade processing capabilities.

The surge suggests a complementary dynamic: as AI applications scale, demand for high-performance data storage, processing, governance, and security solutions is rising in tandem. Rather than competing with AI, big data appears increasingly intertwined with it - forming the backbone of the next generation of digital infrastructure.

Methodology

This report is based on the latest available global venture capital activity data from PitchBook and CB Insights, supplemented with information from LIQUiDITY, DealRoom, and disclosures from leading venture investors. The analysis examines quarterly deal activity, long-term investment trends, regional distribution, and major funding rounds throughout 2025.

funding_news.ai_summary: Scale AI has filed a lawsuit against the US Department of Defence in the Court of Federal Claims over a contract dispute, with court documents sealed due to classified information. The company lost a $708 million contract bid from the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency to Enabled Intelligence last year, filed a bid protest with the Government Accountability Office that was dismissed in January, and filed suit two days later. 2025 AI Infrastructure Investments Ara Eve Leo Sal 1x

[1] Infrastructure components, including chips, data centers, and enabling technologies, emerged as a primary focus, with billion-dollar mega-rounds driving capital inflows despite a notable slowdown in deal activity during the second half of the year.[1] **In 2025, AI infrastructure investments surged amid a record-breaking year for global private AI venture funding, reaching $225.8 billion—nearly double the 2024 total—according to CB Insights' State of AI 2025 report published January 13, 2026.Infrastructure components, including chips, data centers, and enabling technologies, emerged as a primary focus, with billion-dollar mega-rounds driving capital inflows despite a notable slowdown in deal activity during the second half of the year.

[1] AI infrastructure ranked among the leading categories for new unicorns, including companies focused on inference platforms and specialized chips.[1] This funding boom concentrated on scaling the foundational technologies required for advanced AI model training, inference, and deployment. Mega-rounds (deals of $100 million or more) accounted for 79% of total AI funding in 2025, reflecting investor preference for large bets on established players and high-potential infrastructure ventures.AI infrastructure ranked among the leading categories for new unicorns, including companies focused on inference platforms and specialized chips.

[2] AI inference chip startup Groq secured $750 million in the same quarter to meet surging demand for fast, efficient compute.[3] In December 2025, Nvidia entered a $20 billion non-exclusive licensing agreement with Groq for its inference technology, while also integrating key Groq team members.[4] Earlier in the year, Meta invested $14.8 billion in Scale AI in Q2 2025 for a 49% stake, bolstering access to high-quality data labeling and enabling technologies critical for model development.[1] Notable deals underscored the emphasis on infrastructure. In September 2025, AI data center provider Nscale raised $1.1 billion to expand deployment across Europe, North America, and the Middle East, backed by investors including Nvidia and Aker ASA.AI inference chip startup Groq secured $750 million in the same quarter to meet surging demand for fast, efficient compute.In December 2025, Nvidia entered a $20 billion non-exclusive licensing agreement with Groq for its inference technology, while also integrating key Groq team members.Earlier in the year, Meta invested $14.8 billion in Scale AI in Q2 2025 for a 49% stake, bolstering access to high-quality data labeling and enabling technologies critical for model development.

[1] The concentration of capital in infrastructure reflects the growing recognition that advances in chips, data centers, and related systems would determine the pace of AI progress beyond 2025. These investments highlight the strategic priority placed on building robust physical and computational foundations to support frontier AI models, even as overall deal volume declined in the latter half of 2025.The concentration of capital in infrastructure reflects the growing recognition that advances in chips, data centers, and related systems would determine the pace of AI progress beyond 2025.

Overview

Introduction

[1] In 2025, AI infrastructure emerged as a primary focus and key growth area in global venture funding for artificial intelligence, reflecting an important evolution in the sector's investment priorities. Following years of rapid growth in generative AI models and applications after the early 2020s breakthroughs, the escalating demands of frontier model training and inference exposed fundamental constraints in compute power, energy resources, and specialized hardware. This created a clear bottleneck: continued AI advancement required massive scaling of foundational infrastructure—including chips, data centers, and enabling technologies—rather than solely funding end-user applications.

[1] Historically, AI investment cycles have tracked technological inflection points, with enthusiasm building around new capabilities before shifting toward enabling infrastructure to support sustained progress. Over the preceding five years, sectors like robotics maintained consistent deal share amid overall AI funding growth, while others such as digital health and fintech declined in relative prominence, signaling a gradual reorientation toward hardware and systems necessary for scaling. By 2025, this trend accelerated as rising model training costs and competitive pressures divided the market into those with access to substantial resources and those without, compelling investors to prioritize the buildout of an AI-native technology stack to address efficiency, energy, and computational limitations.

[1] These dynamics culminated in a record year for private AI venture funding, with global investments reaching $225.8 billion—nearly double the previous year's total—despite a slowdown in deal volume in the second half of the year. Mega-rounds and larger check sizes across stages underscored a strategic focus on fewer, higher-impact bets on infrastructure to enable long-term scalability and innovation in AI.

CB Insights State of AI 2025 Report

CB Insights State of AI 2025 report, published on January 13, 2026, provides a detailed analysis of global AI investment trends throughout 2025, drawing on CB Insights' proprietary data to track funding, deal activity, and sector shifts.[1] Thereport, published on January 13, 2026, provides a detailed analysis of global AI investment trends throughout 2025, drawing on CB Insights' proprietary data to track funding, deal activity, and sector shifts.

[1] This pattern reflected investors' concentration on large-scale bets to support the scaling of AI capabilities, even as quarterly deal counts declined from mid-year peaks.

Global Funding Landscape

Record Venture Funding Total

[1] This figure represented the highest annual total ever recorded for private AI investments, driven by a concentration of capital into larger deals despite a slowdown in overall deal activity during the year's second half.

[1] AI infrastructure—including chips, data centers, and enabling technologies—served as a primary focus for these investments.

Year-over-Year Growth

[1][5] Global private AI venture funding in 2025 reached a record $225.8 billion, nearly doubling the previous year's total and marking one of the most significant year-over-year increases in the sector's history.

[1][5] This growth represented approximately a 109% increase over 2024's approximately $108 billion, driven primarily by concentrated investments in AI infrastructure such as chips, data centers, and enabling technologies despite a broader venture market context.

[1] The near-doubling reflected sustained investor confidence in the foundational elements required to scale AI capabilities, with mega-rounds and strategic deals contributing disproportionately to the annual total.

Deal Activity Patterns

[1] Deal activity in 2025 AI venture funding displayed a marked temporal pattern, with robust deal volume early in the year giving way to a softening in the second half despite record overall funding totals. Global private AI companies raised $225.8 billion in venture capital, nearly doubling the $114.4 billion from 2024, as reported in CB Insights' State of AI 2025 report.

[6] Deal numbers peaked in the second quarter at 1,937, followed by declines to 1,586 in the third quarter and 1,550 in the fourth quarter, reflecting a broader slowdown in the latter half of the year.

[6] This reduction in deal activity contrasted sharply with funding trends, as quarterly investment remained strong—reaching $27.6 billion in Q1, $29.9 billion in Q2, $28.1 billion in Q3, and surging to $83.2 billion in Q4—driven by a concentration of capital in fewer, larger transactions.

[1] Mega-rounds ($100 million or more) played a pivotal role in sustaining and elevating total funding levels, accounting for 79% of the year's $225.8 billion despite the drop in overall deal count.

[1] These mega-rounds enabled the divergence between declining deal volume and escalating funding amounts, with such large deals comprising 86% of Q4 funding alone.

AI Infrastructure Sector Focus

Definition and Core Components

AI infrastructure refers to the foundational physical and technological elements required to support the development, training, inference, and deployment of advanced artificial intelligence systems at scale. In the context of the 2025 investment landscape, as documented in CB Insights' State of AI 2025 report, AI infrastructure emerged as a significant focus area amid record global private AI venture funding.[1][5] refers to the foundational physical and technological elements required to support the development, training, inference, and deployment of advanced artificial intelligence systems at scale. Investment Drivers

[1] The heavy allocation of capital to AI infrastructure in 2025 stemmed primarily from surging demand for compute power, advancements in inference efficiency, and the urgent expansion of hyperscale data center capacity, as investors sought to address foundational bottlenecks constraining AI progress.

[1] Escalating compute requirements drove much of the investment, as frontier AI models demanded massive hardware resources for training and development amid rising costs in hardware, talent, and energy. This demand concentrated capital on infrastructure to sustain innovation in large language models, robotics, and AI agents, with top AI developers alone channeling significant funds toward these needs.

[1][5] Inference efficiency emerged as another core driver, as the shift from model training to widespread production deployment required optimized technologies to deliver fast, cost-effective performance at scale. Investments targeted specialized chips and platforms that reduced latency and energy use, reflecting a market maturation where operational efficiency became essential for commercial viability.

[7] Hyperscale data center capacity addressed structural constraints, with rapid AI adoption creating pressure on global computing infrastructure, power availability, and cooling systems. Organizations faced acute shortages in capacity and specialized computing resources, prompting investments to enable enterprise-scale deployment and support growing workloads.

[1] These technological and economic forces aligned with market dynamics favoring larger, concentrated bets on infrastructure enablers, even as overall deal activity softened in the year's second half. This infrastructure focus persisted within the broader context of record global private AI venture funding.

Mega-Rounds and Billion-Dollar Deals

[1] The surge in AI infrastructure investments in 2025 was overwhelmingly driven by mega-rounds and billion-dollar deals, which concentrated capital in fewer transactions and propelled overall funding totals despite a marked slowdown in deal volume during the second half of the year. Mega-rounds—defined as deals of $100 million or more—accounted for 79% of total AI funding, creating a top-heavy landscape where large bets on select companies outweighed broader deal activity.

[1][5] Deal activity peaked in the second quarter before declining below 2024 levels in the latter half of 2025, yet funding continued to soar due to these substantial investments in fewer rounds. This pattern was especially pronounced in AI infrastructure—encompassing chips, data centers, and enabling technologies—where billion-dollar rounds sustained momentum amid softening transaction numbers. In the third quarter alone, there were six billion-dollar deals overall, including notable infrastructure examples such as Nscale's $1.1 billion raise, reflecting investor prioritization of foundational technologies essential for scaling AI capabilities.

[5] Notable examples in the infrastructure space included Nscale (AI data centers) and Groq (AI inference processors), alongside major deals such as Meta's investment in Scale AI, illustrating how mega-rounds funneled capital toward critical hardware and compute platforms. This reliance on large-scale financing underscored a shift toward concentrated bets on infrastructure leaders amid broader market caution.

Major Investments and Companies

Nscale AI Data Centers

Nscale is a UK-based provider of AI infrastructure, specializing in the development and operation of data centers and compute platforms optimized for large-scale artificial intelligence workloads. The company focuses on vertically integrated solutions that deliver GPU capacity, leveraging low-cost renewable energy sources and prioritizing regulatory compliance, security, and energy efficiency for enterprise and government clients.

[8][9] The round was led by Norwegian energy conglomerate Aker ASA and included participation from investors such as NVIDIA, Dell, Nokia, Point72, Fidelity Management & Research Company, G Squared, Blue Owl Managed Funds, Sandton Capital, and T.Capital.[8] In September 2025, Nscale raised $1.1 billion in a Series B funding round, described as the largest Series B in European history.The round was led by Norwegian energy conglomerate Aker ASA and included participation from investors such as NVIDIA, Dell, Nokia, Point72, Fidelity Management & Research Company, G Squared, Blue Owl Managed Funds, Sandton Capital, and T.Capital.

[8] This funding supported rapid scaling of GPU-intensive infrastructure to address surging demand for compute resources needed for AI training and inference.[8] The proceeds were allocated to accelerate the global deployment of large-scale "AI factory" data centers, including projects such as Stargate UK and Stargate Norway, while expanding Nscale's AI cloud platform across Europe, North America, and the Middle East.This funding supported rapid scaling of GPU-intensive infrastructure to address surging demand for compute resources needed for AI training and inference.

[1] This deal exemplified the market's emphasis on mega-rounds to build out specialized compute capacity, despite a slowdown in deal activity in the year's second half.[1] Nscale's 2025 raise occurred amid a broader surge in AI infrastructure investments, as documented in CB Insights' State of AI 2025 report, which recorded a record $225.8 billion in global private AI venture funding for the year, nearly double the 2024 total, with infrastructure—including data centers—serving as a primary focus.This deal exemplified the market's emphasis on mega-rounds to build out specialized compute capacity, despite a slowdown in deal activity in the year's second half.

Groq AI Inference Processors

In the third quarter of 2025, Groq, a pioneer in specialized processors optimized for AI inference, raised $750 million in a funding round that elevated its post-money valuation to $6.9 billion.[3][10]

[3][3] The round was led by investment firm Disruptive, which contributed nearly $350 million, with participation from BlackRock, Neuberger Berman, Deutsche Telekom Capital Partners, and other investors including Samsung, Cisco, and Altimeter. This capital influx supported Groq's expansion of global data center infrastructure and its mission to deliver high-speed, low-cost AI inference compute worldwide, reinforcing its position within the American AI technology stack amid surging demand for efficient model execution. Founder and CEO Jonathan Ross emphasized that "inference is defining this era of AI," positioning Groq's technology as critical infrastructure for powering developers and enterprises.

[1][4] Later in December 2025, Groq entered a significant non-exclusive technology licensing agreement with Nvidia, widely reported as a $20 billion deal that granted Nvidia access to Groq's inference technology while integrating key Groq personnel—including founder Jonathan Ross and president Sunny Madra—into Nvidia to scale the licensed innovations. Groq continued operating independently, with Simon Edwards assuming the CEO role, and its GroqCloud service remaining uninterrupted. This arrangement aimed to accelerate global deployment of high-performance, low-cost AI inference capabilities and exemplified the trend of strategic partnerships in the sector.

[1][3] These developments highlighted Groq's prominence in addressing the growing need for specialized inference hardware, distinct from training-focused architectures, as investors and major tech companies prioritized solutions capable of delivering rapid, energy-efficient AI processing at scale.

[1] This transaction, detailed in CB Insights' State of AI 2025 report, valued Scale AI at more than $29 billion and represented one of the largest single investments in the AI infrastructure sector that year.[1][11] In the second quarter of 2025, Meta Platforms invested $14.8 billion to acquire a 49% stake in Scale AI, a leading provider of high-quality labeled data and annotation services essential for training advanced AI models.This transaction, detailed in CB Insights' State of AI 2025 report, valued Scale AI at more than $29 billion and represented one of the largest single investments in the AI infrastructure sector that year.

[11] As part of the agreement, Scale AI founder and CEO Alexandr Wang joined Meta to contribute to its AI initiatives, while remaining a director on Scale's board; Jason Droege, Scale's Chief Strategy Officer, was appointed interim CEO.[11][12] The deal included a substantial expansion of the commercial relationship between Meta and Scale AI, aimed at accelerating the deployment of Scale's data solutions to support Meta's AI development efforts.As part of the agreement, Scale AI founder and CEO Alexandr Wang joined Meta to contribute to its AI initiatives, while remaining a director on Scale's board; Jason Droege, Scale's Chief Strategy Officer, was appointed interim CEO.

[12] This move aligned with broader industry patterns in 2025, where major technology firms pursued significant stakes in data-centric infrastructure providers to bolster their competitive positions amid rapid AI advancement.[1] Strategically, the investment enabled Meta to secure reliable access to high-quality training data, addressing a critical bottleneck in scaling large language models and other AI systems.This move aligned with broader industry patterns in 2025, where major technology firms pursued significant stakes in data-centric infrastructure providers to bolster their competitive positions amid rapid AI advancement.

Other Notable Infrastructure Deals

In addition to the headline-grabbing mega-rounds, 2025 saw a range of significant investments in AI infrastructure companies focused on specialized hardware, cloud compute, and enabling interconnect technologies. These deals, while often smaller than the largest foundation model financings, highlighted sustained investor appetite for building the underlying capabilities needed to support expanding AI workloads despite a late-year slowdown in overall deal volume.

[13] Cerebras Systems, a pioneer in wafer-scale AI chips designed to accelerate large-scale training and inference, raised $1.1 billion in a Series G round at an $8.1 billion valuation.

[13] Lambda, which operates a GPU cloud platform tailored for AI developers and enterprises, secured $480 million in Series D funding at a $2.5 billion valuation to expand its AI cloud infrastructure.

[13] Celestial AI attracted $250 million in Series C financing at a $2.5 billion valuation for its photonic interconnect technology, which aims to reduce bottlenecks in data center-scale AI systems.

[13] Modular raised $250 million to advance its unified compute layer for AI workloads, while Baseten obtained $150 million in Series D funding at a $2.1 billion valuation to enhance its platform for deploying and scaling AI models.

[13] Other notable rounds included Mythic's $125 million venture investment in power-efficient AI compute hardware and TensorWave's $100 million Series A for its AMD-powered AI cloud infrastructure.

[14] These investments collectively illustrate the diversification of capital into alternative chip architectures, specialized cloud providers, and interconnect innovations critical to addressing compute constraints in the AI ecosystem.

Key Players and Partnerships

Leading Investors

[1] The leading investors in AI infrastructure during 2025 encompassed a broad coalition of corporate strategics, asset managers, traditional venture firms, private equity players, and specialized infrastructure funds. These entities channeled capital primarily into chips, data centers, and enabling technologies, often through mega-rounds that concentrated funding amid a broader slowdown in deal volume in the year's second half.

[1] Corporate investors stood out for their strategic involvement, with technology giants like Meta and Nvidia deploying substantial resources to bolster AI infrastructure capabilities through direct investments and technology partnerships. Their participation underscored the integration of AI compute needs with core business objectives in cloud, hardware, and data services.

[15][3] Asset managers and institutional investors, including BlackRock and Neuberger Berman, emerged as increasingly influential players, directing significant capital toward scaling AI chip and inference technologies. This shift reflected growing institutional appetite for the physical and hardware underpinnings of AI growth.

[8][16] Specialized infrastructure and private equity firms, such as Blue Owl, Aker ASA, Blackstone, and Macquarie Asset Management, focused on expanding data center capacity and hyperscale platforms critical for AI workloads. Their expertise in large-scale asset deployment complemented venture-oriented approaches.

[17] Investment conglomerates like SoftBank also drove activity through major commitments to digital infrastructure assets, positioning themselves to capitalize on sustained demand for AI-supporting facilities.

[1] This investor landscape highlighted a maturation in AI infrastructure financing, with diverse capital sources aligning behind the foundational technologies powering the sector's expansion.

Strategic Technology Partnerships

[1] In 2025, strategic technology partnerships—particularly non-equity licensing and collaboration agreements—played a crucial role in advancing AI infrastructure, allowing companies to access specialized capabilities without full acquisitions amid heightened regulatory scrutiny and competitive pressures in the chip and inference markets. These deals enabled rapid integration of innovative technologies while preserving independence for startups and fostering collaboration between established leaders and emerging players.

[4][1] The most prominent example was the December 2025 non-exclusive licensing agreement between Nvidia and Groq, valued at $20 billion. Under the deal, Groq licensed its specialized low-latency AI inference technology—centered on its Language Processing Unit (LPU) chips designed for efficient execution of trained AI models—to Nvidia, enabling broader global access to high-performance, low-cost inference solutions.

[1][18] The agreement also included Nvidia hiring key Groq personnel, including founder Jonathan Ross, president Sunny Madra, and other team members, to help advance and scale the licensed technology. Groq continued as an independent company under new CEO Simon Edwards, with its GroqCloud platform operating uninterrupted. This structure has been characterized as a "quasi-acquisition" approach, allowing Nvidia to secure critical inference expertise while avoiding antitrust risks associated with outright takeovers.

[1] Such partnerships underscored the strategic value placed on inference optimization in 2025, as companies sought to differentiate in a market increasingly focused on efficient deployment of large-scale AI models.

Impact and Outlook

Economic and Technological Implications

[1] The substantial investments in AI infrastructure during 2025 significantly accelerated compute availability across the ecosystem. Record private venture funding of $225.8 billion, nearly doubling the previous year's total, channeled massive capital into hardware, energy resources, and specialized technologies needed to support large-scale model training and deployment.

[19] This influx enabled rapid data-center expansion, as major players committed to constructing hyperscale facilities to meet surging computational demands. Notable examples included Meta's Hyperion project in Louisiana, targeting 5 gigawatts of compute power, and broader initiatives such as the Stargate joint venture planning multiple large-scale data centers to bolster U.S. AI infrastructure capacity.

[1] Technologically, targeted investments in inference-focused hardware and platforms drove reductions in inference costs, making production-scale AI deployment more economical. Specialized inference processors from companies like Groq, bolstered by high-profile deals such as Nvidia's $20 billion technology licensing agreement, improved efficiency and lowered operational expenses for real-time AI applications.

[1] These advancements collectively broadened access to high-performance compute resources, fostering greater innovation and adoption of AI technologies across sectors while strengthening the foundational layer of the AI economy.

Challenges in Late-2025 Market

[5][6] This softening contrasted with sustained high funding levels driven by mega-rounds ($100 million+), which accounted for 79% of total funding, reflecting a shift toward fewer but larger investments.[1] Deal activity peaked in Q2 2025 at 1,937 deals before declining in the latter half of the year, with Q3 falling to 1,586 deals (an approximately 18% quarter-over-quarter drop) and Q4 dropping further to 1,550 deals, an 11% year-over-year decline in the final quarter.This softening contrasted with sustained high funding levels driven by mega-rounds ($100 million+), which accounted for 79% of total funding, reflecting a shift toward fewer but larger investments.

[1] This concentration highlighted emerging risks for smaller startups, including escalating model training costs, high expenses for hardware, talent, and energy, and growing barriers to entry that widened the divide between well-funded leaders and others.[1] The market became increasingly "top-heavy," as investors concentrated capital on established players and frontier model developers, while median check sizes rose across all stages compared to 2024.This concentration highlighted emerging risks for smaller startups, including escalating model training costs, high expenses for hardware, talent, and energy, and growing barriers to entry that widened the divide between well-funded leaders and others.

Future Investment Trends

Building on the surge in AI infrastructure investments observed in 2025, particularly through large-scale funding rounds, industry projections indicate sustained focus on three key areas: inference hardware, energy-efficient data centers, and enabling software.

[20] Inference hardware is expected to become a primary battleground for innovation, as enterprises shift from model training to widespread production deployment of AI applications. Specialized processors, including ASICs and other non-GPU accelerators, are projected to see accelerated adoption due to their advantages in latency, energy efficiency, and cost compared to general-purpose GPUs, with demand for inference-specific solutions growing as workloads scale in data centers. This trend aligns with the increasing recognition of inference as a revenue-generating phase, driving investment in purpose-built chips to support real-time, high-volume AI tasks.

[21] Energy-efficient data centers will remain a priority amid rising power and thermal demands from AI workloads. Advances in cooling technologies, such as liquid and hybrid systems, along with optimized architectures that match resources to specific tasks, are anticipated to address efficiency challenges and enable sustainable scaling of infrastructure.
