Lyra Link integrations (Workday, Alight, ParetoHealth, Salesforce, internal HR tools) and the Carrum Health specialty care partnership (Jan 2026) and Hazelden Betty Ford SUD partnership (Sept 2024) extend Lyra from a mental health point solution into a broader specialty care orchestration layer.

company_assessment.market_position: Lyra Health is a privately held, venture-backed workforce mental health care company founded in 2015 and headquartered in Burlingame, California. The company is the leading workforce mental health benefits provider in the U.S., serving more than 20 million people globally through direct employer contracts and over 100 million through health plan and partner relationships. Lyra reports $890 million in cumulative equity funding (Series F $200M in 2021 at a $4.6B valuation; additional $235M in 2022), is trusted by marquee customers including Starbucks, Salesforce, Morgan Stanley, Genentech, and the School District of Philadelphia, and is the first workforce mental health provider to earn NCQA Credentialing Accreditation (July 2024). The company operates internationally under the Lyra International brand following the 2022 acquisition of ICAS World, extending its reach into 200+ countries and territories.

strengths.details: Lyra Empower and Lyra AI unify HR, provider, and member data into a single AI-powered platform; as member count scales (currently 20M+ direct, 100M+ through partners), the matching algorithm, documentation automation, and predictive insights improve with data, creating a flywheel that pure-play therapy competitors cannot match.
strengths.headline: AI-native platform creates compounding defensibility

strengths.details: Workday Wellness, Alight Partner Network, ParetoHealth (3,500+ employers / 1.2M individuals), Thatch, and Salesforce ecosystem integrations turn Lyra's employer customer acquisition into a partner-led motion; as more benefits platforms embed Lyra, marginal customer acquisition cost declines while reach expands.
strengths.headline: Channel partnerships unlock exponential distribution growth

strengths.details: Acquisition of Bend Health (July 2025) and launch of the Center of Excellence for Pediatric & Young Adult Mental Health expand Lyra beyond adult workforce care into a family mental health model; with 54% reduction in pediatric healthcare spend and 15,500+ pediatric providers, this positions Lyra to capture the underserved youth mental health category.
strengths.headline: Pediatric and family mental health opens a major new TAM

strengths.details: Centers of Excellence for Neurodiversity, Women's Mental Health, and Chronic Conditions, plus the Rogers Behavioral Health partnership and Hazelden Betty Ford SUD program, position Lyra as a full-continuum behavioral health provider; this shifts the conversation from EAP replacement to comprehensive specialty care, raising per-employee revenue and reducing churn.
strengths.headline: High-acuity specialty care deepens wallet share per employer

strengths.details: ICAS World extends Lyra's footprint to 155+ countries with 66 languages; the Lyra International operation under President Andrew Davies is positioned to capture multinational employer demand, opening revenue streams well beyond the saturated U.S. enterprise market.
strengths.headline: Global expansion through ICAS World scales internationally

weakness.details: Spring Health, Modern Health, Headspace Health, and Talkspace are all well-funded and aggressively pursuing the same employer buyers; as the category matures, customers may demand longer outcomes-based guarantees and lower per-employee pricing, eroding Lyra's unit economics despite its scale advantages.
weakness.headline: Competitive intensity could compress pricing and growth

weakness.details: Lyra's revenue is concentrated in B2B employer contracts sold on annual subscription cycles; in a recession or HR budget tightening (as seen in 2024 industry layoffs), mental health benefits are often reduced, paused, or not renewed, creating direct revenue exposure to macroeconomic cycles.
weakness.headline: Macro-driven employer benefit cuts could pressure revenue

weakness.details: Increasingly active regulators (FTC, state medical boards, and emerging federal AI-in-healthcare frameworks) are scrutinizing AI in clinical contexts; an adverse event, model bias finding, or restrictive regulation on AI-driven matching, documentation, or coaching could force product changes and damage Lyra's AI-driven differentiation.
weakness.headline: AI regulatory backlash in mental health is a tail risk

weakness.details: Lyra's $4.6B 2021 valuation was set in a frothy mental health funding environment; in a higher-rate, more disciplined environment, primary capital may come at flat or down valuations, forcing existing investor marks down and complicating future fundraising or M&A optionality.
weakness.headline: Valuation reset risk versus 2021 peak

weakness.details: With ICAS World and Bend Health integrated simultaneously while launching AI products, expanding Centers of Excellence, and onboarding new leadership, Lyra's focus and operational bandwidth are stretched; integration missteps could stall organic growth, inflate costs, and pressure margins that already required a 2024 restructuring.
weakness.headline: Acquisition integration may dilute focus and margins

competitive_moat.details: Lyra distributes through enterprise direct sales plus an unusually deep channel stack: health plan partnerships covering 100M+ lives, Workday Wellness integration, ParetoHealth ecosystem (3,500+ employers, 1.2M individuals), Alight Partner Network, benefits consultants, and the Thatch consumer marketplace. This multi-channel reach is rare for a mental health benefits vendor and meaningfully lowers customer acquisition cost relative to direct-only competitors.

Lyra reports a 99% customer renewal rate and an 80 NPS among HR/benefits leaders, with Lyra Link deeply embedding the platform into HRIS, benefits administration, and workflows. The 8M+ cumulative sessions and longitudinal clinical data locked inside the platform create operational and clinical switching friction that competitors must overcome contract by contract.

The brand is anchored by marquee enterprise logos (Salesforce, Starbucks, Walmart, Morgan Stanley, Genentech, Peraton, TD Bank, Lululemon, School District of Philadelphia), 20+ peer-reviewed publications cited by 200+ research groups, and Lyra being the first and only workforce mental health provider to earn NCQA Credentialing Accreditation (July 2024). Together these signal a clinically credible brand that is difficult for new entrants to replicate quickly.

Lyra operates a curated network of 30,000+ evidenced-based providers across 200+ countries/territories and 66 languages, accepting only 19% of applicants with 100,000+ hours of annual clinical oversight. Larger member volume funds more rigorous vetting and broader geographic coverage, which in turn attracts more employer contracts and more providers, producing a virtuous quality-and-coverage loop.

Lyra has accumulated clinical and operational data from 20M+ directly served members and 8M+ sessions, which feeds AI matching (95% first-recommendation stick rate), outcome benchmarking, and a 20-publication peer-reviewed evidence base. The data flywheel compounds Lyra's ability to personalize matching and demonstrate outcomes to enterprise buyers.

Lyra holds HITRUST CSF, SOC 2 Type 2, HIPAA-compliant operations, and is the first workforce mental health vendor to earn NCQA Credentialing Accreditation (July 2024). These certifications and the Polaris Principles safety framework meaningfully raise the bar for new entrants competing for risk-averse health plan and large employer buyers.

Leadership combines former Experian North America CEO Jennifer Schulz (CEO since Jan 2025), CFO Sandra Beaver (ex-Evolus), Chief Clinical Officer Alethea Varra PhD, Chief Product & Technology Officer Jenny Gonsalves (16+ years CRM), VP Clinical Product & Research Anita Lungu PhD (two PhDs, JAMA Psychiatry publications), and co-founder/Stanford-affiliated Bob Kocher MD. The doctorate-heavy clinical leadership (PhDs in clinical psychology + clinical AI research) is unusual for the category and supports evidence-based product claims.

Lyra Link integrates with Workday Wellness, Alight, ParetoHealth, Salesforce, and internal HR systems, while health plan and benefits consultant channels embed Lyra into the broader benefits stack. Once a buyer's benefits ecosystem routes through Lyra Link, displacement requires re-platforming across multiple vendors rather than swapping a single point solution.

key_risks.details: Lyra laid off approximately 2% of its workforce in November 2024, affecting non-clinicians, indicating margin pressure or right-sizing needs despite a 1,001-5,000 headcount; the move coincided with broader digital health budget tightening and may reflect a path to profitability not previously anticipated.
key_risks.headline: November 2024 workforce reduction signals cost discipline needs amid growth-stage pressures

key_risks.details: CEO transition in January 2025 (Jennifer Schulz replacing prior leadership) and new CFO in June 2025 (Sandra Beaver) coincide with major AI platform launches, two large acquisitions, and a $4.6B-valuation company needing to mature into late-stage financial discipline; multiple simultaneous leadership and strategy changes elevate execution risk.
key_risks.headline: Recent C-suite turnover creates execution risk during critical growth phase

key_risks.details: Lyra's last disclosed post-money valuation was $4.6 billion at the June 2021 Series F; with rising rates, compressed public-market mental health comps, and a 2026 round reportedly smaller in absolute size, the company likely faces valuation pressure versus its 2021 peak.
key_risks.headline: $4.6B 2021 valuation creates potential down-round or mark-down exposure

key_risks.details: Lyra competes against Spring Health, Modern Health, Headspace Health, Talkspace, and others in workforce mental health; many peers are venture-backed with comparable offerings, which can compress pricing, escalate customer acquisition costs, and limit share-of-wallet growth.
key_risks.headline: Highly competitive category with multiple well-funded direct competitors

key_risks.details: Lyra's revenue model is B2B enterprise subscription sales to employers; mental health benefits are often among the first trimmed during macroeconomic slowdowns, layoffs, or HR budget reviews, creating revenue concentration and cyclical exposure.
key_risks.headline: Enterprise customer concentration exposes Lyra to employer cost-cutting cycles

key_risks.details: Lyra completed the ICAS World acquisition in January 2022 (extending reach to 155+ countries) and Bend Health in July 2025 (pediatric mental health); integrating distinct clinical models, technology stacks, provider networks, and cultures while maintaining quality and growth introduces meaningful execution risk.
key_risks.headline: Integration risk from two sizable acquisitions (ICAS World, Bend Health)

key_risks.details: Lyra AI powers clinical co-pilot features, conversational member support, and AI-drafted clinical documentation in a regulated healthcare context; any safety incident, hallucination, or regulatory action against AI in mental health could materially damage brand trust and trigger compliance scrutiny.
key_risks.headline: AI safety and regulatory risk in mental health care delivery

key_highlights.details: Lyra serves more than 20 million people globally through direct employer contracts and more than 100 million through health plan and partner relationships; cumulative equity raised of ~$890M leads the mental health startup category per 2026 market data.
key_highlights.headline: Scaled to 20M+ direct members and 100M+ through partners, the most-funded mental health startup

key_highlights.details: Lyra's enterprise customers include Salesforce, Starbucks, Morgan Stanley, Genentech, Walmart, Lululemon, Uber, Cummins, and others; reports 99% customer renewal among health plan customers and an 80 NPS among HR/benefits leaders, evidencing strong product-market fit and embedded switching costs.
key_highlights.headline: Marquee enterprise customer base with 99% renewal rate and 80 NPS

key_highlights.details: Lyra Empower is the only fully integrated AI-powered platform unifying data across HR leaders, providers, and members; Lyra AI delivers 95% member retention on first AI-matched provider and is grounded in the proprietary Polaris Principles safety framework, with 100,000+ hours of annual clinical oversight.
key_highlights.headline: Differentiated AI platform (Lyra Empower / Lyra AI) with clinical-grade safety framework

key_highlights.details: Lyra reports 3:1 ROI ($1 invested saves $3 in healthcare costs), 26% annual reduction in healthcare claims costs, 9 in 10 members clinically improve, 2x faster recoveries, and 10x utilization over traditional EAPs, validated by Aon analysis and JOEM-published study.
key_highlights.headline: Validated clinical outcomes and ROI drive compelling value proposition

key_highlights.details: Lyra's network spans 200+ countries and territories, 66 languages (post-ICAS World acquisition), and 30,000+ vetted providers with only a 19% acceptance rate; this network depth and quality bar creates a defensible moat that scales with growth.
key_highlights.headline: Global curated provider network spanning 200+ countries with rigorous quality gating

key_highlights.details: Lyra became the first and only workforce mental health provider to earn NCQA Credentialing Accreditation (July 2024), in addition to HITRUST and SOC2 certifications, signaling enterprise-grade regulatory readiness and a credentialing moat relative to peers.
key_highlights.headline: First-and-only NCQA Credentialing Accreditation, plus HITRUST/SOC2 compliance

key_highlights.details: Lyra published its 20th peer-reviewed study in March 2025; research has been cited by 200+ other research groups and is led by a doctorate-level clinical team (Anita Lungu PhD, Jennifer Lee PhD, Alethea Varra PhD), providing evidence-based differentiation in a category often criticized for weak outcomes data.
key_highlights.headline: Strong clinical research engine with 20+ peer-reviewed publications

customer_concentration.details: Customer concentration risk appears Moderate. The customer base is large and diversified across industries (healthcare, construction, retail, finance, defense, education, manufacturing, technology) and includes many large enterprise logos (Salesforce, Starbucks, Walmart, Morgan Stanley, Genentech, TD Bank, Lululemon, SurveyMonkey, Cummins, Peraton, School District of Philadelphia, JE Dunn, Inova, WakeMed, Sheppard Mullin), plus distribution through 100M+ lives via health plan channels and 3,500+ employers via ParetoHealth — indicating meaningful revenue diversification beyond any single account. However, named marquee customers are clustered in the U.S. enterprise segment and large-logo case studies dominate Lyra's public references, suggesting meaningful revenue contribution from a relatively concentrated set of Fortune-class employers even if no single customer appears dominant. The 99% customer renewal rate and quote-based annual contracts imply high revenue predictability but also sensitivity to large employer churn events (e.g., layoffs, M&A, benefit redesigns). Geographic concentration in the United States adds an additional, moderate, dimension of risk.

GlossGenius Becomes Genius AI: Inside the $1.15B Bet on the Physical Economy
July 23, 2026
GlossGenius (Techstars 2015) has rebranded as Genius AI after raising a Series D at a $1.15B valuation, betting that AI will make human expertise more valuable, not less, in the in-person service economy.
GlossGenius (Techstars 2015) just changed its name. Not because the beauty and wellness scheduling app people fell in love with was broken, but because it had outgrown what its old name could hold.
This week, the company announced a Series D at a $1.15 billion valuation, pushing its total capital raised past $125 million. Alongside the raise, the company introduced a new corporate name, Genius AI, with GlossGenius continuing on as its flagship product.
The rebrand isn't cosmetic. As co-founders Danielle Cohen-Shohet and Leah Cohen-Shohet explained in a note published the same day, the customer base has grown well beyond beauty and wellness, and the product has grown well beyond software. The new name reflects both.
From Back-Office Tool to “Physical Economy” AI
GlossGenius launched on a simple premise. Let service professionals focus on their craft instead of their back office. The founders bootstrapped the company for years, deliberately starting with an industry they saw as one of the most technologically underserved in America, beauty and wellness. Every hour a stylist or esthetician spent chasing no-shows, reconciling payments, or managing a calendar was an hour taken from clients.
That focus has scaled. GlossGenius now says it powers more than 125,000 businesses across half of all U.S. ZIP codes, spanning salons, med spas, physical therapy practices, and wellness studios. The company estimates its platform has saved those businesses 112 million hours of administrative work and helped generate more than $2 billion in additional revenue, with the business itself approaching a $200 million revenue run rate this quarter.
The bigger claim in the founders' note is about where AI is headed next. Their argument is that as models automate more knowledge work, in-person, human expertise, think the stylist, the physical therapist, the trainer, becomes more valuable, not less. They point to roughly 8 million U.S. businesses built around this kind of hands-on service work, representing more than $2 trillion in annual spend. Genius AI's bet is that this "physical economy" is entering its best era, and that the winning platform will be the one that runs the admin work autonomously rather than just helping with it.
That shift is already visible in the product. Beyond its core scheduling, payments, and point-of-sale tools, GlossGenius has been rolling out AI agents, including a Growth Agent, a Marketing Agent, and a Reception tool that answers calls and texts around the clock, aimed at automating the busywork that surrounds every appointment rather than just recording it.
The Pitch, in One Line
The announcement's headline captures the thesis the company is now built around. "Your genius is the craft. Let everything else run itself." It's a bet that the value of human expertise rises as AI takes over everything adjacent to it, and that GlossGenius, now under the Genius AI banner, wants to be the layer that disappears so the practitioner doesn't have to think about it.
Learn more at genius.ai.

launches.full_text:
NEW YORK, NY / ACCESS Newswire / July 21, 2026 / Genius AI, the technology platform for in-person service businesses, today announced $44 million in Series D financing at a $1.15 billion valuation. The round was led by Lux Capital, with participation from Bessemer Venture Partners, Imaginary Ventures, L Catterton Growth, 2048 Ventures, StepStone Private Ventures, and other existing investors, bringing the company's total capital raised to more than $125 million. Source: Genius AI (EZ Newswire) Alongside the financing, the company announced its new corporate name, Genius AI. This name reflects the expansion of its customer base and product vision: helping every service business run itself. That work began with GlossGenius, which today is now one of the flagship products of Genius AI. GlossGenius automates workflows like scheduling, payments, marketing, staff, and client management. GlossGenius is used widely across single and multi-location businesses with staff in verticals like beauty, wellness, and health-related services. GlossGenius will be joined by additional agentic products that execute the work end-to-end rather than assist with it, as part of the Genius AI platform. In-person service businesses represent one of the largest opportunities for AI transformation. There are roughly 8 million of these businesses that generate more than $2 trillion in annual spend. Yet the average owner loses nearly a third of every week to administrative work. As advancing model capabilities make it possible to complete multi-step work autonomously, Genius AI believes AI will expand capacity for human-to-human care - making many services more human, not less. "The best work happens with a true partner beside you. As identical twins, we grew up with that - someone who understands you and makes you better. That's what we want for every owner," said Leah Cohen-Shohet, co-founder and Chief Business Officer of Genius AI. Today, more than 125,000 businesses across half of all U.S. ZIP codes run on the platform. The company estimates its products have saved customers 112 million hours of administrative work, helped them generate $2 billion in additional revenue, and facilitated more than 624 million client touchpoints. The company is approaching a $200 million revenue run-rate. "We believe technology in our space will do the opposite of what people fear: not flatten human craft into automation, but free people to be more present, more expressive, and more connected to the people they serve," said Danielle Cohen-Shohet, co-founder and CEO of Genius AI. "One of the most powerful things AI can do isn't to replace what makes us human. It is to give us room to be more human."

Story Continues

launches.full_text:
According to a recent LinkedIn post from Spring Health, the company is emphasizing the growing importance of family mental health as a workplace concern during the back-to-school period. The post outlines practical steps employers can take to support working parents, including flexible schedules, psychological safety, and better awareness of children’s mental health warning signs.

The post suggests that Spring Health is positioning its offerings as relevant to employers seeking year-round mental health support for employees and their dependents. For investors, this focus underscores a potential demand driver in the employer-sponsored mental health benefits market, particularly among enterprises aiming to reduce productivity loss and retention risk tied to parental stress.

By highlighting family-oriented mental health needs, Spring Health appears to be targeting broader utilization of its services beyond individual employees. This framing may support deeper integration with HR and benefits strategies, potentially increasing contract stickiness and expanding addressable spend as organizations seek comprehensive solutions for workforce well-being.

The emphasis on early identification of child and adolescent distress could also signal opportunities for Spring Health to differentiate its product set with specialized resources. If employers respond by enhancing benefits in this area, Spring Health could capture incremental revenue from expanded coverage tiers and larger per-employee-per-month budgets within the competitive digital mental health landscape.

launches.full_text: Whole You, Powered by Spring Health, extends personalized mental health care to more than 245,000 California state employees across 153 departments SACRAMENTO, Calif., July 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- California's firefighters, police officers, parks departments, correctional staff, and many others spend their careers keeping communities safe and helping people through their worst days. Nationally, first responders develop PTSD at up to ten times the rate of the general population, according to a 2025 meta-analysis published in Clinical Psychology Review[1]. It's a toll that builds quietly over the routine weight of emergency response and is compounded during high-intensity stretches like fire season. The California Department of Human Resources (CalHR) is now providing the state's employees and their families access to Whole You, Powered by Spring Health, CalHR's new Employee Assistance Program (EAP) offering confidential, personalized support for care, crisis needs, work-life challenges, and everyday wellbeing. A lifelong mental health platform, Spring Health will deliver mental health care to more than 245,000 California state employees across 153 departments, and their eligible family members. First responders receive the most extensive tier of care under the new program, delivered by trauma-informed providers with direct experience in first responder roles. Support staff within CalFire, the California Highway Patrol and the Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation also receive an elevated level of support, reflecting the higher-stress nature of their roles. The State's 153,000 administrative or desk-based staff will also receive support under the new program. CalHR was drawn to Spring Health's proven outcomes, not just improved access. According to research published in OJPHI and JAMA Network Open, 92% of members reliably improve or recover from depression or anxiety, and members recover 5.9 weeks faster than the leading competitor, with appointments available in less than two days on average, compared to a 48-day average with traditional EAPs. "First responders put themselves in harm's way over and over again to protect the communities they serve. That takes a toll not just on them, but on their families too," said George Michaels, Chief Revenue Officer at Spring Health. "Partnering with CalHR to support more than 245,000 state employees is exactly the kind of large-scale, public-sector commitment we built Spring Health to deliver on, and we're honored to help deliver the mental health support they and their families deserve." "When people go to work, they shouldn't have to leave their hearts at home," said Shannon MacGregor, Statewide Employee Assistance Program Manager at the California Department of Human Resources. "Our first responders carry things most of us never have to. Whole You is our commitment that when they need support, it's there — fast, confidential and built around what they've actually experienced." Whole You, Powered by Spring Health, is available now to California state employees and their eligible dependents through their department's benefits resources. For more information on Spring Health's lifelong mental health platform, visit our webpage. About Spring Health Spring Health is a global mental health company built on one AI-native platform so care follows individuals across every job, move, health plan, and life stage. Independently validated by JAMA Network Open and the Validation Institute, with 92% of members reliably improved or recovered from depression or anxiety and employers seeing a 52% reduction in total mental health claims costs, Spring Health provides personalized lifelong mental health support across self-guided tools, coaching, therapy, medication management, and specialty care. launches.title: Can AI Prevent Suicides? – Communications of the ACM
launches.ai_summary: Spring Health, a mental health organization, has developed VERA-MH (Validation of Ethical and Responsible AI in Mental Health), an open-source clinically validated evaluation framework launched in October 2025 to measure how AI chatbots detect and respond to suicide risk, addressing growing concerns following lawsuits and incidents where AI allegedly contributed to suicides.
launches.author: Esther Shein

industries.name: General Mental Health Therapy Platforms (Talk Therapy)
Safety, Alignment & Content Moderation (Guardrails, Red Teaming)

launches.full_text:
A metal health organization is looking to measure how generative AI tools detect and respond to suicide risk.

As chatbots become more widely used as de facto mental health therapists, news about models encouraging people to commit suicide is growing more common. For example, Google Gemini has been cited in a wrongful-death suit alleging that the chatbot drove a 36-year old Florida man into delusional behavior and ultimately coached him toward committing suicide. The mother of a 14-year-old U.K. teen alleges her son also fell prey to a chatbot and took his life as a result. The parents of a 16-year-old boy who took his own life testified before a Senate subcommittee about the harmful effects of chatbots. The list goes on. Now, a mental health organization called Spring Health is looking to measure how generative AI (GenAI) tools detect and respond to suicide risk. The company has developed VERA-MH (Validation of Ethical and Responsible AI in Mental Health), which it maintains is the industry’s first open-source, clinically validated evaluation framework for this purpose. Adam Chekroud, cofounder of Spring Health, says that just as cars must have seatbelts, technology for mental health needs a safety standard. AI creates enormous potential in mental health by expanding access, reducing stigma, and supporting people between sessions in ways that weren’t possible a few years ago, Chekroud said. But the potential for harm is just as real, he added. “We’re currently in the middle of a massive, unregulated experiment where millions of people are turning to general-purpose AI for support, guidance, and even answers to therapeutic questions,” he said. “These models weren’t designed to work directly with mental health issues. Most lack clinical oversight, regulatory safeguards, and reliable crisis response mechanisms.” This puts individuals at risk in their most vulnerable moments, and puts employers responsible for their workforce’s well-being in an difficult position, Chekroud said. AI has been part of Spring Health’s model since day one, he said, and company officials “held ourselves to a strict internal safety bar: Anything touching a member or provider had to be clinician-co-developed, rigorously tested, and validated as safe.” Yet when Chekroud’s staff went looking for an external standard against which to benchmark their work, they couldn’t find a shared, clinically grounded definition of what “safe” actually means for AI in mental health, he said. “That absence of standards was a gap, not a failure; it was simply that no one had built a way to measure it yet,” Chekroud said. “We weren’t going to wait for a catastrophic failure to change that.” VERA-MH was developed in collaboration with the AI in Mental Health Safety & Ethics Council, an organization convened by Spring Health that includes practicing clinicians, healthcare leaders, ethicists, and AI developers, he said. The framework is designed to evaluate whether an AI system can recognize signs of crisis, respond appropriately, escalate to a human clinician when warranted, and maintain clear safety boundaries. “We started with suicide risk because that’s where getting it wrong carries the greatest potential for harm,” Chekroud explained. The framework was launched in October 2025, followed by an open consultation period that lasted for months and allowed external stakeholders to provide feedback. Chekroud said it was important to his team that VERA-MH be open source from the start. “Our goal was always widespread adoption to raise the bar on the overall safety of AI, not gatekeeping,” he said. The feedback was overall positive, with reviewers “noting that the benchmark is a strong and thoughtful starting framework for evaluating safety in mental health AI,” he said. The most common feedback focused on refining rubric definitions and rating criteria for what is safe vs. unsafe AI behavior; ensuring the set of user personas is diverse and not biased; and emphasizing the ultimate need for real-world validation against clinical standards and outcomes, Chekroud said. In response, the VERA-MH team refined the evaluation rubric for greater clarity and consistency, strengthened the representation and heterogeneity of user personas, and improved the scoring approach to make outputs more actionable and easier to interpret by developers and other stakeholders, Chekroud said. The free open-source code lets any developer plug VERA-MH into their system and infrastructure and receive a structured overall safety score, along with scores for five distinct safety dimensions, so problems can be identified and fixed before they reach users in crisis, Chekroud said. The five dimensions are: detecting potential risk, confirming risk, guiding users to human care when needed, maintaining supportive conversation, and respecting AI boundaries. For employers, health plans, and benefits consultants, Chekroud said VERA-MH offers a consistent clinical benchmark for evaluating and comparing AI mental health and other chatbots on how well they detect and respond to indications of suicide risk, and understanding how safe AI chatbots are in other parts of their benefit systems. For researchers and policymakers, it creates a shared language for developing guidelines and, eventually, regulation, he said. “One of the core problems in this space is that everyone is operating by their own internal definitions of ‘safe.’ VERA-MH won’t solve that overnight, but it gives the field a common starting point.” Mental health providers had mixed opinions on whether a framework for evaluating the safety of chatbots used in mental health will be effective. Dr. Paul Nestadt, a psychiatrist, epidemiologist, and associate professor at Johns Hopkins University, where he serves as medical director of the Center for Suicide Prevention, said a benchmark is a good idea in theory. While not familiar with VERA-MH, Nestadt said it could be a harm reduction measure, but he is concerned a benchmark may be an “imperfect measure.” Right now, AI is unpredictable, Nestadt noted; it’s different than software that people are used to, which is deterministic. In contrast, “AI is probabilistic, so it doesn’t act the same way twice. . . . Let’s say you’re able to train a model that does just what you want it to do; at the end of the day, it’s unpredictable.” That said, Nestadt likes the idea of “a publicly facing benchmark that is independently validated” and judges an AI model on its ability to escalate a situation to a human in the event of a crisis. At the same time, having benchmarks doesn’t preclude accidents from happening. “It just means we sort of agree that there needs [to be] some basic, bare minimum” standard, Nestadt said. It remains to be seen whether AI will ever have clinical judgment. Karla Ivankovich, a licensed clinical therapist, said she is not clear it will. Unfamiliar with VERA-MH, Ivankovich said she’d like to “see it in action” to determine whether it has properly vetted a chatbot. “AI generators are intended to basically help people complete a task,” Ivankovich said. “So if the task is for AI to sound more compassionate, we have to measure whether those benchmarks are going to interrupt [a person] from ideation to action.” The introduction of VERA-MH is “a major advancement,” said Dr. Sam Zand, a psychiatrist and CEO of Anywhere Clinic, which provides psychiatric telemedicine services. “A clinically informed open-source framework that defines how artificial intelligence should identify and respond to crises is precisely what is needed in the healthcare profession. The emphasis on recognition, response, escalation, and safety boundaries connects very closely to our current methods of evaluating suicide risk in the field of psychiatry.” Zand added that the biggest obstacle will be ensuring that the standard is able to effectively capture the nuance of indirect expressions of distress and produce consistent results in real-world situations. “For a standard to take hold in the marketplace, it must demonstrate credibility, be transparent, exhibit collaborative multi-stakeholder support, and obtain some degree of regulatory or institutional endorsement,” Zand said. “Ultimately, how effective these approaches are will determine if they are adopted into practice.” Dr. David Wolff, medical consultant at the New Life Mental Health rehabilitation center in New Jersey, said there is an urgent need for standardized expectations around safety, escalation, empathy, and referral to human care. “Mental health professionals should be involved in the creation of an industry benchmark for how generative AI detects and responds to suicide risk,” Wolff said. “Minimum safety standards for recognizing crisis signals can guide users toward human support.” How a chatbot responds to a person in crisis can “dramatically vary between platforms,” Wolff said. “The inconsistency creates real safety concerns for vulnerable users.” Chekroud said VERA-MH findings reveal significant variation in how commercially available AI chatbots identify and respond to potential suicide risk, highlighting the need for consistent safety standards. “Emerging research and evaluation frameworks like VERA-MH are already showing that some AI systems recognize suicide risk signs far better than others,” Wolff said. “When people disclose suicidal thoughts to an AI model, they shouldn’t be left to chance and having to depend on which app or model they happened to open that day.” Chatbot users may have a false sense of safety and trust when talking to AI, he added. “Unfortunately, these tools might miss warning signs or respond in ways that escalate the situation. Industry benchmarks will result in a safer experience for the millions of people who are already using AI tools while in emotionally vulnerable moments.” Chekroud said the team is encouraged that evaluations of leading general-purpose chatbots by VERA-MH show that “most models have gotten safer over time.” However, “gaps remain in consistently confirming risk in ambiguous situations and effectively guiding users to appropriate human care or support,” he said. “While most models are able to generally maintain supportive conversations and adhere to safety boundaries, there is still room for improvement across those areas, too.” Yet he believes this is a start, and momentum for the benchmark will continue to grow. “Without shared standards, accountability is impossible,” Chekroud said. “You can’t hold an industry to expectations that no one has written down.” Esther Shein is a freelance technology and business writer based in the Boston area.

launches.title: For Caregivers of Neurodivergent Children, Finding the Right Care Is a Full-Time Job
launches.ai_summary: Spring Health, a global mental health company, launched its Neurodiversity Program to provide specialized care for children with neurodivergent needs and their caregivers, requiring no formal diagnosis to begin. Research cited in the announcement shows caregivers spend more than 10 hours per week coordinating care, translating to over $18,000 in lost earnings annually. The program utilizes AI through Spring Health's Guide platform to streamline care navigation, reduce administrative burden, and connect families with clinically appropriate in-network support.
launches.author: Spring Health

industries.name: Behavioral Health for Children & Adolescents (Youth Services)

launches.full_text:
Caregivers of neurodivergent children spend more than 10 hours a week coordinating care, a burden that translates to over $18,000 in lost earnings annually. Spring Health's new Neurodiversity Program is designed to change that. NEW YORK, June 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- For many working parents of neurodivergent children, getting care still means long waitlists, fragmented referrals, and a cycle of trial and error that can stretch on for years. The toll is financial as much as emotional. Studies show that the 10+ hours a week1 spent coordinating care for a neurodivergent child costs families more than $18,000 in lost earnings annually2. That burden shows up every day, in distraction, absenteeism, and the decisions employees make about whether to stay. As the school year ends and summer begins, the pressure intensifies: changes in routine are hard on everyone, the resources families rely on during the school year are often less available, and working caregivers carry more between their child's care and their job. Today, Spring Health, a global mental health company built on one AI-native platform, launched the Neurodiversity Program, specialized care for children with neurodivergent needs and their caregivers, with no formal diagnosis required to begin. The Neurodiversity Program provides care across the full spectrum of needs through specialized care navigation, multidisciplinary support for the child, coaching and skills support for caregivers, and neuropsychological assessments. Powering it all is Guide, Spring Health's AI-led experience built to replace the endless phone calls, paperwork, and administrative burden so caregivers don't need to be case managers. For families already using the Neurodiversity Program, the impact has been immediate. "For once, I feel like I'm not alone in this. I never understood how anxiety and ADHD-related challenges can overlap, or how much they can affect the behaviors I was seeing day to day. That helped me understand my child in a new way. Thank you for helping us get started, giving me direction, and helping us move forward," said a working parent and Spring Health member. "Caregivers spend months, sometimes years, chasing answers, coordinating care across providers who don't talk to each other, and absorbing a weight that follows them everywhere," said April Koh, co-founder and CEO, Spring Health. "The right support, found earlier, changes the trajectory not only for the child's life, but the entire family." For employers, the Neurodiversity Program is designed to restore productivity for working caregivers by providing the most clinically appropriate, cost-effective in-network care for their child and expert, hands-on caregiver support. This gives employees the headspace to show up as the best versions of themselves at home and work. "I know this problem from the inside. My family lives it," said Gijo Mathew, Chief Product Officer at Spring Health. "What breaks caregivers is the years of wrong turns: the wrong referral, the wrong provider, the wrong care. We built the Neurodiversity Program to close that gap with one coordinated system that helps families understand what to do next and how to keep moving forward." The Neurodiversity Program is available now to Spring Health customers. For more information, visit springhealth.com/what-we-do/neurodiversity. Independently validated by JAMA Network Open and the Validation Institute, with 92% of members reliably improved or recovered from depression or anxiety and employers seeing a 52% reduction in total mental health claims costs, Spring Health provides personalized lifelong mental health support across self-guided tools, coaching, therapy, medication management, and specialty care. launches.title: We Spent the Last Decade Building the AI-Native Mental Health Company the Next Decade Will Need
launches.ai_summary: Spring Health co-founders reflect on the company's 10-year anniversary, positioning the first decade as the analog-to-digital transformation of mental healthcare and announcing their vision for an AI-native future. The company cites independently validated clinical outcomes including 92% patient improvement rates, 56% faster recovery times, and $1,796 in annual cost savings per patient. The next decade strategy centers on two new capabilities: Alma, which maintains therapist continuity across coverage changes, and Guide, an AI system providing continuous care support across providers and life stages.
launches.author: Written Byadam Chekroudpresident

industries.name: General Mental Health Therapy Platforms (Talk Therapy)

launches.full_text:
April and I started Spring Health 10 years ago today. When we did, mental healthcare was almost entirely analog. You called a 1-800 number. You worked your way through a phone tree. You waited weeks for an appointment, then left work and drove across town to keep it. The most personal experience in someone's life was delivered through the least personal infrastructure imaginable. The last decade was about closing that gap. We replaced phone trees with a platform. We gave people direct visibility into who their provider is, what they specialize in, and exactly when they are available. That was the analog-to-digital decade. The next one is AI-native. The mental healthcare it produces will look almost nothing like what came before. Where care still breaks Digital solved real problems. Faster access. Better matching. Transparent provider information. Outcomes you could actually measure. The experience, though, was still built around the transaction, not the person.

Better support, better outcomes, stronger teams. Explore how Spring Health helps organizations reduce costs and improve lives. Book a demo Featured articles Why Spring Health Is Joining Forces with Alma Why We Built Guide as a Multi-Agent System Instead of One Big Agent We Need AI Chatbots to Identify Suicide Risk Every Single Time. VERA-MH Can Help Feel better faster Get therapy, coaching, and medication support as low as $0 and as soon as tomorrow. Find care Featured articles Why Spring Health Is Joining Forces with Alma Why We Built Guide as a Multi-Agent System Instead of One Big Agent We Need AI Chatbots to Identify Suicide Risk Every Single Time. VERA-MH Can Help You can see it in the most ordinary version of trying to get help.

They find a therapist. They build trust. They make progress.

Then they change jobs, move, switch health plans, or need a different level of care, and the thread breaks.

The system asks them to start all over again at exactly the moment they have the least energy to do it.

That is the problem that has stayed with us from the start. Even when care worked, it rarely stayed intact across the normal changes in a person's life. Even the best solutions of that era, ours included, optimized the transaction. They could create access to a moment of care. They did not solve for the lifetime. What the digital decade got right We founded Spring Health on a conviction: mental healthcare did not need to be trial and error. We proved a new clinical model, Precision Mental Healthcare, that made care far more personal, identifying the treatments and providers that worked best for each individual. Every match, every outcome, and every signal fed a model that learns what works, for whom, and under what circumstances. Ten years and millions of patients later, the results are independently validated and peer-reviewed: 92% of patients reliably improved or recovered from depression or anxiety, and they get better 56% faster than any other clinical model.

And that patient’s healthcare costs $1,796 per year less as a result

Those numbers matter because they show that better mental healthcare isn’t a vague aspiration or a nice to have. It's here today, it's working, it is saving companies money, and it improves over time as the system learns.

What AI-native actually means The machine learning we built into Spring Health from day one was the first version of this idea. What is possible today is a generational leap beyond it.

The availability and affordability of general-purpose LLMs have revealed more demand for mental and emotional support than ever before. Millions of people are already turning to these tools every day for support, reflection, and guidance. LLMs have exposed just how often the formal system was unavailable, unaffordable, or inaccessible when people needed help.

Legacy mental health systems are responding by bolting AI onto the old system, to speed up workflows, summarize notes, and look more modern. What they lack is a model of care that:

Remembers context.

Learns over time.

Helps support continue across providers, coverage changes, and life stages.

That requires a different foundation: the one we’re building over the next decade. Building lifelong continuity You wouldn't sign up for a 401(k) if you knew you'd lose the balance and start over from zero every time you changed jobs. That is exactly what mental healthcare has asked people to do for decades. Every coverage change, every job change, every move resets the clock.

AI-native architecture changes that. It makes lifelong continuity possible in two layers: a relationship that stays with you, and a thread that carries your story forward. The relationship: Alma Alma’s coverage is what makes it possible to keep the therapist you trust, even when your employer changes plans or you change jobs. With more than 170 million people worldwide now able to access Spring Health, we have the foundation in place to protect the progress a person has built, across the changes that have always interrupted it.

You stay with your care team. You stay with the relationship that is doing the work. The trust you have built does not reset to zero. The thread: Guide Guide is Spring Health's AI that supports people across every stage of their mental health journey, and the part of this that is genuinely new. It carries the context of your care across providers, sessions, and life stages. It provides a continuous thread that stays with you, learns from you, and helps every interaction with care build on every one that came before. Not as an alternative to therapy, but as the kind of memory that has never existed in healthcare before.

‍ Guide is still early, but it is already proving its clinical impact in one of the most fragile periods of any care journey, the first few weeks, when most people fall off. In our first peer-reviewed study, members using Guide attended 5% more therapy sessions in their first seven weeks, completed their second session sooner, and improved continuity of care from 57% to 60%.

People do not just need help finding care. They need help staying engaged with it long enough for it to work.

None of this came at the expense of the human relationship. Members using Guide reported no decline in therapeutic alliance with their providers. AI-native infrastructure does the work humans structurally cannot do, while preserving space for the work only humans can do. For a provider, that means showing up to every session with the full picture, not just what the patient remembers to mention. Together The relationship holds. The thread carries your story forward. Together, they make something possible that has never been possible in mental healthcare before: care that follows you, learns from you, and gets stronger the longer your story is intact.

The bar AI has to clear LLMs revealed the scale of the need. They also revealed their limits. They are immediate, but they are not built for longitudinal care, clinical context, or mental health safety. They have shown both the size of the opportunity and the risk of getting it wrong.

If AI is going to play a meaningful role in mental healthcare, it has to be held to a real standard. That is why Spring Health co-developed and open-sourced VERA-MH: the first open-source AI safety benchmark for mental health. The bar should be public, independently verifiable, and applied to everyone in the category, ourselves included. The next 10 years The first decade of Spring Health was about making mental healthcare digital, measured, and precise.

The next one will make it continuous, lifelong, and AI-native.

That is what we have been building toward for the last decade. It is what the next decade of mental healthcare will require. It is what the next decade will demand from all of us.

launches.title: Spring Health Launches 'Guide,' New AI Experience That Improves Mental Health Outcomes
launches.ai_summary: Spring Health, a global mental health company, has launched Guide, an AI-led mental health experience that the company states is backed by clinical evidence and a safety framework. A recent study by Spring Health found that individuals supported by Guide experienced faster improvement in depression and anxiety symptoms, with those needing care most showing up to 25% greater symptom improvement. Guide is now available to select Spring Health customers as the company positions itself as a lifelong mental health platform.
launches.author: Spring Health

industries.name: General Mental Health Therapy Platforms (Talk Therapy)
Outpatient Mental Health Clinics & Counseling Centers

launches.full_text:
Safety-tested and backed by clinical evidence, Guide helps members improve outcomes faster with continuous, personalized support NEW YORK, April 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Mental healthcare has a continuity problem. Care resets each time something changes. Progress disappears. The next clinician starts from scratch. Today Spring Health, a global mental health company built on one AI-native platform, launches Guide, an AI-led experience with something no other mental health product has: clinical proof that it improves outcomes, and a safety framework developed by worldwide technology and clinical experts to identify and close the failure modes that have caused harm elsewhere. In a recent study by Spring Health, individuals supported by Guide experienced faster improvement in depression and anxiety symptoms. And those who needed care most saw the strongest gains — up to 25% greater symptom improvement. "Mental healthcare has always been treated as a series of one-off events. Context is lost, progress resets, and momentum breaks," said April Koh, co-founder and CEO of Spring Health. "Guide holds the full arc of a person's mental health, not just their most challenging moments. This is what it means to build a lifelong mental health platform, and today marks the beginning of it at scale." Spring Health's platform already produces strong clinical results: 92% of members show clinically significant improvement across its network. Guide extends that model, ensuring context persists as care evolves and that support reaches members between sessions, not only during them. The safety architecture behind those results is equally deliberate. Before deployment, every AI capability in Guide is scored against VERA-MH, the Validated Evaluation and Risk Assessment framework for Mental Health. Guide operates entirely within Spring Health's unified clinical platform — meaning every interaction builds on real clinical context, is coordinated with providers, and is subject to clinical oversight. "No one can hold a decade of context across every session, every life change, every moment of need. Guide can do it safely," said Gijo Mathew, Chief Product Officer at Spring Health. "That's not replacing human care. It's giving people something the system has never offered before: a continuous thread through their entire mental health journey." Guide is available now to select Spring Health customers. For more information, visit www.springhealth.com/guide. About Spring Health Spring Health is a global mental health company that connects members, providers, and organizations on a single AI-native platform so care follows individuals across every job, health plan, and life stage. Independently validated by JAMA Network Open and the Validation Institute for clinical outcomes and net savings, the company's AI platform provides personalized lifelong mental health support across self-guided tools, coaching, therapy, medication management, and specialty care. Today, more than 140 million people worldwide have access to Spring Health, which is trusted by leading employers, health plans, and partners, including Highmark, Target, The Coca-Cola Company, BlackRock, Microsoft, Pfizer, and Wawa. launches.title: Introducing Guide: Spring Health’s AI-Led Experience for Employer Mental Health
launches.ai_summary: Spring Health has introduced Guide, an AI-led mental health experience designed for employer populations that maintains continuous care across providers, coverage changes, and life events rather than resetting when circumstances change. The product addresses a significant engagement gap where approximately 60% of employees never book a first session after enrolling and one in three attend only a single session, leading to low utilization and rising costs for employers. Guide operates within Spring Health's unified platform, using AI to remember clinical context over time, personalize support, and guide members to the right next step between sessions.
launches.author: Written Bygijo Mathewchief Product Officer

industries.name: Care Coordination, Referral Management & Transitions-of-Care Pathways

launches.full_text:
Mental health isn’t episodic; it evolves across a person’s life. But today’s mental healthcare system is built around isolated moments of care: people find a provider, attend a session, and then are left to figure out what comes next on their own.

When a person changes jobs, switches insurance, or their clinical needs evolve, they are often forced to hit a “reset button” on their care, losing access to their provider and the progress they’ve made. When care resets, people drop off.

This impact is felt even among employee populations: ~60% never book a first session after enrolling, and 1 in 3 attend only a single session.

For employers, that shows up as low utilization, inconsistent outcomes, and rising costs without meaningful improvement. What they need is not just access to care, but continuous engagement in care, so people stay long enough to get better, and stay better.

Better support, better outcomes, stronger teams. Explore how Spring Health helps organizations reduce costs and improve lives. Book a demo Featured articles No items found. Feel better faster Get therapy, coaching, and medication support as low as $0 and as soon as tomorrow. Find care Featured articles No items found.

At Spring Health, we’ve spent the last decade building the AI-native infrastructure to make that possible, connecting every member experience, provider interaction, and outcome on a single platform.

With that foundation, it’s now possible to deliver mental healthcare in a fundamentally different way: one that carries context forward across providers, coverage changes, and life events so care doesn’t reset, and progress isn’t lost.

That’s why we are pleased to introduce Guide, Spring Health’s AI-led experience for employer mental health. Guide supports people across every stage of their journey, helping them start care with confidence, stay engaged, and build progress that lasts.

The impact is measurable. Members supported by Guide see faster improvement in depression and anxiety symptoms, with the greatest gains among those who need care most.

A system built for moments, not for lives Mental health isn’t something that happens once. It’s something people carry with them across their lives, through stress at work, relationships, family, growth, and change. But the system was never designed around that reality. It was built for appointments, for isolated episodes, for moments in time, not for what happens between those touchpoints, or how care should evolve as life evolves. That’s where care breaks down.

A shift to AI-led care Guide is a fundamental shift in how mental healthcare works. Instead of care happening only during sessions, support extends into everyday life. Instead of employees having to figure out what to do next, they’re guided to the right next step.

Instead of losing context when something changes, care stays connected. Guide was built to solve a problem we see every day: people open up, make progress, and then have to start over with a new provider, a new system, or a new moment in life. Guide changes that. It remembers context, understands what someone is going through, and guides them to the right next step, whether that’s support in the moment or reinforcing what they’ve already learned. So instead of restarting again and again, care builds.

What makes this possible Delivering care this way requires capabilities that didn’t exist before: remembering context over time, supporting people beyond individual moments, and learning at scale to personalize for each individual. Guide brings these capabilities to life. Because everything is connected in Spring Health’s platform, every interaction builds on real clinical context. Members don’t repeat their story, providers see the full picture, and care evolves as life evolves. What this looks like in practice Take Maya and her therapist, Gene. In session, Maya shares that she’s dreading a difficult conversation with her sister. Together, they unpack Maya’s fears and concerns and make a plan to practice the conversation. Later that week, Guide prompts Maya to roleplay that conversation with her sister. In the next session, Maya and Gene don’t start from scratch. Instead, they discuss how the roleplay went, building on work outside their session, turning insight into concrete progress. Guide was made to counteract the moments where care typically breaks, where engagement is either lost or sustained, like the homework that is never completed, the next session that is never scheduled, or the great insight that is lost after a therapy session ends.

Why AI, and why now AI is already being used for emotional support. In fact, emotional support and companionship is the top use case for generative AI, which means many people are already using AI as their therapist. But most of those tools are not designed for mental healthcare. They lack clinical context, safeguards, and integration with real care. We’ve already seen the consequences, from misleading advice to harmful guidance in moments that require clinical care. That creates real risk for employees in vulnerable moments, and for employers responsible for providing safe, effective support. The answer isn’t to ignore AI. It’s to build it the right way. Guide isn’t a standalone chatbot or generic AI that delivers one-size-fits-all answers. It operates inside Spring Health's unified platform, where every member experience, every provider workflow, and every outcome is connected. That means every interaction builds on real clinical context, support is personalized, and care stays coordinated. Members don’t repeat their story, providers see the full picture, and care evolves as life evolves.

launches.title: VERA-MH Findings Highlight Gaps in How AI Chatbots Respond to Suicidal Ideation
launches.ai_summary: Spring Health announced the development of VERA-MH, an open-source framework to evaluate the safety of AI chatbots in mental health care, especially during high-risk conversations involving suicide risk. The framework has been applied to assess commercial AI models, revealing significant differences in how they handle vulnerable moments. The initiative aims to establish shared safety standards and expand responsible AI practices in mental health support.

industries.name: Crisis Support, Suicide Prevention & Acute Behavioral Triage Platforms
Behavioral Health Managed Care (Medicaid) / BH Carve-In-Carve-Out Plans
Workplace Mental Health & EAP-Integrated Teletherapy Platforms

launches.full_text: NEW YORK, February 11, 2026 — Spring Health, a global mental health company, today announced a major advancement in its work to improve AI safety in mental health care with the application of VERA-MH (Validation of Ethical and Responsible AI in Mental Health), an open-source, clinically grounded framework designed to evaluate how AI chatbots behave in high-risk mental health conversations. As conversational AI tools become increasingly embedded in how people seek emotional and mental health support, including during moments of crisis, concerns have grown among clinicians, researchers, and policymakers about the safety of these systems when they encounter suicide risk and acute psychological distress. Without shared standards, developers and decision-makers lack a consistent way to assess whether AI systems respond appropriately when the stakes are highest. “AI is already present in some of the most vulnerable moments in people’s lives,” said Adam Chekroud, President and co-founder at Spring Health. “In mental health care, clinicians are held to clear standards designed to prevent harm. As AI increasingly operates in these same moments, it must be held to similarly rigorous expectations.” From Concept to Application In October 2025, Spring Health partnered with leaders across healthcare, technology, and ethics to launch VERA-MH, the first open-source, clinically grounded standard for evaluating the safety and effectiveness of AI chatbots in mental health care. Since opening the framework to the field, dozens of academic, clinical, and technology experts have joined the effort to help shape a common foundation for responsible innovation. Today’s announcement marks the next step in that work. VERA-MH has now been applied to assess commercially available AI models, beginning with conversations that may involve suicide risk. Suicide risk was selected as the first focus area because it represents the moment where getting safety wrong carries the greatest potential for harm. Major commercially available AI models showed meaningful differences in how they evaluate potential risk, respond supportively, guide users to human care, and maintain appropriate boundaries. These findings are not intended to indict individual systems but instead invite universal industry participation. Without widespread adoption of shared benchmarks, the field lacks a common definition of what “safe enough” means in practice. Shared Infrastructure for a Growing Ecosystem VERA-MH provides a structured way to define and evaluate safety expectations in high-risk mental health conversations, including recognizing suicide risk, responding appropriately, and escalating to human support when needed. “Shared safety standards are not a constraint on innovation,” said Dr. Millard Brown, Chief Medical Officer at Spring Health. “They keep people safe. Standards help developers innovate responsibly, enable employers and health plans to make informed decisions, and most importantly, help protect those in crisis. We all deserve confidence that if a loved one turns to an AI tool for support, it has been rigorously tested and proven safe.” An Invitation to the Field VERA-MH is designed to evolve over time as AI capabilities, use cases, and risks change. Suicide risk is the first milestone in a broader, multi-year effort to expand shared safety standards across additional mental health risk areas. Spring Health is calling on the industry to engage with VERA-MH and contribute to the development of future safety standards. Developers and researchers can immediately apply the open-source codebase to evaluate solutions against the benchmark. Employers, benefits consultants, and policymakers can advance responsible adoption by requiring the standard in AI implementation decisions. “Our goal is to raise the bar together,” said Dr. Millard Brown, Chief Medical Officer at Spring Health. “So that wherever AI shows up in someone’s hardest moments, the field can stand behind what ‘safe’ means. When safety fails in moments of suicide risk, lives are at stake.” For more information about VERA-MH and to access the open-source framework, visit https://www.springhealth.com/blog/vera-mh-for-suicide-risk About VERA-MH VERA-MH (Validation of Ethical and Responsible AI in Mental Health) is an open-source evaluation framework that provides a transparent, clinically grounded way to assess whether AI systems meet essential safety requirements in high-risk mental health conversations. Built in collaboration with clinicians, researchers, and the AI in Mental Health Safety & Ethics Council, VERA-MH is designed to make AI safety measurable, comparable, and accountable. For future updates and ongoing work, follow VERA-MH on LinkedIn. ‍

launches.title: What the Spring Health, Alma Deal Means for the Future of Digital Health Dealmaking
launches.ai_summary: Spring Health announced plans to acquire therapist enablement platform Alma, with the combined entity expected to generate $1 billion in revenue in its first year and valued at between $6 billion and $7 billion. Both companies target different payer markets but address the same challenge of connecting patients to mental health care, with Alma providing backend support for providers and helping them contract with insurance while Spring Health works with employers. The deal is expected to signal a growing number of mega deals in the digital behavioral health space as venture-backed companies explore exit strategies amid a difficult fundraising environment.
launches.author: Laura Lovett

industries.name: Behavioral Health & Psychiatry Virtual Care (Payer Network)

launches.full_text:
This is an exclusive BHB+ article During the post-pandemic investment boom, venture firms poured billions of dollars into the digital behavioral health sector. In 2021, at the peak of investor interest, digital behavioral health providers raised $4.8 billion in funding, according to Rock Health. ​While the sector attracted plenty of venture capital, it has had few mega M&A deals. But that may be shifting.​ This morning, mental health benefits platform Spring Health announced its plans to acquire therapist enablement platform Alma. Advertisement While the terms of the deal were not disclosed, both companies have raised hundreds of millions of dollars – and according to a Wall Street Journal report, the combined entity expects to see $1 billion in revenue in its first year and is valued at between $6 billion and $7 billion. I would not be surprised if the deal was valued north of $1 billion and investors got a healthy payout. I think the deal could signal a growing number of mega deals in the digital behavioral health space. I’m also interested to see what this deal could indicate for the futures of other therapist-enablement platforms such as Headway and Rula. Advertisement While Spring Health and Alma came from different corners of the market, these platforms could be attractive acquisition targets — particularly for payers looking to build or expand provider networks. ​In this week’s exclusive BHB+ Update, I will explore: – What we know about the Spring Health-Alma deal – What’s next for digital health M&A – Why payers might begin looking at therapist-enabled platforms Inside the Spring Health, Alma deal ​Spring Health’s acquisition of Alma is interesting because the two companies target different payer markets. Spring Health works with employers to give their staff members access to contract therapists through its platform. ​Meanwhile, Alma provides backend support for behavioral health providers and helps them contract with insurance providers. Adam Checkround, co-founder and president of Spring Health, told my colleague Ashleigh Hollowell that the acquisition made sense because both companies were addressing the same issue: connecting patients to mental health care. ​“Individually, Spring Health and Alma each reached significant scale addressing different parts of that challenge,” Chekroud said. “Together, this is the moment to accelerate impact by expanding access while reducing the total cost of care, strengthening provider infrastructure, and supporting continuity of care across more points in a person’s mental health journey.” I think the deal could work for Spring Health for a few reasons. First, it could help diversify revenue and tap into Alma’s extensive relationships with health plans. This comes as Spring Health’s core employer customers face point-solution fatigue — and publicly traded competitors like Talkspace (Nasdaq: TALK) report declining revenue in that same market. Companies are responding by diversifying beyond the employer market. Headspace, long known for employer-sponsored virtual therapy, rolled out a direct-to-consumer option in June that lets patients use their insurance — opening up an entirely new revenue stream.​ Chekroud also noted that the deal could help the combined entities support care transition for clients who move between employer-sponsored and health plan-sponsored care. While Alma and Spring Health will remain separate operating entities, coming under one roof means a much bigger company. This could be a tactic in moving towards a public offering. PitchBook speculated that Spring Health is a company to watch for an IPO in 2026. What does this mean for other therapist-enabled platforms? Over the past half a dozen years, payers have struggled with ghost networks and keeping up with patient access demands in behavioral health. This gave rise to therapist-enablement platforms, such as Alama, Headway and Rula. These platforms helped more independent therapists become in-network with payers and, in turn, gave payers access to thousands of therapists. Like Alma, many of these companies have raised significant funding. Take Headway: The company closed a $100 million funding round in 2024, raising its valuation to $2.3 billion. While these companies wouldn’t come cheap, they may be exploring exit strategies. So, which acquirer has deep pockets and needs an access expansion play? Payers. As more payers consider expansion opportunities, therapist enablement platforms could be a natural fit. Still, I could see many independent providers getting the “yuck” at paying a major insurance company for their tech stack and the up-front contracting expenses, just to turn around and bill that payer for a session. Alternatively, some of these companies might grow to the scale that the best exit strategy is public. And there are enough of these platforms out there that consolidation could still occur in the market. ​Digital health M&A picking up ​Digital health M&A never stopped, but it never matched the pace of venture investment either. However, I think we are poised to see some more dealmaking in 2026. For starters, many companies that took advantage of the digital behavioral health funding frenzy of the early 2020s are finding it a difficult environment to raise additional rounds. ​This could mean that some companies will be forced to find a deal or close their doors. We have already seen some smaller behavioral health providers close up shop. And many digital providers have shuttered; for example, virtual ketamine provider Noma closed its doors in September and Mindstrong shut down in 2023. ​Additionally, those investors who poured funds into those funding rounds are looking for a payout. And there seems to be some interesting moves in the space. Earlier this week, NOCD announced the acquisition of trauma-informed provider Rebound Health. At the same time, it announced that the pair will operate under a new parent company, Noto, which will act as a specialty behavioral health services provider. It’s an interesting move for the company because it allows it to expand into new areas of behavioral health, while keeping its specialty care at the center. ​At the end of last year, pediatric provider Handspring Health bought adolescent therapy Joon Care in a more cut-and-dry merging of the same specialty type companies. Similarly, virtual provider Kooth purchased Kismet Health’s pediatric telehealth platform in November. ​But I do expect to see some interesting and innovative mergers that help digital players, and dare I even say, more traditional players, get into new and innovative areas of the industry.

Companies featured in this article: Spring Health

Each session combines guided breathwork, binaural beats for brainwave entrainment, hypnotic suggestion, Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP), and subliminal messaging. Customization Drives Engagement: One size does not fit all. Look for partners that allow you to tailor offerings to different employee demographics, job functions, and stress levels. As a study in the American Journal of Health Promotion noted, personalized wellness programs see higher participation rates and greater long-term success. Your Immediate Next Steps Transforming insight into action is the final, crucial step. Use this checklist to build momentum and make a confident, informed decision for your team. Survey Your Team (Again): Before you sign any contract, gather fresh, anonymous feedback. Action: Use a simple tool like Google Forms to ask, “What is the #1 thing impacting your well-being at work today?” and “If you had a $50 monthly wellness stipend, what would you spend it on?” This data provides immediate direction. Audit Your Current Offerings: What do you already have in place? An underutilized EAP? A basic health insurance plan? Identify the gaps that a new program needs to fill. Action: Create a simple two-column list: “What We Have” and “What We Need.” This visual gap analysis prevents overlap and ensures you’re investing where it matters most. Request Targeted Demos: Approach vendors with your specific needs. Instead of a generic overview, ask platforms like Spring Health or Personify Health to demonstrate exactly how they would address your top three employee challenges. Action: Provide your top challenge from the survey (e.g., burnout) to vendors beforehand and ask them to tailor their 30-minute demo to solving that specific problem. Pilot a Program: If possible, run a small-scale pilot with a specific department. For example, introduce a somatic tool like 9D Breathwork to a high-stress team, like your sales or customer support departments. Measure feedback and engagement before committing to a company-wide rollout. Research from the Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine confirms that pilot programs are effective for testing feasibility and ROI. Ultimately, investing in employee wellness is one of the most powerful investments you can make in your organization’s future. It’s a commitment to building a resilient, engaged, and thriving workforce capable of navigating any challenge. By choosing thoughtfully and integrating strategically, you create a culture where every employee feels seen, supported, and empowered to do their best work. launches.title: The Future of Mental Healthcare Is Continuous Care
launches.ai_summary: Spring Health is promoting its 'Continuous Care' model, which utilizes AI-driven tools like Guided Intake and Summaries & Takeaways to support mental health patients between therapy sessions. The company also introduced VERA-MH, an open-source framework for evaluating the safety and ethics of AI in mental healthcare.
