Nationally recognized Gold Seal of Approval® reflects clinical excellence behind Talkiatry's in-network psychiatric and therapy care, delivered to over 170 million covered lives nationwide NEW YORK, Oct. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Talkiatry, the nation's largest psychiatric provider group and the preferred in-network psychiatry partner for more than 70 U.S. health systems, has earned The Joint Commission's Gold Seal of Approval® for Behavioral Health. This distinction reflects Talkiatry's continued commitment to providing comprehensive, high-quality care, with more than 170 million covered lives, coming shortly after the company surpassed four million patient visits to date. Talkiatry's Joint Commission accreditation is a testament to the rigor of the provider group's processes, clinical oversight, and safety practices behind its model. The accreditation reflects Talkiatry's pursuit of clinical excellence and its focus on meeting the same clinical standards held by the country's leading brick-and-mortar healthcare institutions. As demand for behavioral healthcare continues to outpace access nationally, an increasing number of psychiatric care providers have moved to virtual and hybrid settings. With this, patients, providers, and payers have fewer ways to assess whether providers meet consistent, independently audited standards for quality and safety. The Gold Seal of Approval® is a reflection of Talkiatry's robust clinical standards and an integrated care model that brings therapy and psychiatry together to support better patient outcomes. "Earning Joint Commission accreditation is validation of our clinical infrastructure, further strengthening confidence across the board for our patients, clinicians on staff, and the providers who trust us with their patients," said Dr. Georgia Gaveras, DO, co-founder and Chief Medical Officer of Talkiatry. "Joint Commission congratulates Talkiatry for achieving accreditation by demonstrating its focus on delivering safe and effective care of the highest quality and value," says Ken Grubbs, DNP, MBA, RN, executive vice president of Accreditation and Certification Operations and chief nursing officer, Joint Commission. "Through the accreditation process, we worked closely with Talkiatry to enable and affirm the highest standards of healthcare quality and patient safety. Together, we are elevating care for all patients, and we appreciate Talkiatry's collaboration throughout this process." funding_news.title: 5 Behavioral Health VC Investors to Watch
funding_news.ai_summary: VC funding in behavioral health rebounded in 2026 after a 2024 low, with large rounds like Talkiatry's $210M Series D and Grow Therapy's $150M Series D. The article highlights five firms—GreyMatter, Goldman Sachs Alternatives, Kaiser, General Catalyst, and HealthQuest—backing tech-enabled providers and specialized services.
funding_news.author: Ashleigh Hollowell
funding_news.full_text:
This is an exclusive BHB+ story.

Venture capital investments in behavioral health are emerging from a lull as firms recalibrated their priorities in 2024 and have since identified new strategic targets as the sector has matured.

Behavioral health, and in particular digital mental health solutions, saw an influx of capital in 2021, driven by the pandemic, with funding peaking around $4.9 billion, according to Rock Health. After that, there was talk of VC capital “drying up” around early 2022. Since then, VC funding dipped to a low of $1.4 billion in 2024. But behavioral health venture capital funding has recently been reinvigorated by investor conviction, a wave of new mental health startups and large growth funding rounds that target specialized, high-acuity services.

VC investments in behavioral health began the year with large capital rounds paid to platforms that target access and infrastructure, including a $210 million Series D round for Talkiatry, a $150 million Series D round for Grow Therapy, $80 million out of stealth for Salma Health and $40 million for AnswerNow’s telehealth applied behavioral analysis (ABA) services. All four of those mega fundraises took place during the first quarter of 2026.

Advertisement

VC investments across behavioral health during the second quarter of 2026 looked a bit different, with more attention to specialty services and slightly smaller, though still noteworthy, capital raises, including deals like Click Therapeutics’ $50 million Series D and a $30 million round for Instride Health.

Now that the market has matured past the COVID-induced telehealth arms race, venture capital funding is being prioritized for providers and solutions that have promising infrastructure and aim to improve access rather than merely investing in the promise of digital mental health.

Across all five VC firms that Behavioral Health Business is watching, one theme is clear: behavioral health is embracing technology, and the future belongs to strategic providers with scalable, tech-enabled, payer-aligned care models.

Advertisement

GreyMatter Capital

Noteworthy behavioral health investments:

Anna Health

Blackbird Health

Coral Care

Era

FamilyWell

firsthand

Kyan Health

Flourish

Luna Family Autism

Manatee

Nema

Pelago

Talkiatry

TownHome Health

Valera Health

Vanna Health

Willow Health

Why BHB is watching:

San Francisco-based GreyMatter Capital is a venture firm that invests solely in mental health founders. It has a swath of behavioral health providers and tech-enabled solutions in its investment portfolio, but a handful have raised significant capital to scale in the last year.

In February, virtual psychiatry provider Talkiatry raised a $210 million Series D round, which was almost the total of all the funding it had received up to that point, bringing its total funding to roughly $452 million. The company will use much of the new funding to bolster its AI capabilities.

Another one of GreyMatter’s portfolio companies, pediatric psychiatric care provider Flourish Health, raised $26 million for its Series A round in July. Its goal is to scale high-acuity psychiatric care for youth populations.

Serious mental illness provider Vanna Health secured $17 million in a Series B round earlier this summer and will use the capital to enter new markets soon. The company also named a new CEO shortly before the fundraise. One of the new CEO’s goals is to deepen payer partnerships and wraparound services for patients.

Pediatric speech, occupational and physical therapy provider Coral Care, another GreyMatter investment, secured a $13 million Series A in February, and aims to connect families with therapists for in-home services. The company noted that with this funding, it will move to scale nationally.

Other noteworthy developments among GreyMatter’s portfolio companies this year include the acquisition of Valera Health by Mindoula in July. Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but Mindoula noted the deal was a move to expand its collaborative care model with established psychiatric services.

Another one we’re watching in this portfolio is Pelago’s announcement that it will transition from being historically a substance use disorder (SUD) care provider and expand into general behavioral health. Its first move in this vein was a wellness support chatbot capable of escalating issues to Pelago’s in-house clinical team.

Goldman Sachs Alternatives Growth Equity

Noteworthy behavioral health investments:

Grow Therapy

Why BHB is watching:

Goldman Sachs Alternatives Growth Equity’s portfolio company Grow Therapy made headlines earlier this year when it secured a whopping $150 million Series D round in March 2026. That brought the digital mental health platform’s projected annual revenue to more than $1 billion. Prior to the large capital round, Grow Therapy made a strategic investment and acquired the AI scribe tool Tenor Therapy in February. The company’s last funding round prior to its Series D was an $88 million Series C in 2024. The new infusion of capital, coupled with its latest acquisition, positions it to make additional, scalable investments going forward in the sector.

Kaiser Permanente Ventures

Noteworthy behavioral health investments:

Headspace

Groups Recover Together

Mind 24-7

Noto (formerly NOCD)

Why BHB is watching:

Kaiser Permanente Ventures made BHB’s list of VC firms to watch in 2025, as well, but for different reasons. This year, the firm’s portfolio companies Headspace, Groups Recover Together and NOCD all were part of significant, strategic transactions.

Virtual mental health provider Headspace is set to be acquired by Sword Health in a cash deal reportedly valued at $300 million. The valuation is lower than some in the industry expected, particularly as many have had Headspace on their bingo cards as a company that could potentially IPO. The transaction comes just about one year after Headspace launched its direct-to-consumer therapy services. Sword Health, a New York City-based digital health provider, began making moves into behavioral health last summer and its valuation jumped to $4 billion. Sword Health’s CEO Virgilio Bento previously told HB that expanding capabilities into SMI care and growing its AI offerings, are part of its trajectory on its path toward a possible 2028 IPO.

Addiction treatment provider Groups Recover Together, another investment in Kaiser’s portfolio, made its first-ever acquisition in March 2026 and hinted that more activity in that vein is likely on the horizon. Its purchase of Better Life Partners deepens its resources throughout New England and introduces new care model elements that will allow the company to expand into new territories. Better Life Partners had been a bit of a distressed asset, with a series of financial and operational issues. Still, it had two assets that Groups wanted: virtual responsive care and walk-in clinic capabilities, CEO Cooper Zelnick, told BHB. Those are likely to scale further across the company over time.

Virtual OCD provider NOCD, another one of Kaiser’s portfolio companies, acquired trauma care provider Rebound Health earlier this year. Now the two entities operate under the new brand identity “Noto.” The transaction follows a market trend BHB has been keeping tabs on, where several new providers entering the market are entering niche areas of care and adding on, rather than starting broad and trying to narrow. The deal added trauma-focused care capabilities, which NOCD did not previously provide. An ongoing priority now for the newly formed company Noto is to continue to add new services for other complex behavioral health conditions.

General Catalyst

Noteworthy behavioral health investments:

Radial

Birches Health

Ophelia Health

Cortica

Elemy

Cartwheel Care

Eleanor Health

Equip Health

InStride Health

Osmind

Rippl

SonderMind

Spring Health

Why BHB is watching:

General Catalyst has long been a powerhouse investment firm known for backing successful healthcare companies with venture investments. Throughout 2026, several of its portfolio companies were part of sizable transactions or on the receiving end of large capital infusions.

Late last year, General Catalyst led a $50 million funding round for New York City-based Radial, which provides clinic-based interventional psychiatry services like transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), Spravato, and neuromodulation treatments. Not only was the funding a vote of confidence from its investors, zooming out, interventional psychiatry is also on the rise across the industry as the latest hot commodity.

Following the $50 million Series A round, Radial acquired Mindful Health Solutions, a larger and older outpatient operator, this August for an undisclosed amount. Mindful Health Solutions has similar interventional psychiatry offerings and this single deal exponentially multiplied Radial’s geographic footprint. Radial is less than one year into its hold period with General Catalyst and anticipates tailwinds from the boom in interventional psychiatry will propel it further.

Also, as part of General Catalyst’s massive investment portfolio, Spring Health disclosed its plans to acquire digital mental health platform Alma in January. The transaction took place amid a wave of digital health dealmaking that began in 2026. Digital mental health is an area that is likely to continue to see consolidation following the explosion of solutions out of the pandemic, which is starting to balance out. Spring’s move to buy Alma skyrocketed its revenue expectations to $1 billion in its first year following the close of the deal, with its valuation rising to between $6 billion and $7 billion.

Other noteworthy developments among General Catalyst’s investments this year were also InStride Health’s $30 million Series C and Birches Health’s $20 million capital raise. Pediatric behavioral health provider InStride raised the capital at the beginning of 2026 and told BHB it plans to use it to expand into new markets. Birches Health’s funding came late in 2025, but has remained noteworthy in 2026, as both public and private audiences have renewed their attention on gambling addiction, which is one of its primary service lines. It’s likely there will be more expansion or consolidation in this area of behavioral and process addictions over time as concerns about gambling and social media rise.

HealthQuest Capital

Noteworthy behavioral health investments:

AnswersNow

Why BHB is watching:

Virtual autism therapy provider AnswersNow secured a $40 million Series B in January, marking its first fundraise since 2023. The company provides ABA care via telehealth with board-certified behavior analysts (BCBAs), which is typically a clinic-based service. AnswersNow executives said that following the new capital infusion, its focus will be on “aggressively” scaling its platform, eventually adding new service lines and expanding its use of AI. HealthQuest Capital successfully exited AmWell, another behavioral health company, in the past.

funding_news.title: Patience is not caution: The case for rethinking capital in youth mental health
funding_news.ai_summary: The article argues that the behavioral health sector's reliance on traditional venture capital creates a boom-bust cycle that harms early-stage youth mental health companies due to misaligned growth expectations and regulatory complexities. It advocates for patient capital models, citing examples like Talkiatry's large funding round and Flourish Health's strategic Series A, to allow time for clinical validation and operational stability. The author urges investors to adopt blended-capital approaches that prioritize long-term impact over rapid scaling.
funding_news.author: Nathaan Demers

industries.name: Behavioral Health for Children & Adolescents (Youth Services)

funding_news.full_text:
Patience is not caution: The case for rethinking capital in youth mental health

With rates of anxiety and depression among young people near all-time highs, there is no shortage of founders working within the youth mental health space. And they are not short on innovation, passion or capabilities. However, the funding boom-bust cycle in the behavioral health sector following the influx of investment capital during COVID leaves many companies struggling to secure funding that is aligned with the nuances of innovation in a highly regulated, fragmented behavioral healthcare system. In prior clinical roles, I have supported hundreds of young people coping with mental health challenges and families navigating care systems with long waitlists and countless access barriers. The challenges felt tangible, human and present. Now, working at Hopelab in an impact investing capacity, I see a different systemic barrier — the mismatch between how early-stage mental health companies grow and how they’re funded. That mismatch shapes whether young people have access to the supports they need or are left without them. Boom and bust The behavioral health funding environment tells a stark story. Venture capital deployment peaked at roughly $5 billion in 2021 at the height of COVID, up from approximately $2 billion in 2020. Since then, investments have returned to 2020 levels and, according to some reports, have contracted further. While the causes are many, a key factor is the growth expectations associated with venture capital, which can be misaligned with the realities of early-stage behavioral health companies. From lengthy payor contracting cycles to the complexities of scaling clinical operations across state lines, early-stage growth in this space is time and resource intensive. As a result, much of the capital deployed from 2023 through the present has concentrated on later-stage companies — specifically high-margin service providers such as psychiatry — that have cleared early-stage growing pains and are ready for massive scale. For example, the telepsychiatry provider Talkiatry raised a $210 million Series D in February 2026. While that shift has expanded access to services for many in need, the challenge lies in the constriction of capital for early-stage companies innovating in the space, especially those serving traditionally underserved populations. Seeking patient capital The boom-bust cycle has left many early-stage companies caught between a rock and a hard place: either accepting venture capital that pushes for rapid scale before their care models, compliance infrastructure and reimbursement pathways are stable, or endlessly seeking a rare funding source that tolerates slower, evidence-driven growth. As a result, many run out of time and are forced to close their doors before achieving lasting impact and commercial success. Venture timelines reward velocity, not validation, and in behavioral health, that imbalance often derails both mission and business. Not all sectors are created equal. Tech-first companies like the newest email copilot or AI assistant can grow as fast as consumer markets allow, unencumbered by regulatory oversight, clinical safeguards and complex reimbursement models. Mental health innovators cannot — and should not — because the regulations in place serve an important purpose. But the industry’s highly regulated nature, spanning HIPAA compliance, data governance, licensure requirements and clinical supervision, means responsible scaling takes longer in the early stages than in other sectors. Rushing risks eroding clinical outcomes and consumer trust, both of which are essential to long-term viability for youth-serving behavioral health companies. But how do we — as investors and funders — change this dynamic? Based on primary research and conversations with colleagues and organizations across the field, we propose an alternative path: aligning funding timelines with market realities through more patient capital. Laying the groundwork for growth Patient capital gives youth-serving behavioral health companies the room to go deep within specific markets rather than reaching for wide geographic scale too early, providing the runway needed to become venture ready. By initially focusing within a state or several states, companies can build on a smaller set of clinical and operating regulations and demonstrate clinical outcomes, operational efficiency and financial performance under real-world conditions. With roughly 30 million youth on Medicaid in the United States, the reality is that many states have enough market share to prove out these models. As companies mature in these select markets, they can improve operational efficiency and margins, prioritizing new states with large target populations, favorable reimbursement rates and analogous regulations. This approach builds staying power rather than hype, fostering trust among consumers and buyers — and, in time, making these companies ready for the growth expectations of traditional venture. For example, Flourish Health, a company serving youth and young adults on Medicaid living with severe and persistent mental illnesses, just announced a $26 million Series A. Its growth model involved going deep within a select few markets in the early stage, allowing for the fine-tuning of clinical and operational efficiency, while also allowing enough time for evidence generation. In line with this growth trajectory, the company sought a bridge round that Hopelab co-led with Acumen America, with the understanding that funding was to be used for depth in existing markets, as opposed to scale, an approach less aligned with the orientation of traditional venture funds. Doing so afforded the company additional time and focus to establish a strong foundation and achieve margin expansion within Medicaid populations, which then positioned it to raise a large Series A focused on scale. An ask for investors It’s worth being honest: Not all companies innovating in any space are a fit for traditional venture capital, and the behavioral health field is no exception. However, that does not mean they are weak businesses that should not exist. The caveat is that many require capital that understands the nuances of the space in the early stages, giving them the time to become venture-ready before meeting the growth expectations of traditional venture capital. This is not a call for caution; patient capital is often mistaken for playing it safe, when in fact it is the de-risking work — proving outcomes, stabilizing reimbursement and building trust — that venture-scale growth depends on. Our ask for fellow investors and funders is specific: Consider co-investing in, or helping to create, patient and blended-capital models that bring together grants, philanthropic capital and other nondilutive funding for early-stage behavioral health companies. These instruments provide the runway required to drive innovation and outcomes — and ultimately to determine whether the young people and families I saw in clinical practice will have access to the supports they need. Speed is not synonymous with success. In youth mental health innovation, patience is not caution; it is a prerequisite for lasting impact. Nathaan Demers is principal investor at Hopelab. funding_news.title: Investors Want It All: Digital Behavioral Health Companies Dish on Fundraising Secret Sauce
funding_news.ai_summary: Early-stage investors in digital behavioral health have shifted their expectations, now demanding that startups demonstrate solid fundamentals, profitability (current or near-term), scale, and tech-driven differentiation rather than prioritizing speed of expansion. Three companies detailed their recent fundraising experiences: Avela Health raised approximately $10 million, AnswersNow secured $40 million in a Series B round, and Talkiatry closed a $210 million Series D led by Perceptive Advisors with Banc of California providing debt financing. Industry leaders note that investors have become more sophisticated and skeptical, focusing on unit economics, care quality, and long-term sustainability while also evaluating companies' approaches to AI integration in clinical and operational applications.
funding_news.author: Chris Larson
funding_news.full_text:
Early-stage investors are demanding that digital behavioral health providers have it all, regardless of the organization’s level of development. In short, industry insiders expect digital behavioral health startups to have rock-solid fundamentals, profitability now or in the near term, some degree of scale and a compelling vision for differentiation with tech innovation. Investors have also become more sophisticated in assessing digital behavioral health. They have also become more skeptical of the space, with some investors expressing disappointment with the present results. On the other hand, that increased savvy and skepticism has helped providers and investors set more realistic expectations for what each wants in entrepreneurship in this slice of behavioral health. Advertisement “The conversations centered on unit economics, care quality, and long-term sustainability — not just speed of expansion,” Robin McIntosh, co-founder and CEO of Avela Health, told BHB. “That reflects where the broader market is today.” Avela Health is a digital autism diagnostics and therapy provider. Its services encompass caregiver support and coordinated services that include occupational therapy, speech therapy, psychiatry and feeding specialists. It recently raised about $10 million, including a simple agreement for future equity (SAFE) and $6.4 million that was later disclosed in public filings. “Investors understand that this space requires clinical depth, operational rigor, and economic sustainability. That level of sophistication wasn’t always present a few years ago,” McIntosh said. Advertisement Still, venture capitalists often bring prior expectations and assumptions about digital services that don’t necessarily fit with growing behavioral health companies. McIntosh said that there were some investors who asked for a plan for Avela Health to get to $100 million in revenue in three to five years. “That’s a fair question in many categories, but hyper-acceleration isn’t our objective,” McIntosh said. “We’re building in a complex health care space where responsible growth matters. “We chose partners who value durable, sustainable expansion.” With the increased familiarity, providers can also better gauge the investors they bring into their work. Jeff Beck, CEO of AnswersNow, a digital autism therapy provider, told BHB that it was able to, in part, distinguish between investors who would and would not be a good fit based on their level of awareness of the ABA space. “There have been times where I’ve met with an investor, and they say, ‘Explain to me how ABA works,'” Beck said. “And that’s how I know this is not going to work.” AnswersNow announced it raised $40 million as part of a Series B round in January. The company has developed its own software and, in addition to a geographic and payer partner expansion, is using about “half a million” hours of recorded virtual therapy to optimize and deeply personalize the most effective treatment for children with autism and their families. On the whole, Beck and AnswersNow largely pitched investors on a new vision for the delivery model for applied behavior analysis (ABA), the most widely used therapy in the autism space. Its digital-only, heavily parent-moderated model is profoundly different from most autism therapy providers. This kind of tech-forward, what’s-next approach is usually what venture capitalists look for. However, during the effort to raise the Series B round, Beck heard from multiple venture capitalists that they had overindexed and were overexposed to the digital health sector. In other cases, they presented a more bullish stance for in-person services for behavioral health care, a departure from the digital-focused past. With heightened investor demands, there are also more realistic expectations that companies will show additional results to some degree, Beck added. “I think investors, from my perspective at a digital health company, are looking for ways to change the way that health care is delivered while maintaining quality,” Jeff Beck, CEO of AnswersNow, a digital autism therapy provider, told BHB. “If you can do those two things, you’re going to get a lot of interest.” Focus on quality Robert Krayn, co-founder and CEO of digital psychiatry provider Talkiatry, told Behavioral Health Business that the key to both fundraising and payer relations is care quality. “They’re looking for scale. They’re looking for you to operate appropriately. But they’re also looking for good outcomes,” Krayn said. “I think we’ve seen investors pass on folks that have great financials, but they don’t see what they need to see clinically.” More and more, investors are bringing in “physician experts” into potential investment processes who have a “much, much deeper understanding” of health care than other staff. Overall, Krayn posits that digital health generally struggles to deliver impressive care outcomes. “Most people are not good at it. I’m not saying that they’re wrong,” Krayn said. “I’m saying that it has not been common to find people that do this well — it’s very, very hard.” This makes companies that can control quality at scale appealing. This was the key for Talkiatry’s latest funding round, Krayn said. In turn, the key to that is a W-2 employment model for Talkiatry’s psychiatry and therapist workforce. The company announced a $210 million Series D funding round, led by Perceptive Advisors. Banc of California provided a debt facility to the round. On the other end of the investment round spectrum, McIntosh and Avela Health shared a similar sentiment about quality. “What resonated with investors is that we operate with disciplined economics, strong clinical leadership, and were profitable when we raised this round,” McIntosh said. “That combination — clinical rigor plus financial sustainability — is not common in early-stage health care.” Providers setting their own course on AI With so much of every industry influenced by AI directly, or through the idea of AI, it may be surprising to learn that provider organizations ultimately set their own vision for AI use in their organizations. “I would say that we were volun-telling investors how we should think about AI,” Beck said. Beck said he looks at three segments for AI application in digital health: increasing individual employee capacity, improving operational efficiency/leverage and clinical enhancement. “We can truly individualize the care and the environment virtually,” Beck said, noting the company’s corpus of session recordings. Beck and Krayn said they see clinical applications insofar as they make clinicians’ lives easier. At Talkiatry, AI has helped the company to build a revenue cycle management apparatus that is disproportionately efficient compared to traditional models. AI has also eased the intake process and helps ID patients’ insurance coverage even if they don’t have their insurance card handy. Talkiatry offers tools for clinicians, such as AI scribes, but it doesn’t force clinicians to use them, Krayn said. Dr. Georgia Gaveras, co-founder and chief medical officer, told BHB that it looked to its clinicians to identify and test tools and filter learnings on best uses to the leadership team. “They want to be able to focus more on patient care — the direct practice of care,” Gaveras said. “We really wanted them to feel comfortable with how we were integrating things that they would use in their day-to-day work.” While the jury is still out on AI in digital mental health, it is clear that it will have a place in the digital behavioral health. Part of the present allure of digital health is its capacity to test the latest in digital tools. “Folks are really interested in digital health because it is a bit of a click ahead from an innovation perspective,” Beck said.

Companies featured in this article: AnswersNow, Avela Health, Talkiatry

funding_news.title: Mental Health Startup Talkiatry Raises $5 Million As Demand For Telepsychiatry Skyrockets — Relevance Ventures
funding_news.ai_summary: Talkiatry, a mental health startup providing telepsychiatry services, has raised $5 million in Series A funding led by Sikwoo Capital Partners, with participation from Relevance Ventures and Dr. Richard Park. The company, which currently employs 16 clinicians and accepts insurance from major providers including UnitedHealthcare, Cigna, Humana, Anthem, and Aetna, plans to use the capital to expand operations and develop a proprietary technology platform to onboard more providers amid surging demand for mental health services. The funding reflects a broader trend of record investment in digital behavioral health startups, driven by a sharp rise in Americans reporting anxiety or depression symptoms from 11% in early 2019 to 36% by January 2021.
funding_news.author: Relevance Ventures

sic_codes.name: SERVICES-OFFICES & CLINICS OF DOCTORS OF MEDICINE

funding_news.full_text: A year after Covid-19 arrived in the U.S., many are hitting a “pandemic wall.” But as the state of Americans’ mental health declines, the mental health market is heating up. Investors have taken note of skyrocketing demand for tele-mental health services and poured record investment into companies that are addressing rising depression and anxiety. Among the latest mental health startups to attract investors is Talkiatry, which today announced it has raised $5 million in Series A funding to expand its operations and develop a proprietary technology platform. The round was led by Sikwoo Capital Partners, with participation from Relevance Ventures and Dr. Richard Park, founder and former CEO of CityMD. Talkiatry offers telepsychiatry around the country and in-person visits at its New York City headquarters. The company employs its 16 clinicians—mostly psychiatrists—and plans to grow to 30 providers by the summer. Cofounders Robert Krayn and Dr. Georgia Gaveras say they will use the influx of capital, in part, to make sure they can efficiently onboard providers to accommodate growing demand to join the practice. “We’re looking to solve the provider’s problem [and] the insurance company’s problem,” Krayn said. “We think if we solve both of those we’ll ultimately solve the patient’s problem.” The problem for many patients during the pandemic has been deteriorating mental health. According to CDC data, 36% of Americans reported symptoms of anxiety or depression at the end of January 2021. In the first six months of 2019, that rate was 11%. “Americans are already experiencing a mental health crisis today, which will only get worse as mental health issues stemming from the extraordinary stress of living through a global pandemic go untreated,” said Park, who will join Talkiatry’s board of directors. “It’s hard to even quantify what effect the pandemic is going to have on mental health in this country,” said Cameron Newton, general partner at Relevance Ventures, who will also take a board seat. “I think most folks, and us included, realize and predict that it’s going to be a considerable problem going forward.” Widespread mental health needs have fueled growth for businesses like Talkiatry. “You've had people that had a tremendous amount of anxiety over the past year,” said Gaveras. “It's really created a huge demand in the system.” The Talkiatry team and its new investors see a silver lining in increased mental health burdens and demand for services: mental health may have finally lost its taboo. “Mental health has become something that more and more people are seeing as essential, not a luxury,” said Gaveras. Reducing Cost Barriers Through Insurance The cost of mental health care can put essential mental health services out of reach. Before the pandemic, 40% of adults with unmet mental health needs cited cost as the barrier to care. More recent data suggests one-quarter of adults are not getting treatment for symptoms of anxiety or depression. Patients who use mental health services tend to pay more out-of-pocket for out-of-network care, nearly $350 more than patients with diabetes. Higher out-of-pocket costs reflect the fact that many mental health providers do not accept insurance. For example, psychiatrists are less likely than other medical specialists to accept health insurance—55% compared to 89%, according to one study. Talkiatry takes a different approach; it accepts insurance. The company has negotiated favorable contracts with several large health insurers, including UnitedHealthcare, Cigna, Humana, Anthem, and Aetna. It also contracts with Medicare and TriCare, the health insurance program for active-duty and retired military service members and their families. These arrangements have allowed the company to operate profitably on a per patient basis. They also make it easier for patients who can’t afford to pay out-of-pocket to get care they need. “Talkiatry sits at the intersection of two great American problems: the shortage of mental health providers and the disconnect between insurers and patients,” Park said. Mental health provider shortages affect an estimated 120 million Americans and are projected to get worse by 2025. According to Greg Yap, partner at Menlo Ventures (which is not involved with Talkiatry), telehealth can improve access to care and give patients a better chance of finding a provider that meets their needs. “Virtual providers help to balance supply and demand by removing geographic constraints,” said Yap. Several of Talkiatry’s providers are credentialed to practice in multiple states, which allows them to see patients where provider shortages are more common. But according to Krayn, there are even “mental health deserts” in New York City. “I can’t tell you how many patients can’t find a psychiatrist who takes their insurance and has availability,” he said. “Even though we’ve got the highest concentration of psychiatrists in the country, there’s still a massive desert. How is that possible in today’s world?” Betting On Digital Behavioral Health Talkiatry’s funding reflects a broader trend: record investment in digital behavioral health startups. In the first half of 2020, 27 behavioral health companies raised $588 million, more than behavioral health startups raised in all of 2019, according to Rock Health. “We’re very bullish on the mental health space,” said Newton. Pandemic stresses may have spurred the growth in tele-mental health, but Yap believes it’s here to stay. “I think the most impactful digital mental health companies will provide holistic treatment that includes both therapy delivered through telemedicine and medication management,” Yap said. “One size does not fit all, and patients should get the best combination of treatment for them.”

funding_news.full_text: Virtual psychiatry provider Talkiatry has raised a $210 million Series D funding round, nearly matching the total funding it has raised across previous rounds. The move signals that venture capital sees a lane for the virtual delivery of high-level outpatient care in AI-powered work environments. The company will double down on its AI capabilities to be the “de facto in-network psychiatry partner for U.S. health systems, payers, and employers” as it further scales up. “Talkiatry has built a national full-stack provider group that sits on a proprietary AI-powered technology platform, giving it greater control over the quality and care being delivered at scale,” Michael Altman, head of strategy for lead investor Perceptive Advisors, said. “The company’s consistent results across outcomes, engagement, and patient experience position it as defining the next era of psychiatric care in the United States. Advertisement “Our investment supports that long-term vision.” Talkiatry leans on AI to automate its back office, support current and prospective patient engagement and enable alternative payer arrangements. The use of AI by clinicians leads to an 80% reduction in feelings of burnout, the company says. Perceptive Advisors led the round. The following firms also participated — Sofina, Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), blisce/ and Left Lane Capital. Banc of California provided a debt facility to the round. Advertisement Talkiatry employs more than 800 full-time psychiatrists. It operates in 45 states. It also has in-network arrangements with over 60 health plans. Including previous funding rounds tracked by Crunchbase, the round brings the company’s total funding to $452 million. The digital mental health segment of behavioral health is no stranger to big bets by the investor class for several years now. In 2024, Spring Health raised $100 million with a $3.3 billion valuation. Grow Therapy raised $88 million in its Series C. Cerebral, the digital mental health industry’s living cautionary tale, raised a $300 million Series C funding round in 2021. This round by Talkiatry is an aberration in the current digital mental health finding landscape. After an accelerated phase of investment jumping in at the opportunity COVID revealed, many learned harsh lessons about the dynamic world of digital mental health — the challenges of working with payers, the internal dynamics that keep therapists engaged, the difficulty of retaining patients ethically, to name a few. The funding dynamic today is also defined by smaller organizations staying relatively small while a handful of others grow at accelerated clips — creating a land of proverbial Davids and Goliaths. Despite the quickly tilting dynamic favoring a handful of scaled providers, so much venture capital has been pumped into the space that several enterprises are likely to float along for quite some time without a terminal exit. This has staved off the long-anticipated implosion of closures and consolidation predicted for this industry. The funding also comes during what might be a fundamental shift in mental health services consumer behavior. Since reaching a peak in 2021, the share of telehealth visits for behavioral health has dropped by 25%, according to Trilliant Health data. That’s not to say Americans aren’t consuming as much behavioral health. The amount of care consumed in behavioral health now eclipses that of primary care, according to the same data.

funding_news.full_text:
The funding will help the company scale its AI-powered, in-network virtual psychiatry platform, which employs more than 800 full-time psychiatrists.

Talkiatry, a virtual mental healthcare platform that employs more than 800 full-time psychiatrists, announced an oversubscribed $210 million Series D funding round, bringing its total raise to more than $400 million.

Perceptive Advisors led the round, with participation from Sofina and existing investors Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), blisce/ and Left Lane Capital. It also secured a debt facility from Banc of California.

WHAT IT DOES

Talkiatry is an AI-powered virtual health platform that privately employs psychiatrists. Its providers cover various conditions, such as anxiety, depression, insomnia, mood disorders, postpartum depression, children's mental health, bipolar disorder, OCD, PTSD and substance use disorder.

The company said it helps with back-office functions, patient engagement between visits, and helping health systems get patients into care. It also enables "innovative payment models with payers."

Talkiatry touts that it is an in-network psychiatric care provider through more than 100 insurers nationwide.

The New York-based company will use the funds to enhance its technology and scale its reach.

"Talkiatry has built a national full-stack provider group that sits on a proprietary AI-powered technology platform giving it greater control over the quality and care being delivered at scale," Michael Altman, head of strategy at Perceptive Advisors, said in a statement.

"The company's consistent results across outcomes, engagement, and patient experience position it as defining the next era of psychiatric care in the United States. Our investment supports that long-term vision."

MARKET SNAPSHOT

In 2024, Talkitary secured $130 million in equity and debt financing, bringing its total raise to $245 million.

The equity round was led by Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), with participation from Perceptive Advisors, and debt financing was provided by Banc of California.

That same year, the company announced a referral collaboration with HCA Healthcare, enabling it to become part of HCA's network and for patients to be referred to Talkiatry psychiatrists when HCA Healthcare or community resources lack capacity.

It also partnered with Magellan Health in 2024, a collaboration that would help extend telepsychiatry services across California, and with the direct-to-consumer mental health therapy provider BetterHelp.

In 2023, Quest Behavioral Health, an administrator of mental health and substance use disorder benefits, partnered with Talkiatry to provide Quest members and their families with access to virtual psychiatric care.

Talkiatry and NOCD partnered that year as well to improve access to therapists and psychiatric services for people suffering from OCD.

In 2021, Talkiatry completed a $37 million Series A round of funding.

funding_news.full_text: Telepsychiatry provider Talkiatry picked up $210 million in fresh funding to expand its offerings and build out its technology. Perceptive Advisors led the round, which the company said was oversubscribed. Brussels-based investor Sofina also participated along with prior lead investors Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), blisce/ and Left Lane Capital, alongside a debt facility from Banc of California. The company has raised $400 million to date. Talkiatry is not disclosing its valuation. Between 2021 and 2024, the company's revenue grew 1,745%, executives said. The company claims to be the largest private employer of psychiatrists and directly employs more than 800 full-time psychiatrists. Talkiatry is now in network with more than 100 insurers nationwide covering more than 170 million lives. The company has delivered 3 million patient visits to date. Talkiatry, which launched in 2020 and was named to Fierce Healthcare’s Fierce 15 in 2024, was co-founded by Robert Krayn and Georgia Gaveras. The New York City-based company's model partners with payer and provider networks as well as employers. It launched its Mindshare Partner Program in late 2023, and the company now works with more than a third of the country's top 20 health systems and more than 50 total systems to deliver in-network psychiatric care across their populations. The Mindshare Partner service allows healthcare providers to refer patients to the provider while working with their own electronic medical record systems and referral workflows. Talkiatry plans to use the fresh funding to build out its technology and expand its services across the acuity spectrum. Currently, Talkiatry provides psychiatry services for a range of mental health conditions including anxiety, depression, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, bipolar disorder, mood disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, among others. The company is looking to expand across the full acuity spectrum, building some capabilities in-house and partnering with specialized providers for others, according to a Talkiatry spokesperson. Talkiatry has extended its offerings to lower-acuity services like couples therapy. In the future, it may offer higher-acuity services like intensive outpatient support. Related Talkiatry closes $130M series C to expand telepsychiatry model The company is focused on tighter clinical integration and better care coordination as it grows, according to executives. “Talkiatry is setting the standard for how psychiatry is delivered and measured, with a proven national operating model centered on employed psychiatrists built upon a proprietary technology platform,” Krayn, who serves as CEO, said in a statement. “Health systems, payers, and employers continue to choose Talkiatry as their psychiatry partner of record to deliver consistent, superior outcomes across their patient populations. This funding supports expansion into more complex care and deeper partnerships as institutional demand grows.” Talkiatry built an artificial-intelligence-powered technology platform for its clinical operations to drive efficiency and outcomes. The tech manages care delivery, streamlines clinical operations and engages members, according to the company. The tech platform combined with a rigorous physician-led model allows the company to maintain the highest level of quality and consistency as it continues to scale and expand across the acuity spectrum, executives assert. Talkiatry touts its strong clinical outcomes with 87% of anxiety patients and 86% of depression patients reporting symptom improvement after just two visits, with 67% and 62%, respectively, reporting no longer having clinically significant symptoms. The company says its early dropout rates are 60% lower than industry benchmarks. These strong outcomes lead to cost savings for its partners, the company says, as its care model supports stronger continuity of care and dramatically reduces the likelihood of escalation into higher-cost settings. Cost of care reductions reach up to $700 per member per month, the company said. "Talkiatry has built a national full-stack provider group that sits on a proprietary AI-powered technology platform giving it greater control over the quality and care being delivered at scale,” said Michael Altman, head of strategy at Perceptive Advisors, in a statement. “The company’s consistent results across outcomes, engagement, and patient experience position it as defining the next era of psychiatric care in the United States. Our investment supports that long-term vision.”

This post about Talkiatry is a great example of how to use the natural movement of numbers to claim you did something ... when, in fact, what occurred was just a standard statistical outcome. The OP notes that patients who engaged with the company experienced improvement by the second visit in both depression and anxiety. The implication is that the treatment from the telemedicine platform is responsible for the change in severity of depression and anxiety. There is no way to determine if this is true, but there is a reason to suspect that it has nothing to do with the action taken by the telemedicine provider. There is a statistical concept called regression to the mean. This was discovered by Sir Francis Galton, the father of modern statistics. He originally termed it regression to mediocrity. Sir Francis wanted to prove that the children of a successful British royal families were more successful than their peers who came from less successful families. Much to his horror, he discovered that the opposite was true! The children of powerful houses were less likely to be successful than those of commoners. He went on to demonstrate that the children of tall parents are more likely to be shorter than their parents, and the children of short parents are more likely to be taller than their parents, on average. This is not because being short causes tall children, and it's not because being tall causes shortness in your offspring. It's because extreme values in any data set will become less extreme overtime, if random variation acts up upon them. If you flip a coin 10 times, and get 10 heads, which happens some of the time, you would be impressed. If you flip that same coin 10 more times, the likelihood is that the number would not be all heads again. It's more likely that you'd have a mixture of heads and tails that would approximate 50-50. Similarly, in any group of patients who are suffering from depression or anxiety, and you are seeking care, they are likely to have higher scores at baseline. They were suffering, and found care. Natural regression to the mean would mean that any measured value related to the severity of their symptoms would decrease over any subsequent period of time. That's what extreme values in a data set do. They regress to the mean. Thus, we should be careful when the claims are made about the outcome of a healthcare service leading to improvement, with no randomization, no comparison, and no control group. We can't know if the outcome was due to random chance, which is always acting on data scale, or due to an actual effect of the intervention in question. Thank you for attending my lecture on statistics here on LinkedIn. I have a link to my article on the topic in the comments. Separately, congratulations to talkiatry on their massive series D fundraise!

Talkiatry has built the nation’s largest full-stack psychiatry provider group, employing more than 800 full-time psychiatrists, delivering over 3 million patient visits, and partnering with leading health systems, payers, and employers nationwide. The company’s scale is matched by strong clinical and economic outcomes: 87% of anxiety patients and 86% of depression patients report symptom improvement after two visits, with dropout rates up to 60% lower than industry benchmarks. Congratulations to Robert Krayn, Georgia Gaveras, and the entire Talkiatry team! funding_news.ai_summary: Talkiatry, a virtual psychiatry company, announced it raised $210 million in funding led by Perceptive Advisors, with participation from Sofina and Andreessen Horowitz, to expand its insurance-covered psychiatric services. The company employs 800 psychiatrists and contracts with insurers to serve as a referral partner for health systems providing psychiatric care. CEO Robert Krayn said the funding provides a financial cushion to maintain payroll for employed clinicians during potential revenue interruptions, citing the 2024 Change Healthcare ransomware attack as an example of such disruptions.

funding_news.full_text:
Mario Aguilar covers technology in health care, including artificial intelligence, virtual reality, wearable devices, telehealth, and digital therapeutics. His stories explore how tech is changing the practice of health care and the business and policy challenges to realizing tech’s promise. He’s also the co-author of the free, twice weekly STAT Health Tech newsletter . You can reach Mario on Signal at mariojoze.13.

Talkiatry, a virtual psychiatry company, announced Thursday it raised $210 million as it looks to build on its insurance-covered services in a critical and difficult-to-access chunk of mental health care.

Since the Covid-19 pandemic, investors have fueled the rise of a number of large mental health tech companies. But Talkiatry’s focus on psychiatric conditions that require medication management stands out from other companies that focus on wellness, coaching, and therapy. Among Talkiatry’s strategic advantages is an employed workforce of 800 psychiatrists. The company contracts with insurers and serves as a referral partner for health systems whose patients need psychiatric care.

Advertisement

CEO and co-founder Robert Krayn said the new funding, led by Perceptive Advisors, in part provides a cushion to ensure the company can keep meeting its payroll for all those employed clinicians if there are revenue interruptions. He cited as an example the 2024 ransomware attack on clearinghouse Change Healthcare that delayed payments to many providers. Talkiatry declined to comment on a new company valuation or its progress toward profitability. Other backers include Sofina and Andreessen Horowitz.

funding_news.title: Talkiatry Raises Oversubscribed $210M Series D to Expand Nation's Largest Full-Stack Psychiatry Provider
funding_news.ai_summary: Talkiatry announced a $210 million Series D funding round led by Perceptive Advisors, with participation from Sofina and existing investors Andreessen Horowitz, blisce/, and Left Lane Capital, bringing total capital raised to over $400 million. The company, which directly employs more than 800 psychiatrists and is in-network with over 100 insurers covering 170 million lives, will use the proceeds to expand its proprietary AI-powered technology platform and extend care across the acuity spectrum. The funding reflects growing institutional demand from health systems, payers, and employers seeking psychiatric care partnerships.
funding_news.author: Access Intercomm
funding_news.full_text:
Talkiatry Raises Oversubscribed $210M Series D to Expand Nation's Largest Full-Stack Psychiatry Provider Share This Article • With more than 800 full-time psychiatrists, Talkiatry strengthens its position as the de facto in-network psychiatry partner for U.S. health systems, payers, and employers



• Talkiatry's clinical outcomes and cost savings lead the industry, with 87 percent of anxiety patients and 86 percent of depression patients reporting symptom improvement after just two visits, dropout rates 60 percent lower than industry benchmarks, and cost of care reductions reaching up to $700 per member per month



• Series D capital will fuel Talkiatry's continued investment in industry-leading technology and support continued expansion across the acuity spectrum NEW YORK, February 12, 2026-- Talkiatry today announced $210 million in Series D financing to support the next phase of growth for its nationally scaled, full-stack provider group. The oversubscribed round was led by Perceptive Advisors, with participation from Sofina and prior lead investors Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), blisce/, and Left Lane Capital, alongside a debt facility from Banc of California, bringing total raise to date to over $400 million.



As the nation's largest private employer of psychiatrists, Talkiatry directly employs more than 800 full-time psychiatrists. The company has delivered 3 million patient visits to date and is in-network with more than 100 insurers nationwide covering over 170 million lives. Since the launch of its Mindshare Partner Program in late 2023, Talkiatry has established partnerships with more than a third of the country's top 20 health systems and 50+ total systems to deliver high-quality, in-network psychiatric care across their populations.



Payers and health systems turn to Talkiatry because its care model produces superior outcomes across large patient populations. 87 percent of Talkiatry patients treated for anxiety and 86 percent treated for depression experience symptom reduction after two visits, with 67 percent and 62 percent respectively reporting no longer having clinically significant symptoms. Additionally, Talkiatry's early dropout rate is up to 60 percent lower than industry benchmarks, supporting stronger continuity of care and dramatically reducing the likelihood of escalation into higher-cost settings.



Talkiatry's clinical operations are built on a proprietary AI-powered technology platform that drives efficiency and outcomes, automating back office functions, engaging patients between visits, supporting health systems in getting patients into care, and enabling innovative payment models with payers. As Talkiatry's patient population continues to grow, its technology platform combined with a rigorous physician-led model allows it to maintain the highest level of quality and consistency as it continues to scale and expand across the acuity spectrum.



"Talkiatry is setting the standard for how psychiatry is delivered and measured, with a proven national operating model centered on employed psychiatrists built upon a proprietary technology platform," said Robert Krayn, CEO and cofounder of Talkiatry. "Health systems, payers, and employers continue to choose Talkiatry as their psychiatry partner of record to deliver consistent, superior outcomes across their patient populations. This funding supports expansion into more complex care and deeper partnerships as institutional demand grows."



In its most recent clinician satisfaction survey, 90 percent of psychiatrists said they would recommend Talkiatry as a place to practice. Talkiatry clinicians report 80 percent less burnout than the industry average, including less emotional exhaustion and a stronger sense of personal accomplishment. Talkiatry also reports therapeutic alliance ratings 22 percent higher than industry peers, with 92 percent of patients building a strong rapport with their clinicians.



"Talkiatry has built a national full-stack provider group that sits on a proprietary AI-powered technology platform giving it greater control over the quality and care being delivered at scale," said Michael Altman, Head of Strategy, Perceptive Advisors. "The company's consistent results across outcomes, engagement, and patient experience position it as defining the next era of psychiatric care in the United States. Our investment supports that long-term vision."



Treating conditions including anxiety, bipolar disorder, depression, postpartum depression, OCD, and PTSD, Talkiatry reports a 76 NPS rating, reflecting consistent patient satisfaction across its practice. Talkiatry was ranked among the fastest-growing companies in North America on the Deloitte Technology Fast 500™ in 2025, and is repeatedly recognized as one of the best companies to work for in the country by Fortune and Great Place to Work.



About Talkiatry



Talkiatry is a full-stack provider group delivering in-network psychiatric care across the United States. The company directly employs more than 800 full-time psychiatrists, making it the largest private employer of psychiatrists in the country, and has delivered 3 million patient visits to date. Talkiatry serves as the preferred psychiatry partner for health systems, payers, and employers seeking dependable access and superior outcomes. The company's care model is underpinned by proprietary AI-powered technology to manage care delivery, streamline clinical operations, and engage members. Talkiatry was co-founded by Robert Krayn and Georgia Gaveras, DO.



Learn more at talkiatry.com and follow us on LinkedIn, Facebook, and Instagram. Contact:

product_offering.product_overview: Talkiatry operates as a single integrated telepsychiatry platform with several interconnected products and modules serving patients, providers, and health systems. Talkiatry Connect is an add-on EMR referral module integrated into over 30 cloud-based EMRs, enabling health systems and referring clinicians to route patients into Talkiatry's provider network. Launched Talkiatry Connect, a cloud-based psychiatric referral product embedded within 30+ cloud-based EMRs that enables referring providers to place referrals in-workflow and receive clinical updates back.

Partnered with New York Cancer & Blood Specialists (NYCBS) to deliver integrated psychiatric care to oncology and hematology patients across more than 30 NYCBS locations in New York.
Raised $130 million in a round led by Andreessen Horowitz with Perceptive Advisors participating, cited among the major H1 2024 digital mental health financings.

Ranked 56th on the 2025 Deloitte Technology Fast 500, validating three-year revenue growth that reflects workforce expansion from a regional New York operation to 800+ psychiatrists and 300+ therapists across 45 states.

expansion_highlight.description: April 2026 partnership with New York Cancer & Blood Specialists (NYCBS) signals a deliberate move into integrated oncology/hematology psychiatry, targeting the up to 25% of cancer patients who experience clinical depression and opening a specialty-care vertical beyond Talkiatry's core D2C anxiety/depression/ADHD base.

April 2026 AMGA partnership and the Mindshare Partner Program across 50+ health systems, combined with Talkiatry Connect's embedding in 30+ EMRs, mark a strategic shift from pure D2C acquisition to enterprise/B2B distribution through payer, employer, and provider channels.

Launch of Talkiatry Connect in April 2026 expands the product surface from a patient-facing telepsychiatry service into a SaaS-style B2B referral and care-coordination module integrated into third-party EMRs, creating a new revenue and partnership surface.

The February 2026 $210M Series D (largest round to date, led by Perceptive Advisors with Banc of California debt) brings cumulative funding above $400M and is explicitly earmarked to maintain clinician payroll continuity and fund expansion; the capital cushion signals investor confidence in continued scaling.

Talkiatry's employed psychiatrists now operate across 45 U.S. states (versus initial Northeast/Mid-Atlantic focus from the 2021-2022 Series A use of funds), with state-specific professional entities (MCCD FL/CA/KS/NJ Psychiatry Services) indicating methodical state-by-state licensing build-out.

The integration footprint across 30+ cloud-based EMRs (via Talkiatry Connect) and a 50+ health-system partner network, supported by an affiliated medical group structure (MCCD Psychiatry Services, PLLC and state entities), indicates deliberate ecosystem lock-in around referral and care-coordination workflows.

company_assessment.market_position: Talkiatry is a New York City-based, venture-backed telepsychiatry provider founded in 2019 that operates as the nation's largest full-stack psychiatry practice. It employs more than 800 full-time psychiatrists and 300 therapists, delivers care in 45 U.S. states, has completed more than 3 million patient visits, and is in-network with more than 100 commercial insurers covering roughly 170 million lives. The company has raised more than $400 million in cumulative funding across multiple rounds, most recently a $210 million Series D in February 2026 led by Perceptive Advisors. It was ranked 56th on the 2025 Deloitte Technology Fast 500 and named to CB Insights' Digital Health 50 in 2024.

strengths.details: Talkiatry employs 800+ full-time psychiatrists across 45 states, self-described as the nation's largest full-stack telepsychiatry group. In a market characterized by 6+ week waits and a national psychiatrist shortage, this employed-supply scale is a defensible moat that marketplaces cannot replicate quickly, enabling continued share-take from in-person psychiatry practices and gig platforms.
strengths.headline: Largest employed psychiatrist network captures supply scarcity

strengths.details: Talkiatry Connect is embedded in 30+ cloud-based EMRs and pairs with 50+ health system Mindshare partnerships. Each new EMR integration and enterprise contract compounds the referral moat — referring providers place referrals in-workflow, generating warm inbound demand that DTC-only competitors must pay full CAC to match.
strengths.headline: EMR-embedded referral channel compounds distribution

strengths.details: Talkiatry's measurement-based care platform tracks standardized PHQ-8/PHQ-9 and GAD-7 outcomes, demonstrating 86% symptom improvement after 2 visits and 65% remission in ~5 visits. As payers shift toward value-based mental health contracting, Talkiatry's longitudinal outcomes dataset and AI-powered analytics position it to negotiate premium, capitated, or risk-sharing arrangements unavailable to less instrumented competitors.
strengths.headline: Outcomes data unlocks value-based payer contracts

strengths.details: Specialty-care partnerships like NYCBS oncology (treating the ~25% of cancer patients with clinical depression) and AMGA point to expansion beyond DTC psychiatry into embedded specialty behavioral health — a higher-acuity, harder-to-replicate segment that commands better unit economics than generalist virtual care.
strengths.headline: Specialty and oncology integrations expand TAM

strengths.details: 3M+ visits delivered, 13,000+ five-star reviews, and in-network status with 100+ insurers covering ~170M lives provide the volume base and contracted-revenue leverage to layer in adjacent services (medication-assisted treatment, pediatric psychiatry, ADHD management) where Talkiatry already has clinical capability and demand signals.
strengths.headline: Scale supports adjacent service line expansion

weakness.details: Talkiatry's dominant revenue stream is per-visit fees billed to commercial insurers (in-network with 100+ carriers covering ~170M lives) and the company explicitly does not accept Medicaid and offers no self-pay option. Any material payer reimbursement cut, network exit, or shift in employer benefit design toward competitors would compress unit economics and volume simultaneously, with limited offset given the commercial-only positioning.
weakness.headline: Payer concentration threatens unit economics

weakness.details: Talkiatry's CEO Robert Krayn explicitly framed the Series D as a "financial cushion to maintain payroll for employed clinicians during potential revenue interruptions," citing the 2024 Change Healthcare ransomware attack as an example. With 800+ employed psychiatrists as fixed cost, revenue disruptions (cyber, payer, regulatory) flow directly to margin.
weakness.headline: Employed-clinician model magnifies revenue shocks

weakness.details: The Talkiatry website publicly notes that "one of our vendors was impacted by a security incident, which affected some of our patients'…protected health information". HIPAA-regulated breaches on top of the healow/eClinicalWorks infrastructure dependency create compounding exposure as Talkiatry scales into more enterprise contracts.
weakness.headline: Third-party vendor breach exposes patient data

weakness.details: Talkiatry relies on eClinicalWorks/healow (mycw135.ecwcloud.com) for the patient portal and visit infrastructure. A migration, outage, or pricing change at eClinicalWorks would directly affect Talkiatry's core delivery surface, and competitors building on more modern stacks could outpace on user experience.
weakness.headline: Core EMR/portal rides on third-party infrastructure

weakness.details: Cerebral, Lyra, Headspace Care, Spring Health, Grow Therapy, Rula, and others are pursuing the same in-network telepsychiatry opportunity and competing for the limited pool of prescribing psychiatrists. Wage inflation and clinician attrition could erode the talent moat that anchors Talkiatry's differentiation.
weakness.headline: Competitive crowding pressures talent and pricing

competitive_moat.details: Talkiatry employs more than 800 full-time, vetted psychiatrists with an average of 10 years of clinical experience across 26 subspecialties and 30+ languages. Unlike gig or marketplace competitors, this is an employed (not contractor) clinical workforce that is difficult and expensive to replicate at scale.

Talkiatry Connect is embedded in 30+ cloud-based EMRs and the Mindshare Partner Program covers 50+ health systems, creating warm inbound referral channels competitors lack. In-network status with 100+ insurers covering ~170M lives gives unparalleled patient-acquisition leverage via insurance routing.

Talkiatry is described as the nation's largest full-stack psychiatry provider group with 3M+ patient visits delivered, generating scale economies in clinician recruitment, payer contracting, and technology amortization. Back-to-back Deloitte Technology Fast 500 rankings (2024 and 2025) validate the rate-of-scale advantage.

Measurement-based care using PHQ-8/PHQ-9 and GAD-7 across millions of visits has produced proprietary outcome datasets used for predictive analytics (e.g., early-dropout thresholds, matching algorithms) and published validation (JMIR Form Res 2023 study of 1,826 patients showing 65% remission).

State-by-state licensing is delivered through affiliated medical groups (MCCD Psychiatry Services, PLLC plus FL/CA/KS/NJ professional entities), and in-network contracts with 100+ commercial payers represent a multi-year regulatory and contractual barrier. Talkiatry does not accept Medicaid, narrowing its addressable market but reducing regulatory exposure.

EMR-embedded Talkiatry Connect referrals create workflow dependency for referring providers, and continuity of care with the same psychiatrist across visits builds patient retention. However, switching costs are lower on the patient side given the commoditized nature of telepsychiatry supply.

key_risks.details: Talkiatry does not accept Medicaid and offers no self-pay option, leaving its addressable market limited to commercially insured patients. This shrinks the population it can serve and leaves it exposed to employers dropping mental health benefits or shifting carriers.
key_risks.headline: Commercial-only model excludes major patient segments

key_risks.details: Patient portal, scheduling, and telehealth visits run on eClinicalWorks/healow (mycw135.ecwcloud.com), while a third-party vendor security incident has already affected some patients' PHI. Outages, vendor pricing changes, or further breaches flow directly to Talkiatry's core delivery surface.
key_risks.headline: Heavy reliance on third-party platform infrastructure
Payer mix concentration risk

key_highlights.details: Talkiatry self-describes as the nation's largest full-stack psychiatry provider group with 800+ employed psychiatrists and 300+ therapists operating in 45 states. This employed-clinician scale is hard for marketplace competitors to replicate quickly.
key_highlights.headline: Largest employed telepsychiatry group in the U.S.

key_highlights.details: Measurement-based care data shows 86% of patients feel better after 2 visits, 65% achieve remission in an average of 5 visits, and 87% anxiety / 86% depression symptom reduction after 2 visits.
key_highlights.headline: Strong unit-level clinical outcomes

key_highlights.details: In-network with 100+ commercial insurers covering ~170M lives, with an in-network guarantee on first visits. Average patient out-of-pocket is ~$30/visit, which Talkiatry's own research links to lower early-dropout rates.
key_highlights.headline: Broad payer coverage creates revenue durability

key_highlights.details: Talkiatry Connect is integrated into 30+ cloud-based EMRs and pairs with 50+ health system Mindshare partnerships. This generates warm, in-workflow referrals that pure-DTC competitors must pay full CAC to match.
key_highlights.headline: EMR-embedded referral channel is a defensible moat

key_highlights.details: Over 3 million patient visits completed and 13,000+ five-star reviews, with the company ranked 56th on the 2025 Deloitte Technology Fast 500 and included on CB Insights' 2024 Digital Health 50.
key_highlights.headline: Massive patient traction and brand proof

key_highlights.details: Total funding raised exceeds $400M, most recently an oversubscribed $210M Series D led by Perceptive Advisors with a16z, Sofina, blisce/, and Left Lane Capital plus debt from Banc of California. CEO Robert Krayn explicitly described the round as cushion for clinician payroll continuity.
key_highlights.headline: Strong capital position supports growth runway

customer_concentration.details: Talkiatry's patient base is a long-tail of millions of individual visits across 45 states (3M+ cumulative visits), making D2C patient concentration inherently low. However, revenue is concentrated in commercial insurance payers (100+ insurers covering ~170M lives), and the company does not accept Medicaid, creating payer-mix concentration. On the enterprise side, only two named partners are disclosed (AMGA and NYCBS), and the AMGA partnership was just announced in April 2026, so enterprise revenue concentration is currently low but could rise as the B2B motion scales. The Copay estimator, $30 average out-of-pocket, and absence of self-pay suggest pricing is payer-controlled, which moderates Talkiatry's ability to offset churn in any single payer relationship.

launches.title: Alexa+ just quietly became way more useful, if your gadgets are on this list
launches.ai_summary: Amazon is launching a new AI-powered smart home developer toolkit for Alexa+ that enables device makers to integrate their full feature sets directly into the voice assistant, eliminating the need for users to navigate separate app menus. The toolkit currently supports devices from Bosch, Whirlpool, iRobot, Govee, Yale Home, and Eufy, with Amazon reporting that customers who upgraded to Alexa+ already increased smart home engagement by nearly 50% in their first month. Amazon is also adopting the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to enable third-party integrations with brands including Priceline, Lyft, Headspace, Virgin Atlantic, Atom Tickets, and Fandango, positioning Alexa+ as an orchestration layer for voice-assisted tasks.
launches.author: Shikhar Mehrotra

industries.name: Agents & Autonomous Workflows (Tool Use, Planning, Multi-Agent)

launches.full_text:
You might have asked Alexa to do plenty of dumb things over the years, but “figure out which of my washer’s 30 cycles actually means cold wash” might not have been one of them. Turns out, Amazon just built the toolkit that makes exactly that possible, and it’s rolling out across a genuinely huge list of brands today. So what’s actually changing for your smart home gadgets? Amazon’s launching a new AI-powered smart home developer toolkit that lets device makers plug their full feature set into Alexa+ instead of forcing you to dig through app menus yourself. Recommended Videos 1/1 Continue watching after the ad Visit Advertiser website GO TO PAGE Amazon says customers who upgrade to Alexa+ already boost their smart home engagement by nearly 50% in the first month. This toolkit is clearly aimed at pushing that number higher. The washer example above is real. Tell Alexa your kid’s soccer jersey needs a deep clean but only allows cold water, and it’ll pick the exact cycle for you. For now, devices from Bosch, Whirlpool, iRobot, Govee, Yale Home, and Eufy are supported. What about booking, spending, and third-party apps? Amazon’s also adopting the Model Context Protocol (MCP), letting brands bring their own MCP server so Alexa+ can inspect it and hand developers a ready-to-build integration path.
